qs.q: Which of the following is characterized by effacement of foot processes with weakening of the slit pore membrane?
qs.a:
a. Minimal change disease ✓

b. Membranous nephropathy

c. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)

d. IgA nephropathy

Answer: a

Minimal change disease = podocyte injury with diffuse foot-process effacement (EM only) and loss of the slit-diaphragm charge barrier → selective albuminuria.

Key point: Foot-process effacement only = minimal change.

qs.q: By light microscopy, uniform thickening of the basement membrane along the peripheral capillary loops is characteristic of:
qs.a:
a. Membranous nephropathy ✓

b. Minimal change disease

c. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)

d. IgA nephropathy

Answer: a

Membranous nephropathy shows diffuse uniform GBM thickening on light microscopy (subepithelial deposits, 'spike and dome' on silver stain).

Key point: Thick GBM + spikes = membranous.

qs.q: A patient with kidney impairment and proteinuria requires pharmacological control of proteinuria. Which drug class is most appropriate?
qs.a:
a. ARBs ✓

b. Loop diuretics

c. Calcium channel blockers

d. Beta-blockers

Answer: a

ACE inhibitors/ARBs reduce intraglomerular pressure (efferent dilatation) and lower proteinuria — renoprotective first-line.

Key point: Reduce proteinuria = ACEi/ARB.

qs.q: A patient with a 15-year history of rheumatoid arthritis, treated with methotrexate and sulfasalazine for 3 years, presents with severe weakness, loss of appetite, breathlessness, and swelling of the legs, face, and abdomen. On examination: puffy face, marked anemia, pitting lower limb edema, blood pressure 160/110 mmHg, pulse 76 beats/min. Laboratory findings: serum creatinine 2 mg/dL, BUN 30 mg/dL, albumin 2.8 g/dL, total cholesterol 375 mg/dL, urine protein ++++ (4+). What is the diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Nephritic syndrome

b. Nephrotic syndrome ✓

c. Renal tubular acidosis

d. Goodpasture syndrome

Answer: b

Heavy proteinuria (4+), hypoalbuminaemia, edema/anasarca and marked hypercholesterolaemia = nephrotic syndrome (in long-standing RA think secondary AA amyloidosis or drug-induced membranous).

Key point: Proteinuria + low albumin + edema + high lipids = nephrotic.

qs.q: Which of the following causes kidney enlargement despite chronic renal failure?
qs.a:
a. Systemic sclerosis

b. Analgesic nephropathy

c. Amyloidosis ✓

d. Hypertensive nephrosclerosis

Answer: c

Infiltrative diseases (amyloidosis, also diabetes, HIV nephropathy, PKD, myeloma) keep kidneys large despite CKD.

Key point: Big kidneys + CKD: amyloid, DM, PKD, HIV.

qs.q: Specific biopsy findings for diabetic nephropathy include:
qs.a:
a. Eosinophilic nodules called nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules) ✓

b. Diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane

c. Focal thickening and sclerosis of the basement membrane

d. Crescent formation in Bowman's capsule

Answer: a

Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules (nodular intercapillary glomerulosclerosis) are specific for diabetic nephropathy.

Key point: Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules = diabetic nephropathy.

qs.q: A 60-year-old male presents with a two-week history of fatigue, swelling in his legs, and foamy urine. His blood pressure is elevated at 160/100 mmHg. Urinalysis reveals significant proteinuria and hematuria. Which of the following glomerulonephritis is most likely to be the cause of his symptoms?
qs.a:
a. Minimal change disease

b. Membranous glomerulonephritis ✓

c. IgA nephropathy

d. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

Answer: b

Older adult with nephrotic-range proteinuria and edema: membranous nephropathy is the commonest primary cause (microscopic hematuria can occur). Screen for malignancy in > 60s.

Key point: Adult nephrotic (esp. > 60) = membranous — screen for cancer.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT a diagnostic criterion of nephrotic syndrome?
qs.a:
a. Massive proteinuria

b. Hyperlipidemia

c. Anasarca

d. Hypertension ✓

Answer: d

The core features are heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hyperlipidaemia. Hypertension is not required. (Source: Kumar Ch.6 Q9)

Key point: The core features are heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hyperlipidaemia.

qs.q: What is the most common histological type of nephrotic syndrome in children?
qs.a:
a. Minimal change disease ✓

b. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis

c. Mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis

d. Membranous nephropathy

Answer: a

Minimal change disease causes ~80–90% of nephrotic syndrome in children.

Key point: Child + nephrotic = minimal change.

qs.q: What is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults overall?
qs.a:
a. Membranous nephropathy

b. Minimal change disease

c. Diabetes mellitus ✓

d. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis

Answer: c

Overall (including secondary causes), diabetes mellitus is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults.

Key point: Adult nephrotic overall = diabetes; primary = membranous/FSGS.

qs.q: What is the most common organism causing urinary tract infections?
qs.a:
a. Staphylococcus

b. Escherichia coli ✓

c. Streptococcus

d. Klebsiella

Answer: b

E. coli (uropathogenic) causes about 75–90% of UTIs.

Key point: UTI = E. coli.

qs.q: A 19-year-old man presents with malaise, nausea, and oliguria. Examination reveals elevated JVP and a pericardial rub. Urinalysis shows which finding most strongly suggests acute glomerulonephritis?
qs.a:
a. Red blood cell casts ✓

b. White blood cell casts

c. Granular casts

d. Hyaline casts

Answer: a

RBC casts indicate glomerular inflammation (acute glomerulonephritis); the uraemic pericardial rub and fluid overload support acute renal failure.

Key point: RBC casts = glomerulonephritis.

qs.q: Which of the following is an indication for treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria?
qs.a:
a. All elderly patients

b. All diabetic patients

c. Pregnant women ✓

d. All healthy adults

Answer: c

Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnant women (and before urological procedures).

Key point: Asymptomatic bacteriuria → treat only in pregnancy.

qs.q: Which investigation may be used in the evaluation of suspected pyelonephritis, particularly when complications or obstruction are suspected?
qs.a:
a. Ultrasound of the kidneys and urinary tract ✓

b. Thyroid scan

c. MRI pituitary

d. Echocardiography

Answer: a

Renal ultrasound is the first imaging to look for obstruction, abscess or stones in pyelonephritis (CT if complex).

Key point: Complicated pyelonephritis → US (then CT).

qs.q: Which condition is associated with large kidney size despite advanced kidney damage?
qs.a:
a. Chronic pyelonephritis

b. Hypertensive nephrosclerosis

c. Reflux nephropathy

d. Amyloidosis ✓

Answer: d

Amyloidosis keeps kidneys large despite advanced damage.

Key point: Large kidneys + CKD = amyloidosis.

qs.q: Minimal change disease is characterized by:
qs.a:
a. Subepithelial spike and dome pattern

b. Crescents in more than 50% of glomeruli

c. Tram-track appearance of the basement membrane

d. Nephrotic syndrome with normal light microscopy and effacement of foot processes on electron microscopy ✓

Answer: d

Minimal change disease: nephrotic syndrome with normal light microscopy and foot-process effacement on EM (no immune deposits).

Key point: Normal LM + effaced foot processes = MCD.

qs.q: A patient with stage V (membranous) lupus nephritis typically presents with:
qs.a:
a. Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis

b. Nephrotic syndrome ✓

c. Isolated hematuria

d. Acute nephritic syndrome

Answer: b

Class V (membranous) lupus nephritis presents with nephrotic syndrome (heavy proteinuria, edema).

Key point: Lupus class V = nephrotic.

qs.q: A 16-year-old otherwise healthy female on no medications presents complaining of swelling and is found to have a BP of 150/93 mmHg, periorbital edema, 3+ peripheral edema, and the following lab values: creatinine 0.7 mg/dL, albumin 2.2 g/L, urinalysis 3+ protein, 0 RBC/HPF, 0 WBC/HPF, 1+ oval fat bodies. What should be the first diagnostic test ordered?
qs.a:
a. Renal ultrasound

b. Measurement of urine albumin ✓

c. Serum protein electrophoresis

d. Test for anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA)

Answer: b

Per the key, first quantify the proteinuria (urine albumin/protein measurement, e.g. ACR/PCR or 24-h) to confirm nephrotic range before further work-up.

Key point: Suspected nephrotic → quantify proteinuria first.

qs.q: A 16-year-old otherwise healthy female on no medications presents complaining of swelling and is found to have a BP of 150/93 mmHg, periorbital edema, 3+ peripheral edema, and the following lab values: creatinine 0.7 mg/dL, albumin 2.2 g/L, urinalysis 3+ protein, 0 RBC/HPF, 0 WBC/HPF, 1+ oval fat bodies. Which of the following should be AVOIDED?
qs.a:
a. An ACE inhibitor

b. Diuretic therapy

c. High fat in diet ✓

d. Low sodium diet

Answer: c

Nephrotic patients already have hyperlipidaemia; a high-fat diet should be avoided.

Key point: Nephrotic diet: low salt, avoid high fat; ACEi + diuretics.

qs.q: A 65-year-old female with no significant past medical history presents with pedal and periorbital edema progressive over a couple of months. The exam shows normal blood pressure. Urinalysis reveals 4+ proteinuria but no other findings. Renal function is normal, but there is decreased albumin. Select the most likely diagnosis.
qs.a:
a. Lupus nephritis

b. Membranous glomerulopathy ✓

c. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis

d. Diabetic nephropathy

Answer: b

Older patient with isolated heavy proteinuria (no hematuria, normal BP and renal function) = membranous glomerulopathy (commonest primary cause in older adults).

Key point: Elderly + bland nephrotic = membranous.

qs.q: Hypercoagulability is most commonly associated with which of the following nephrotic diseases?
qs.a:
a. Minimal change disease

b. Membranous nephropathy ✓

c. IgA nephropathy

d. Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

Answer: b

Membranous nephropathy has the highest risk of hypercoagulability (renal vein thrombosis, DVT/PE) among the nephrotic lesions, due to urinary loss of antithrombin III and high fibrinogen, especially when albumin is very low.

Key point: Renal vein thrombosis → think membranous nephropathy.

qs.q: A 7-year-old child presents with generalized edema, periorbital puffiness, heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and hyperlipidemia. What is the most likely underlying histopathological diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)

b. Membranous nephropathy

c. Minimal change disease (MCD) ✓

d. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis

Answer: c

A child with full nephrotic syndrome (oedema, heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, hyperlipidaemia) most likely has minimal change disease — the commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, steroid-responsive. FSGS and membranous are adult causes; MPGN is nephritic/nephrotic with low complement.

Key point: Nephrotic child = minimal change disease until proven otherwise.

qs.q: What is the treatment of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)?
qs.a:
a. ACE inhibitors ✓

b. Antibiotics only

c. Immediate dialysis

d. Heparin alone

Answer: a (and corticosteroids in primary FSGS)

FSGS is treated with ACE inhibitors/ARBs to reduce proteinuria and slow progression; primary FSGS also needs corticosteroids. Antibiotics, dialysis or heparin alone are not the treatment.

Key point: FSGS: ACEi/ARB (+ steroids in primary FSGS).

qs.q: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection most commonly results in which type of glomerulonephritis?
qs.a:
a. Membranous nephropathy ✓

b. IgA nephropathy

c. Focal segmental glomeruloscelerosis

d. Minimal change disease

Answer: a

The key lists membranous nephropathy. (Note: HCV is classically linked to MPGN with cryoglobulinaemia; membranous is the classic HBV association — be ready for both.)

Key point: HBV → membranous; HCV → MPGN/cryoglobulinaemia (key here: membranous).

qs.q: A man with multiple myeloma and elevated serum creatinine. What is the most likely renal diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Amyloidosis (light chain amyloidosis) ✓

b. Minimal change disease

c. IgA nephropathy

d. Membranous nephropathy

Answer: a

Myeloma light chains cause AL amyloidosis (nephrotic), cast nephropathy (renal failure) and light-chain deposition disease; the keyed answer is light-chain amyloidosis.

Key point: Myeloma + kidneys: cast nephropathy, AL amyloid.

qs.q: What is the gold standard in the diagnosis of renal disease?
qs.a:
a. Renal biopsy ✓

b. Ultrasound

c. CT scan

d. MRI

Answer: a

Renal biopsy (LM, IF, EM) is the gold standard for diagnosing parenchymal/glomerular disease.

Key point: Gold standard = renal biopsy.

qs.q: What is the most common cause of chronic renal failure?
qs.a:
a. Diabetes mellitus ✓

b. Hypertension

c. Glomerulonephritis

d. Polycystic kidney disease

Answer: a

Diabetic nephropathy is the leading cause of CKD/ESKD worldwide, then hypertension.

Key point: CKD #1 = diabetes, #2 = hypertension.

qs.q: A 28-year-old woman with Hodgkin lymphoma develops an abrupt onset of periorbital edema and proteinuria on urinalysis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Minimal change disease ✓

b. Membranous nephropathy

c. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis

d. IgA nephropathy

Answer: a

Hodgkin lymphoma is classically associated with minimal change disease (T-cell cytokines).

Key point: Hodgkin's → minimal change.

qs.q: How is proteinuria diagnosed?
qs.a:
a. Protein in urine more than 150 mg per 24 hours ✓

b. Protein in urine more than 4 mg per 24 hours

c. Protein in urine more than 3.5 g per 24 hours

d. Protein in urine more than 30 mg per 24 hours

Answer: a (proteinuria is defined as >150 mg/24 hours; nephrotic-range

Proteinuria = > 150 mg/24 h.

Key point: Proteinuria > 150 mg/day.

qs.q: Which of the following factors contributing to hypercoagulability is associated with nephrotic syndrome?
qs.a:
a. Decreased platelet activation

b. Elevated levels of anticoagulants

c. Increased urinary excretion of antithrombin, protein C, and protein S ✓

d. Reduced clot formation

Answer: c

Urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins (antithrombin III, protein C and S) plus ↑ hepatic fibrinogen → hypercoagulability.

Key point: Nephrotic thrombosis = urinary loss of antithrombin III.

qs.q: What type of nephropathy is associated with hepatitis B?
qs.a:
a. Membranous nephropathy ✓

b. IgA nephropathy

c. Minimal change disease

d. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis

Answer: a

Hepatitis B is classically associated with membranous nephropathy (especially children) and also PAN.

Key point: HBV → membranous (and PAN).

qs.q: A 64-year-old man presents with weight gain, shortness of breath, easy bruising, and leg swelling. On examination, BP is 140/80 mmHg, pulse 100/min, JVP 4 cm, heart sounds normal, lungs clear. There is 3+ pedal and some periorbital edema. Investigations include normal CXR, ECG with low voltages, anemia, high urea and creatinine, and 4 g/day of protein in the urine. A renal biopsy shows nodular deposits that have apple-green birefringence under polarized light when stained with Congo red. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Amyloidosis ✓

b. Multiple myeloma

c. Diabetic nephropathy

d. Minimal change disease

Answer: a

Nephrotic syndrome with easy bruising, low-voltage ECG (cardiac infiltration) and Congo red apple-green birefringence = amyloidosis.

Key point: Congo red apple-green = amyloid.

qs.q: A 42-year-old man notices leg and facial swelling but no other symptoms. His examination is pertinent for 3+ pedal edema including periorbital edema. A 24-hour urine collection reveals 5 g of proteinuria. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Sickle cell disease

b. Medullary sponge kidney

c. Radiation nephritis

d. Membranous nephropathy ✓

Answer: d

Middle-aged adult with nephrotic-range proteinuria (5 g/day) and edema = membranous nephropathy among the options.

Key point: Adult nephrotic = membranous.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT a criterion for diagnosis of nephrotic syndrome?
qs.a:
a. Hypertension ✓

b. Massive proteinuria

c. Hyperlipidemia

d. Anasarca

Answer: a

Nephrotic syndrome = proteinuria > 3.5 g/day + hypoalbuminaemia + edema ± hyperlipidaemia. Hypertension is a NEPHRITIC feature.

Key point: Nephrotic ≠ hypertension; nephritic = hypertension.

qs.q: A 24-year-old woman has nephrotic syndrome due to minimal change disease. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
qs.a:
a. Protein restriction

b. No treatment

c. ACE inhibitor

d. Diuretic

e. Prednisolone ✓

Answer: e

Minimal change disease is highly steroid-responsive; prednisolone (1 mg/kg) is first-line.

Key point: MCD = prednisolone.

qs.q: A 55-year-old man has 3.6 g of protein in a 24-hour urine collection. Which disorder would account for this?
qs.a:
a. Persistent UTI

b. Acute tubular necrosis (ATN)

c. Transitional cell carcinoma

d. Chronic interstitial nephritis

e. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) ✓

Answer: e

3.6 g/day = nephrotic-range (glomerular) proteinuria — FSGS fits; tubular/urothelial disorders give < 1–2 g/day.

Key point: > 3.5 g/day = glomerular disease.

qs.q: A 26-year-old man presents with nephrotic syndrome. Which condition is most likely to be the underlying cause?
qs.a:
a. Acute tubular necrosis (ATN)

b. Membranous nephropathy ✓

c. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN)

d. Anti-GBM disease

e. Small-vessel vasculitis

Answer: b

Among the options, only membranous nephropathy is a nephrotic disorder; the rest are nephritic or tubular.

Key point: Nephrotic option = membranous.

qs.q: Which glomerular disease is most likely to respond to corticosteroids?
qs.a:
a. Minimal change nephropathy ✓

b. IgA nephropathy

c. Primary FSGS

d. Diabetic nephropathy

Answer: a

Minimal change disease shows > 90% steroid response in children (slightly less in adults).

Key point: Most steroid-responsive = minimal change.

qs.q: What is the most likely outcome following minimal change nephropathy in a 10-year-old boy?
qs.a:
a. CKD requiring RRT within 30 years

b. Full recovery with no further episodes

c. Full recovery but with later relapses ✓

d. CKD without RRT

e. CKD requiring RRT within 10 years

Answer: c

Children with MCD usually achieve full remission but many relapse (frequent relapsers/steroid dependent); progression to CKD is rare.

Key point: MCD in children: remission + relapses, rarely CKD.

qs.q: In renal failure, what causes renal osteodystrophy?
qs.a:
a. Hypocalcemia

b. Impaired renal production of 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol ✓

c. Hypophosphatemia

d. Excess erythropoietin

Answer: b

Damaged kidneys fail to 1α-hydroxylate vitamin D → low calcitriol → low calcium absorption, phosphate retention and secondary hyperparathyroidism → renal osteodystrophy.

Key point: Renal osteodystrophy starts with ↓ 1,25-(OH)₂D.

qs.q: Ultrasound helps differentiate chronic from acute kidney disease. Which finding favors CKD?
qs.a:
a. Normal-sized kidneys

b. Enlarged, edematous kidneys

c. Isolated hydronephrosis

d. Small, shrunken kidneys with a thin cortex ✓

Answer: d

Small (< 9 cm), echogenic kidneys with a thin cortex indicate chronic kidney disease.

Key point: Small kidneys on US = CKD (exceptions: DM, amyloid, PKD, HIV).

qs.q: A patient with non-specific symptoms and serum creatinine 9 mg/dL. What is the next step?
qs.a:
a. Repeat creatinine after one month

b. Start oral corticosteroids

c. Initiate dialysis ✓

d. Do nothing and observe

Answer: c

Creatinine 9 mg/dL with uraemic symptoms indicates advanced/end-stage kidney failure — dialysis is indicated (after checking hyperkalaemia, acidosis, fluid overload).

Key point: Symptomatic very high creatinine = start dialysis.

qs.q: Which of the following structures is located in the renal cortex?
qs.a:
a. Proximal convoluted tubule ✓

b. Renal pyramid

c. Loop of Henle

d. Collecting duct

Answer: a

The cortex contains glomeruli, proximal and distal convoluted tubules.

Key point: Cortex = glomeruli + PCT + DCT; medulla = loops + collecting ducts.

qs.q: Which of the following structures is primarily located in the renal medulla?
qs.a:
a. Proximal convoluted tubule

b. Distal convoluted tubule

c. Loop of Henle ✓

d. Renal corpuscle (glomerulus)

Answer: c

The loop of Henle lies mainly in the medulla (creating the concentration gradient).

Key point: Loop of Henle = medulla.

qs.q: Which hormone is secreted from the kidney to stimulate red blood cell production?
qs.a:
a. Erythropoietin ✓

b. Renin

c. Calcitriol

d. Aldosterone

Answer: a

Erythropoietin from peritubular interstitial cells stimulates red cell production; deficiency causes the anaemia of CKD.

Key point: Kidney hormones: EPO, renin, calcitriol.

qs.q: Which of the following is freely filtered in the normal glomerulus?
qs.a:
a. Albumin

b. Glucose ✓

c. Red blood cells

d. Platelets

e. Fibrinogen

Answer: b

Glucose (small, uncharged) is freely filtered, then almost completely reabsorbed in the PCT (SGLT2).

Key point: Freely filtered: glucose, electrolytes, urea — not albumin or cells.

qs.q: Which investigation provides the most information about the relative contribution of each kidney to overall renal function?
qs.a:
a. Renal biopsy

b. Renal ultrasound

c. MRI

d. Isotope renogram ✓

e. Renal arteriogram

Answer: d

Isotope renography (DMSA/MAG3) gives split (differential) function of each kidney.

Key point: Split renal function = isotope renogram.

qs.q: A patient presents with hematuria and RBC casts on urine microscopy. What is the most likely source of bleeding?
qs.a:
a. Glomerular ✓

b. Extraglomerular

c. Lower urinary tract

d. Renal pelvis

Answer: a

RBC casts form in the tubules from glomerular bleeding — they localise hematuria to the glomerulus.

Key point: RBC casts = glomerular.

qs.q: A 75-year-old male presents with hematuria and normal laboratory findings. Which of the following is the most important diagnosis to EXCLUDE?
qs.a:
a. Bladder cancer ✓

b. IgA nephropathy

c. Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (APSGN)

d. Urinary tract infection (UTI)

Answer: a

Painless hematuria in an elderly man is bladder (urothelial) cancer until proven otherwise → cystoscopy + CT urogram.

Key point: Old + painless hematuria = exclude bladder cancer.

qs.q: A patient develops hematuria after strenuous exercise. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Myoglobinuria (exercise-induced rhabdomyolysis) ✓

b. IgA nephropathy

c. Acute glomerulonephritis

d. Renal stone disease

Answer: a

Red/brown urine after strenuous exercise = myoglobinuria from rhabdomyolysis (dipstick positive for blood without RBCs).

Key point: Dark urine after exercise = myoglobin.

qs.q: A hallmark of nephritic syndrome is:
qs.a:
a. Hypoalbuminemia

b. Hyperlipidemia

c. Proteinuria

d. RBC casts ✓

Answer: d

Nephritic syndrome = glomerular inflammation with hematuria (RBC casts), oliguria, hypertension and mild proteinuria.

Key point: Nephritic hallmark = RBC casts.

qs.q: Proteinuria is diagnosed when urinary protein excretion exceeds:
qs.a:
a. >4 mg per 24 hours

b. >3.5 g per 24 hours

c. >30 mg per 24 hours

d. >150 mg per 24 hours ✓

Answer: d

Proteinuria is defined as > 150 mg/24 h (albuminuria > 30 mg/24 h); nephrotic range > 3.5 g/24 h.

Key point: Proteinuria > 150 mg/day; nephrotic > 3.5 g/day.

qs.q: All of the following cause glomerular hematuria EXCEPT:
qs.a:
a. IgA nephropathy

b. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

c. Alport syndrome

d. Renal stone ✓

Answer: d

Renal stones cause NON-glomerular (urothelial) hematuria with normal-shaped RBCs and pain.

Key point: Stone = non-glomerular hematuria.

qs.q: A patient develops red urine after exercise with muscle pain. The diagnosis is:
qs.a:
a. IgA nephropathy

b. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

c. Urinary tract infection

d. Rhabdomyolysis ✓

Answer: d

Red urine after exertion with muscle pain = rhabdomyolysis: muscle breakdown releases myoglobin (dipstick 'blood' positive without RBCs) and raises CK.

Key point: Exercise + myalgia + dark urine → rhabdomyolysis (myoglobinuria).

qs.q: Which of the following is an indication for treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria?
qs.a:
a. Pregnancy ✓

b. Urinary catheter

c. Elderly patients

d. Diabetes mellitus

Answer: a

Asymptomatic bacteriuria is treated in pregnancy (risk of pyelonephritis and preterm labour) and before urological procedures. It is not treated in catheterised, elderly or diabetic patients.

Key point: Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria: pregnancy + before urological surgery.

qs.q: Renal imaging is indicated in which of the following situations?
qs.a:
a. Persistent fever for more than 3 days despite appropriate antibiotics ✓

b. The pathogen is E. coli

c. Urine culture with 10,000–50,000 colonies

d. Uncomplicated cystitis

Answer: a

Imaging (US/CT) is indicated when fever persists > 72 h despite appropriate antibiotics, to look for obstruction, abscess or emphysematous infection.

Key point: Image UTI if no response in 72 h.

qs.q: A patient with pyelonephritis is treated with antibiotics, but fever persists for more than 48 hours. What is the next step in management?
qs.a:
a. Start empirical antibiotics

b. Perform CT scan ✓

c. Perform cystoscopy

d. Repeat urine culture

Answer: b

Persistent fever on antibiotics in pyelonephritis → CT to look for obstruction, abscess or emphysematous pyelonephritis.

Key point: Non-resolving pyelonephritis → CT.

qs.q: Emphysematous urinary tract infection is most commonly caused by:
qs.a:
a. Gas-forming Enterobacteriaceae (e.g., E. coli) ✓

b. Staphylococcus aureus

c. Streptococcus pyogenes

d. Pseudomonas aeruginosa

Answer: a

Emphysematous pyelonephritis/cystitis (mostly diabetics) is caused by gas-forming Enterobacteriaceae, especially E. coli and Klebsiella.

Key point: Gas in the kidney = E. coli/Klebsiella in a diabetic.

qs.q: The most common organism in complicated UTI is:
qs.a:
a. Staphylococcus saprophyticus

b. Pseudomonas aeruginosa

c. Proteus mirabilis

d. Escherichia coli ✓

Answer: d

E. coli remains the most common organism in complicated UTI (although Proteus, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Enterococcus are more frequent than in simple UTI).

Key point: Commonest UTI organism (simple or complicated) = E. coli.

qs.q: All of the following are risk factors for UTI EXCEPT:
qs.a:
a. Male sex ✓

b. Diabetes mellitus

c. Urinary catheterization

d. Pregnancy

Answer: a

Female sex (short urethra) is the risk factor; male sex is protective (except older men with prostate disease).

Key point: Women > men for UTI.

qs.q: A 71-year-old male presents to the hospital with groin and loin pain. His relatives report that he has been disoriented for the last two days and has been feverish. Urine analysis shows pus cells over 100. What is the most common organism that causes this condition?
qs.a:
a. Streptococcus pyogenes

b. Klebsiella

c. Proteus mirabilis

d. E. coli ✓

Answer: d

Elderly man with fever, loin pain, confusion and heavy pyuria = acute pyelonephritis/urosepsis; E. coli is the commonest cause.

Key point: Pyelonephritis organism = E. coli.

qs.q: Renal imaging is useful in patients with acute urinary tract infections when:
qs.a:
a. The pathogen is E. coli

b. The urine culture has 10,000–50,000 col/ml

c. The patient presented with fever

d. The patient has persistent fever for more than 3 days despite appropriate antibiotics ✓

Answer: d

Imaging (ultrasound/CT) is indicated when a UTI does not respond — persistent fever beyond 72 hours of appropriate antibiotics — to look for obstruction, abscess or stones.

Key point: UTI not improving after 72 h of antibiotics → image the kidneys.

qs.q: A procedure which often predisposes a hospitalized patient to a urinary tract infection is:
qs.a:
a. Urinary catheterization ✓

b. Antibiotic therapy

c. Colonization of periurethral areas with hospital organisms

d. Immunosuppressive therapy

e. Diabetes

Answer: a

Urinary catheterization is the main cause of hospital-acquired UTI.

Key point: Catheter = commonest cause of nosocomial UTI.

qs.q: What is the most common causative organism of complicated urinary tract infections?
qs.a:
a. Staphylococcus saprophyticus

b. Escherichia coli ✓

c. Enterococcus faecalis

d. Pseudomonas aeruginosa

Answer: b

E. coli (uropathogenic) causes about 75–90% of UTIs.

Key point: UTI = E. coli.

qs.q: All of the following are risk factors for urinary tract infection (UTI) EXCEPT:
qs.a:
a. Female sex

b. Urinary catheterization

c. Urinary tract obstruction

d. Male sex ✓

Answer: d

Female sex (short urethra) is the risk factor; male sex is protective (except older men with prostate disease).

Key point: Women > men for UTI.

qs.q: Which test compares the creatinine in a 24-hour sample of urine to the creatinine level in the blood?
qs.a:
a. BUN

b. Serum creatinine

c. Creatinine clearance ✓

d. Albumin-to-creatinine ratio

Answer: c

Creatinine clearance = (urine creatinine × urine volume) / plasma creatinine — estimates GFR.

Key point: Creatinine clearance = urine vs blood creatinine.

qs.q: Indications for treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria include:
qs.a:
a. Pregnancy ✓

b. Elderly patients

c. Diabetic patients

d. Patients with urinary catheters

Answer: a

Asymptomatic bacteriuria is treated in pregnancy (pyelonephritis, preterm birth risk) and before urological procedures.

Key point: Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria only in pregnancy (and before urological surgery).

qs.q: The colony count in a symptomatic UTI is:
qs.a:
a. >10³/mL

b. >10⁴/mL

c. >10⁵/mL ✓

d. >10²/mL

Answer: c

Significant bacteriuria is classically ≥ 10⁵ CFU/mL (lower counts may be significant in symptomatic women or catheter samples).

Key point: Significant UTI count = 10⁵/mL.

qs.q: Which patient has increased risk for asymptomatic bacteruria?
qs.a:
a. Pregnant females and increase risk of preterm labor ✓

b. Diabetic males

c. Elderly patients

d. Postmenopausal women

Answer: a

Pregnant women are at increased risk from asymptomatic bacteriuria: it can progress to pyelonephritis and is linked to preterm labour, so they are screened and treated.

Key point: Pregnancy: screen and treat asymptomatic bacteriuria.

qs.q: A hallmark of nephritic syndrome is:
qs.a:
a. Hypoalbuminemia

b. Hyperlipidemia

c. Proteinuria

d. RBC casts ✓

Answer: d

Nephritic syndrome = glomerular inflammation with hematuria (RBC casts), oliguria, hypertension and mild proteinuria.

Key point: Nephritic hallmark = RBC casts.

qs.q: After an infection, what is the typical latency period before developing post- infectious glomerulonephritis?
qs.a:
a. 1–2 weeks ✓

b. 4–6 weeks

c. 1–2 days

d. Same day

Answer: a

Post-infectious (post-streptococcal) GN follows the infection after a latent period: ~1–2 weeks after pharyngitis (2–4 weeks after skin infection).

Key point: Latency 1–2 weeks = PSGN; 1–2 days = IgA.

qs.q: The treatment of anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome) is:
qs.a:
a. Plasmapheresis + steroids + cyclophosphamide ✓

b. Aspirin

c. Antibiotics

d. Dialysis alone

Answer: a

Anti-GBM disease: remove antibodies with plasma exchange and stop production with steroids + cyclophosphamide.

Key point: Goodpasture's = plasma exchange + steroids + cyclophosphamide.

qs.q: The classic biopsy appearance of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) is:
qs.a:
a. Mesangial proliferation + thickening of the basement membrane ✓

b. Crescent formation

c. Diffuse podocyte effacement

d. Spike and dome pattern

Answer: a

MPGN (mesangiocapillary GN) shows mesangial proliferation with GBM thickening and duplication ('tram-track').

Key point: MPGN = mesangial proliferation + tram-track GBM.

qs.q: A patient develops hematuria 3 weeks after a sore throat infection, with dysmorphic RBCs in the urine and a high ASO titer. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis ✓

b. IgA nephropathy

c. Cryoglobulin-associated glomerulonephritis

d. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis

Answer: a

Hematuria ~3 weeks after a sore throat with dysmorphic RBCs and high ASO = acute post-streptococcal GN (low C3 expected).

Key point: Sore throat → 2–3 weeks → hematuria + ↑ASO = PSGN.

qs.q: A patient presents with hematuria following gastroenteritis, with dysmorphic RBCs in the urine analysis and normal C3 and C4 levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. IgA nephropathy ✓

b. Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

c. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis

d. Goodpasture syndrome

Answer: a

Hematuria soon after a mucosal infection (pharyngitis/gastroenteritis) with NORMAL complement = IgA nephropathy.

Key point: Mucosal infection + hematuria + normal C3 = IgA.

qs.q: A patient presents with malar rash and photosensitivity, then develops renal affection. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Lupus nephritis (systemic lupus erythematosus with renal involvement) ✓

b. Dermatomyositis

c. IgA nephropathy

d. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

Answer: a

Malar rash and photosensitivity = SLE; renal involvement = lupus nephritis.

Key point: Malar rash + kidney = lupus nephritis.

qs.q: A patient with a known history of rheumatoid arthritis develops hepatitis C, with low C3 and low C4 levels. What is the best laboratory test to add to confirm the diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Cryoglobulins ✓

b. Anti-GBM antibodies

c. C-ANCA

d. Anti-dsDNA

Answer: a

HCV + low C3 and C4 (classical pathway) + RA-like symptoms → check serum cryoglobulins (mixed cryoglobulinaemia, rheumatoid factor positive).

Key point: HCV + low C4 → cryoglobulins.

qs.q: A kidney biopsy is performed on a patient with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Immunofluorescence shows linear IgG deposits along the glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM antibodies). What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Goodpasture syndrome ✓

b. IgA nephropathy

c. Lupus nephritis

d. Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (APSGN)

Answer: a

Linear IgG along the GBM on immunofluorescence = anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture).

Key point: Linear IgG = anti-GBM.

qs.q: A case of hematuria with RBC casts. What is the possible cause?
qs.a:
a. Glomerular ✓

b. Extraglomerular

c. Contamination from the urethral meatus

d. Dehydration

Answer: a

RBC casts form only when blood enters the tubule from the glomerulus.

Key point: RBC casts → glomerular.

qs.q: What criteria differentiate between nephritic and nephrotic syndrome?
qs.a:
a. Proteinuria (nephrotic >3.5 g/day; nephritic <3.5 g/day) and hematuria ✓

b. Blood pressure

c. Serum creatinine

d. Edema

Answer: a

The key difference is the urine: nephrotic = heavy proteinuria >3.5 g/day with bland sediment; nephritic = haematuria (RBC casts) with proteinuria <3.5 g/day. BP, creatinine and oedema can occur in both.

Key point: Nephrotic: protein >3.5 g · Nephritic: haematuria + RBC casts.

qs.q: Red cell casts on urine microscopy are most likely due to:
qs.a:
a. Urethral trauma

b. UTI

c. Bladder carcinoma

d. Ureteric stone

e. Post-streptococcal GN ✓

Answer: e

RBC casts point to glomerulonephritis — here post-streptococcal GN.

Key point: RBC casts = GN.

qs.q: What is the most common cause of nephritic syndrome?
qs.a:
a. IgA nephropathy ✓

b. Membranous nephropathy

c. Minimal change disease

d. Diabetic nephropathy

Answer: a

IgA nephropathy is the most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide and the commonest cause of nephritic presentation.

Key point: Most common GN worldwide = IgA.

qs.q: Nephritic syndrome is characterized by:
qs.a:
a. Glomerular hematuria ✓

b. Proteinuria of 5 g/day

c. Hypotension

d. Polyuria

Answer: a

Nephritic syndrome = glomerular hematuria (dysmorphic RBCs/casts), oliguria, hypertension and sub-nephrotic proteinuria.

Key point: Nephritic = hematuria + HTN + oliguria.

qs.q: Which of the following is TRUE regarding post-infectious glomerulonephritis?
qs.a:
a. Adults are more likely to fully recover, while children are more prone to severe disease

b. Corticosteroid therapy is the treatment of choice

c. Light microscopy shows a diffuse proliferative pattern of injury ✓

d. It usually occurs 2–3 months after infection

Answer: c

Post-infectious GN shows diffuse proliferative (endocapillary) GN with neutrophils; subepithelial 'humps' on EM.

Key point: PSGN = diffuse proliferative GN; supportive Rx; children recover.

qs.q: A 16-year-old female presents with generalized fatigue and exertional dyspnea for the past four weeks. For the past two weeks, she has also started to pass dark-colored urine, especially at night and in the morning on waking. Laboratory investigations show hemoglobin 7.1 g/dL, WBC 2200/mm³, and platelets 80,000/mm³. What is the most likely complication of this condition that can lead to death?
qs.a:
a. Liver cell failure

b. Thrombosis

c. Respiratory failure

d. Acute kidney injury ✓

Answer: d

Dark urine on waking + pancytopenia in a young patient = paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria. The key gives acute kidney injury (haemoglobin pigment nephropathy). Note: in standard references thrombosis (e.g. Budd-Chiari) is the leading cause of death in PNH.

Key point: PNH: morning dark urine + pancytopenia; complications: thrombosis, AKI, aplasia.

qs.q: Which of the following conditions can cause glomerular hematuria?
qs.a:
a. IgA nephropathy

b. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

c. Alport syndrome

d. All of the above ✓

Answer: d

IgA nephropathy, PSGN and Alport syndrome all cause glomerular hematuria.

Key point: Glomerular hematuria: IgA, PSGN, Alport, thin BM, lupus.

qs.q: A 40-year-old man presents with malaise, nausea, and decreased urine output. He was previously well, and his physical examination is normal except for an elevated JVP and a pericardial rub. His electrolytes reveal acute renal failure. Which of the following findings on urinalysis is most likely in keeping with acute glomerulonephritis?
qs.a:
a. White blood cell casts

b. Granular casts

c. Hyaline casts

d. RBC casts ✓

Answer: d

RBC casts are diagnostic of acute glomerulonephritis.

Key point: AKI + RBC casts = GN.

qs.q: A patient presents with nephritic symptoms and mesangial proliferation with IgA deposits. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. IgA nephropathy ✓

b. Wegener granulomatosis

c. Post-infectious glomerulonephritis

d. Goodpasture syndrome

Answer: a

Mesangial proliferation with IgA deposits = IgA nephropathy (Berger's).

Key point: Mesangial IgA = Berger's disease.

qs.q: All of the following cause hemoptysis and renal affection EXCEPT:
qs.a:
a. IgA nephropathy (Berger disease) ✓

b. Goodpasture syndrome

c. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener)

d. Microscopic polyangiitis

Answer: a

Pulmonary-renal syndromes: Goodpasture's, GPA, MPA, (SLE). IgA nephropathy does not cause hemoptysis.

Key point: Lung + kidney bleeding: anti-GBM, ANCA vasculitis — not IgA.

qs.q: Which of the following is one of the nephritic criteria?
qs.a:
a. Glomerular hematuria ✓

b. Hypotension

c. Polyuria

d. Proteinuria >5 g

Answer: a

Nephritic syndrome = glomerular haematuria (dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts), hypertension, oliguria, oedema and sub-nephrotic proteinuria. Hypotension, polyuria and proteinuria >5 g do not fit.

Key point: Nephritic: haematuria, HTN, oliguria, oedema.

qs.q: Which of the following is found in a nephritic case?
qs.a:
a. RBC casts ✓

b. WBC casts

c. Granular casts

d. Hyaline casts

Answer: a

RBC casts are the urinary hallmark of nephritic syndrome.

Key point: Nephritic = RBC casts.

qs.q: A man presents with 3 years of intermittent hematuria and oliguria with no history of associated infection. He has no symptoms at the moment. What is the most likely pathological finding on kidney biopsy?
qs.a:
a. Mesangioproliferative glomerulonephritis with IgA deposits ✓

b. Mesangioproliferative glomerulonephritis with IgM deposits

c. Proliferative glomerulonephritis with IgM, IgG, and C3 deposits

d. Crescentic glomerulonephritis

Answer: a

Recurrent episodes of hematuria over years without infection link = IgA nephropathy: mesangial proliferation with IgA deposits.

Key point: Recurrent hematuria for years = IgA.

qs.q: A 40-year-old man presents with hematuria and proteinuria of 1.4 g/day. What is the gold standard for diagnosis of his condition?
qs.a:
a. Renal biopsy ✓

b. Renal angiogram

c. Intravenous urogram

d. CT scan

Answer: a

Hematuria + proteinuria (glomerular disease) → renal biopsy is the gold standard diagnosis.

Key point: Glomerular disease = biopsy.

qs.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with a recent episode of coughing up some blood, frequent nosebleeds, and now decreased urine output. A nasal mucosa ulcer is seen on inspection. Her urinalysis is positive for protein and red cells consistent with glomerulonephritis. CXR shows two cavitary lesions, and serology is positive for antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Wegener's granulomatosis (Granulomatosis with polyangiitis) ✓

b. Bacterial endocarditis

c. Goodpasture's syndrome

d. Lupus erythematosus

e. Post-streptococcal disease

Answer: a

Upper airway (epistaxis, nasal ulcer) + lung cavities + GN + ANCA (c-ANCA/PR3) = granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's).

Key point: Nose + lung + kidney + c-ANCA = GPA.

qs.q: A patient presents with RBCs and WBCs in urine, associated with flank pain. Urine bacteriology is negative. What is the first investigation of choice?
qs.a:
a. CT abdomen and pelvis

b. Ultrasonography of the kidneys ✓

c. Plain X-ray KUB

d. Intravenous urography (IVU)

e. Urine culture and sensitivity

Answer: b

Flank pain with hematuria/pyuria and sterile urine → renal ultrasound first (stones, obstruction, TB, papillary necrosis), then CT if needed.

Key point: Sterile pyuria + flank pain → US first (think stones/TB).

qs.q: A patient presents with a nephritic picture, low C3 and C4, positive HCV, vasculitic purpura, and cold distal limbs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Goodpasture syndrome

b. Mixed cryoglobulinemia ✓

c. IgA nephropathy

d. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN)

Answer: b

HCV + low C3/C4 + vasculitic purpura + cold extremities + GN = mixed (type II) cryoglobulinaemia.

Key point: HCV + purpura + low C4 = cryoglobulinaemia.

qs.q: Which of the following is a cause of nephritic syndrome?
qs.a:
a. Minimal change disease

b. IgA nephropathy ✓

c. Membranous nephropathy

d. Diabetic nephropathy

Answer: b

IgA nephropathy is a nephritic cause (haematuria, often after URTI). Minimal change, membranous and diabetic nephropathy cause nephrotic syndrome.

Key point: IgA nephropathy = nephritic; MCD/membranous/diabetic = nephrotic.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT a cause of nephritic syndrome?
qs.a:
a. Post-streptococcal GN

b. IgA nephropathy

c. Henoch-Schönlein purpura

d. Minimal change disease ✓

Answer: d

Minimal change disease is a NEPHROTIC disease.

Key point: MCD = nephrotic, not nephritic.

qs.q: Complement C3 is characteristically low in all EXCEPT:
qs.a:
a. Membranoproliferative GN

b. SLE

c. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis ✓

d. Post-streptococcal GN

Answer: c

FSGS is not complement-mediated — C3 is normal.

Key point: Low C3 GN: PSGN, MPGN, SLE, cryo, endocarditis.

qs.q: Which is associated with a better prognosis in IgA nephropathy?
qs.a:
a. Heavy proteinuria

b. Male gender

c. Hyperlipidemia

d. Frank hematuria ✓

e. ACE genotype DD

Answer: d

Episodic frank (macroscopic) hematuria with infections is associated with a better prognosis in IgA nephropathy.

Key point: IgA good sign = frank hematuria; bad = proteinuria, HTN, raised creatinine, male.

qs.q: What is the most common type of SLE-associated renal disease?
qs.a:
a. Class II mesangial GN

b. Class III focal proliferative GN

c. Class IV diffuse proliferative GN ✓

d. Class V membranous GN

e. Class VI sclerosing GN

Answer: c

Class IV diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis is the commonest and most severe form.

Key point: Commonest lupus nephritis = class IV.

qs.q: Linear IgG deposits along the GBM are most characteristic of:
qs.a:
a. SLE

b. IgA nephropathy

c. Minimal change disease

d. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN)

e. Goodpasture syndrome ✓

Answer: e

Linear IgG deposition along the GBM = Goodpasture's (anti-GBM).

Key point: Linear IgG = Goodpasture's.

qs.q: Goodpasture syndrome is due to:
qs.a:
a. Bacterial infection

b. Metabolic derangement

c. Immune-complex deposition

d. Anti-GBM antibodies ✓

e. Enzymatic deficiency

Answer: d

Goodpasture's is caused by autoantibodies to the α3 chain of type IV collagen in glomerular and alveolar basement membranes.

Key point: Goodpasture's = anti-GBM (type IV collagen).

qs.q: Which cause of glomerulonephritis is associated with normal complement levels?
qs.a:
a. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN)

b. Mesangiocapillary GN

c. Subacute bacterial endocarditis

d. Goodpasture syndrome ✓

e. SLE

Answer: d

Anti-GBM disease has normal complement levels.

Key point: Normal complement GN: anti-GBM, IgA, ANCA vasculitis.

qs.q: Which glomerulonephritis is also characteristically associated with normal complement levels?
qs.a:
a. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN)

b. Membranoproliferative GN (MPGN)

c. IgA nephropathy ✓

d. Lupus nephritis

Answer: c

IgA nephropathy characteristically has normal complement levels.

Key point: IgA = normal complement.

qs.q: A 10-year-old boy develops hematuria two days after a sore throat. What would renal biopsy most likely show?
qs.a:
a. Proliferation of endothelial cells

b. No change

c. Mesangial hypercellularity ✓

d. Basement membrane thickening

e. Capillary wall necrosis

Answer: c

Hematuria 1–2 days after a sore throat (synpharyngitic) = IgA nephropathy → mesangial hypercellularity with IgA deposits.

Key point: Hematuria 2 days after sore throat = IgA → mesangial proliferation.

qs.q: A 13-year-old girl develops purpura of the lower limbs and buttocks with microscopic hematuria. She has mild persistent renal impairment. What is the most likely renal outcome?
qs.a:
a. Hypertension within 20 years

b. Persistent proteinuria

c. End-stage renal failure (ESRF)

d. Full renal recovery ✓

e. Frequent relapses

Answer: d

HSP nephritis in children with mild renal involvement usually recovers fully (keyed answer); heavier proteinuria/impairment predicts worse outcomes.

Key point: Childhood HSP nephritis: mostly full recovery.

qs.q: Which type of GN is most characteristically associated with streptococcal infection in children?
qs.a:
a. FSGS

b. Diffuse proliferative GN ✓

c. Membranous GN

d. Mesangiocapillary GN

e. Rapidly progressive GN (RPGN)

Answer: b

Post-streptococcal GN in children = diffuse (endocapillary) proliferative GN.

Key point: Post-strep GN = diffuse proliferative.

qs.q: A 33-year-old man with celiac disease has recurrent macroscopic hematuria. His urine is typically brown with no clots. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Diffuse proliferative GN

b. IgA nephropathy ✓

c. Membranous GN

d. Minimal change disease

e. Rapidly progressive GN (RPGN)

Answer: b

Recurrent macroscopic brown hematuria in a young adult, associated with celiac disease (mucosal IgA) = IgA nephropathy.

Key point: Celiac + recurrent hematuria = IgA nephropathy.

qs.q: A 45-year-old woman with nephrotic syndrome develops marked loss of subcutaneous tissue from the face. What is the most likely underlying renal disease?
qs.a:
a. MPGN type II ✓

b. FSGS

c. Minimal change GN

d. Renal vein thrombosis

e. Membranous GN

Answer: a

Partial lipodystrophy (loss of facial fat) with C3 nephritic factor is associated with MPGN type II (dense deposit disease / C3 glomerulopathy).

Key point: Partial lipodystrophy = MPGN type II (C3 nephritic factor).

qs.q: An African American woman with joint pain presents with renal impairment. Which urinalysis finding is expected?
qs.a:
a. Hyaline casts

b. Protein 4+ / hematuria / RBC casts ✓

c. Muddy brown casts

d. Fatty casts only

Answer: b

Young black woman with arthralgia and renal impairment = lupus nephritis → active nephritic sediment: heavy proteinuria, hematuria and RBC casts.

Key point: Lupus nephritis urine: protein + blood + RBC casts.

qs.q: All of the following cause thrombocytopenia EXCEPT:
qs.a:
a. ITP (immune thrombocytopenic purpura)

b. TTP (thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura)

c. Henoch–Schönlein purpura ✓

d. DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation)

Answer: c (Henoch–Schönlein purpura is a small-vessel vasculitis with a normal

Henoch-Schönlein purpura is a small-vessel IgA vasculitis with palpable purpura and NORMAL platelets.

Key point: HSP = purpura with normal platelets.

qs.q: Which condition does NOT cause hemoptysis with renal involvement?
qs.a:
a. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (ANCA)

b. Microscopic polyangiitis (ANCA)

c. IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease) ✓

d. Goodpasture syndrome

Answer: c

Pulmonary–renal syndromes (haemoptysis + GN) are ANCA vasculitis (GPA, MPA) and Goodpasture (anti-GBM). IgA nephropathy affects the kidney only and does not cause haemoptysis.

Key point: Pulmonary–renal: GPA, MPA, Goodpasture — not IgA.

qs.q: A nephritic picture with low C3 and C4, positive HCV, vasculitic purpura, and cold distal limbs suggests:
qs.a:
a. Cryoglobulinemic glomerulonephritis ✓

b. IgA nephropathy

c. Anti-GBM disease

d. Minimal change disease

Answer: a

HCV + low C3 and C4 + vasculitic purpura + cold extremities + nephritic urine = mixed cryoglobulinaemia causing membranoproliferative (cryoglobulinaemic) GN.

Key point: HCV + low C4 + purpura → cryoglobulinaemic GN.

qs.q: A patient with stage V (membranous) lupus nephritis typically presents with:
qs.a:
a. Nephrotic syndrome ✓

b. Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis

c. Isolated hematuria

d. Acute nephritic syndrome

Answer: a

Class V (membranous) lupus nephritis presents with nephrotic syndrome (heavy proteinuria, edema).

Key point: Lupus class V = nephrotic.

qs.q: In renal failure, what causes renal osteodystrophy?
qs.a:
a. Hypocalcemia

b. Impaired renal production of 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol ✓

c. Hypophosphatemia

d. Excess erythropoietin

Answer: b

Damaged kidneys fail to 1α-hydroxylate vitamin D → low calcitriol → low calcium absorption, phosphate retention and secondary hyperparathyroidism → renal osteodystrophy.

Key point: Renal osteodystrophy starts with ↓ 1,25-(OH)₂D.

qs.q: Most common complication of dialysis in a diabetic patient:
qs.a:
a. Hypotension ✓

b. Disequilibrium syndrome

c. Air embolism

d. Peritonitis

Answer: a

Hypotension is the commonest complication of haemodialysis, especially in diabetics (autonomic neuropathy, impaired vasoconstriction).

Key point: Dialysis + diabetic → hypotension (commonest).

qs.q: Which of the following is a recognized complication of chronic renal failure?
qs.a:
a. Liver cirrhosis

b. Hyperglycemia

c. Pericarditis ✓

d. Peptic ulcer

Answer: c

Uraemic pericarditis is a recognised complication of CKD (uraemic toxins irritate the pericardium); it can present with a friction rub.

Key point: Uraemia → pericarditis.

qs.q: Criteria for hemodialysis include:
qs.a:
a. Hyperkalemia that is responding to treatment

b. Uremic encephalopathy ✓

c. Metabolic acidosis that is responding to treatment

d. Mild anemia

Answer: b

Uraemic encephalopathy is a true indication for dialysis. Hyperkalaemia and acidosis count only when they do NOT respond to medical treatment.

Key point: Dialysis for REFRACTORY K/acidosis/fluid + uraemic encephalopathy/pericarditis.

qs.q: A diabetic patient underwent dialysis, then developed hypotension, headache, confusion, and seizures; CT confirms brain edema. What is the cause of the complication?
qs.a:
a. Hypotension

b. Disequilibrium syndrome ✓

c. Air embolism

d. Access infection

Answer: b

Headache, confusion, seizures and cerebral oedema during/after (often first) dialysis = dialysis disequilibrium syndrome: rapid urea removal makes plasma hypotonic relative to brain, so water moves into the brain.

Key point: Brain oedema after dialysis = disequilibrium syndrome.

qs.q: Which urinary finding favors chronic kidney disease over acute kidney injury?
qs.a:
a. Broad waxy casts ✓

b. Muddy brown granular casts

c. Red cell casts

d. White cell casts

Answer: a

Broad waxy casts form in dilated, atrophic tubules of chronically damaged kidneys, so they favour CKD. Muddy brown casts = ATN; RBC casts = GN; WBC casts = pyelonephritis/AIN.

Key point: Broad waxy casts → CKD.

qs.q: Ultrasound helps differentiate chronic from acute kidney disease. Which finding favors CKD?
qs.a:
a. Normal-sized kidneys

b. Enlarged, edematous kidneys

c. Isolated hydronephrosis

d. Small, shrunken kidneys with a thin cortex ✓

Answer: d

Small (< 9 cm), echogenic kidneys with a thin cortex indicate chronic kidney disease.

Key point: Small kidneys on US = CKD (exceptions: DM, amyloid, PKD, HIV).

qs.q: A patient on peritoneal dialysis develops complications. What should she be expected to have?
qs.a:
a. Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome

b. Peritonitis ✓

c. Air embolism

d. Vascular access thrombosis

Answer: b

Peritonitis (cloudy effluent, abdominal pain, fever) is the commonest serious complication of peritoneal dialysis. Disequilibrium, air embolism and access thrombosis belong to haemodialysis.

Key point: PD complication = peritonitis.

qs.q: Which condition is associated with large kidney size despite advanced kidney damage?
qs.a:
a. Chronic pyelonephritis

b. Amyloidosis ✓

c. Hypertensive nephrosclerosis

d. Reflux nephropathy

Answer: b

Amyloidosis keeps kidneys large despite advanced damage.

Key point: Large kidneys + CKD = amyloidosis.

qs.q: A patient with non-specific symptoms and serum creatinine 9 mg/dL. What is the next step?
qs.a:
a. Repeat creatinine after one month

b. Start oral corticosteroids

c. Initiate dialysis ✓

d. Do nothing and observe

Answer: c

Creatinine 9 mg/dL with uraemic symptoms indicates advanced/end-stage kidney failure — dialysis is indicated (after checking hyperkalaemia, acidosis, fluid overload).

Key point: Symptomatic very high creatinine = start dialysis.

qs.q: A patient with renal failure and on dialysis has GFR:
qs.a:
a. 30-60

b. 15-30

c. 5-15 ✓

d. None of the above

Answer: c

Patients on dialysis have a GFR around 5–15 mL/min, which is the range of end-stage renal failure where dialysis is needed.

Key point: Dialysis ≈ GFR 5–15.

qs.q: What is the dietary modification for a patient with chronic kidney failure?
qs.a:
a. Adequate calories, low carbohydrates, high proteins

b. Adequate calories, high carbohydrates, limited proteins ✓

c. Low calories, high carbohydrates, limited proteins

d. Low calories, low carbs, limited proteins

Answer: b

CKD diet: adequate calories (mainly from carbohydrates) to prevent catabolism, with limited protein to reduce urea load; plus salt, potassium and phosphate restriction.

Key point: CKD: enough calories, high carbs, limited protein.

qs.q: What is the cause of anemia in chronic renal failure?
qs.a:
a. Iron deficiency

b. Decreased erythropoietin ✓

c. Vitamin B12 deficiency

d. Folate deficiency

Answer: b

The main cause of anaemia in chronic renal failure is reduced EPO production; uraemia, blood loss and shortened red-cell survival add to it.

Key point: CRF anaemia: mainly ↓EPO.

qs.q: Which of the following is INCORRECT (least common) regarding CKD?
qs.a:
a. Hyperparathyroidism

b. Hyperphosphatemia

c. Hypokalemia ✓

d. Hypocalcemia

Answer: c

CKD typically causes hyperkalaemia, not hypokalaemia; hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism are common.

Key point: CKD → K up, phosphate up, Ca down, PTH up.

qs.q: Which is not found in Lupus Nephritis?
qs.a:
a. Psychosis ✓

b. Hematuria

c. Proteinuria

d. Hypertension

Answer: a

Haematuria, proteinuria and hypertension are features of lupus nephritis. Psychosis is a neuropsychiatric (CNS) lupus feature, not a finding of the nephritis itself.

Key point: Lupus nephritis = haematuria, proteinuria, HTN.

qs.q: What is wrong related to diet in a renal patient?
qs.a:
a. Na restriction

b. Protein restriction

c. Increase cholesterol intake ✓

d. Potassium restriction

Answer: c

The wrong statement is 'increase cholesterol intake'. Renal patients with hyperlipidaemia need less fat and cholesterol.

Key point: CKD diet: ↓ Na, ↓ protein, ↓ fat/cholesterol.

qs.q: How to differentiate between acute renal failure and chronic kidney disease?
qs.a:
a. Small echogenic kidneys on ultrasound ✓

b. Anemia

c. Hyperphosphatemia

d. Hyponatremia

Answer: a

Small, echogenic kidneys with thin cortex on ultrasound indicate chronic disease. Anaemia, hyperphosphataemia and hyponatraemia can occur in both AKI and CKD.

Key point: Small kidneys on US = CKD (exceptions: diabetes, amyloid, PKD).

qs.q: A patient taking a statin, diuretics, and 3 anti-hypertensive drugs. What is the cause of death in renal dialysis patients?
qs.a:
a. Anaphylaxis

b. GI hemorrhage

c. Pulmonary embolism

d. Cardiovascular ✓

Answer: d

Cardiovascular disease is the commonest cause of death in dialysis patients (accelerated atherosclerosis, LVH, arrhythmia, sudden death).

Key point: Dialysis patient dies of → cardiovascular.

qs.q: Which of the following is not an absolute contraindication for renal transplant?
qs.a:
a. Active infection

b. Active glomerulonephritis

c. Hepatitis C ✓

d. Overt hepatitis

Answer: c

Hepatitis C is no longer an absolute contraindication to transplantation (it can be treated with antivirals). Active infection, active GN and overt (decompensated) liver disease are contraindications at that time.

Key point: HCV is a relative, not absolute, contraindication to kidney transplant.

qs.q: What is an absolute indication for dialysis?
qs.a:
a. Serum K+ level > 6 mEq/L

b. Serum urea level > 200 mg/dL

c. Serum creatinine level > 4 mg/dL

d. Clinical evidence of pericarditis ✓

e. HCO3 level < 10 mEq/dL

Answer: d

Uraemic pericarditis is an absolute (emergency) indication: it can progress to tamponade and only dialysis treats it. The lab numbers alone (K, urea, creatinine, HCO₃) are not absolute; what matters is refractoriness or clinical effect.

Key point: Absolute dialysis = uraemic pericarditis / encephalopathy; labs only if refractory (AEIOU).

qs.q: A patient with CKD complains of fatigue without shortness of breath. He takes calcium and oral iron. Serum ferritin is normal, reticulocyte count is normal, and Hb is 8 g/dL. What is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a:
a. Shift from oral to IV iron

b. Use oral acid to increase iron absorption

c. Blood transfusion

d. Erythropoiesis-stimulating agent (ESA) ✓

Answer: d

Hb 8 in CKD with normal ferritin (iron replete) and no response = anaemia from EPO deficiency, so start an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent. IV iron is for iron deficiency; transfusion is for symptomatic/severe anaemia.

Key point: CKD anaemia + adequate iron → ESA.

qs.q: Which of the following electrolyte abnormalities is LEAST commonly associated with CKD?
qs.a:
a. Hyperparathyroidism

b. Hyperphosphatemia

c. Hypokalemia ✓

d. Hypocalcemia

Answer: c

Hypokalaemia is the least common: CKD retains potassium (hyperkalaemia). Hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism are typical.

Key point: CKD = hyperkalaemia, not hypokalaemia.

qs.q: What is the main cause of anemia in chronic renal failure?
qs.a:
a. Increased RBC destruction

b. Decreased erythropoietin production ✓

c. Increased iron absorption

d. Increased vitamin B12 production

Answer: b

The main cause of anaemia in chronic renal failure is reduced EPO production; uraemia, blood loss and shortened red-cell survival add to it.

Key point: CRF anaemia: mainly ↓EPO.

qs.q: In which CKD stage is renal replacement therapy usually considered based on clinical indications?
qs.a:
a. GFR above 90

b. GFR below 60 in every patient

c. GFR below 15 mL/min/1.73 m² ✓

d. Mild proteinuria

Answer: c

Renal replacement therapy is usually planned when GFR falls below 15 mL/min/1.73 m² (stage 5), guided by symptoms and complications.

Key point: Stage 5 CKD (GFR <15) → prepare RRT.

qs.q: Which of the following statements regarding the assessment of proteinuria in patients with chronic kidney disease is INCORRECT?
qs.a:
a. Albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR) is more sensitive than protein:creatinine ratio

b. An ACR of 30 mg/mmol is approximately equal to a PCR of 50 mg/mmol.

c. An ACR sample is collected over 24 hours ✓

d. Women typically have higher ACR values.

e. An ACR of 3.1 mg/mmol in a diabetic man is clinically significant.

Answer: c

ACR is measured on a spot (early morning) urine sample, not a 24-hour collection — so that statement is incorrect. ACR is more sensitive than PCR, ACR 30 ≈ PCR 50, women have higher values, and ACR >3 mg/mmol is significant in diabetes.

Key point: ACR = spot urine sample.

qs.q: Which of the following adverse features of chronic renal failure is least effectively treated by haemodialysis?
qs.a:
a. Accumulation of uraemic toxins

b. Abnormal electrolyte balance

c. Fluid overload

d. Anaemia ✓

e. Acidosis

Answer: d

Dialysis removes toxins, corrects electrolytes and acidosis, and removes fluid. It does not replace erythropoietin, so anaemia persists and needs EPO.

Key point: Dialysis doesn't fix anaemia (or bone disease).

qs.q: Which of the following biochemical abnormalities in venous blood is least likely to be present in a patient with untreated chronic renal failure?
qs.a:
a. Reduced bicarbonate

b. Elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH)

c. Reduced phosphate ✓

d. Elevated cholesterol

e. Reduced calcium

Answer: c

Untreated CRF causes phosphate RETENTION (high phosphate), so reduced phosphate is least likely. Low bicarbonate, high PTH, high cholesterol and low calcium are expected.

Key point: CKD: high phosphate, low calcium.

qs.q: Which of the following statements about the management of anaemia in patients with chronic renal failure is most accurate?
qs.a:
a. Treatment with human recombinant erythropoietin is only beneficial in patients with a subnormal plasma erythropoietin level.

b. Target haemoglobin should be 13–14 g/dL to achieve maximal benefit.

c. Transferrin saturation should be maintained below 20% to avoid iron overload.

d. Patients not receiving dialysis should receive oral rather than parenteral iron. ✓

Answer: d

In non-dialysis CKD, oral iron is tried first; IV iron is mainly for dialysis or failed oral iron. EPO works regardless of measured EPO levels, the Hb target is about 10–12 (not 13–14, which raises stroke/CV risk), and transferrin saturation should be kept above 20%.

Key point: Non-dialysis CKD: oral iron first; Hb target ~10–12.

qs.q: Which of the following are complications of erythropoietin therapy?
qs.a:
a. Hypertension

b. Hypercoagulability

c. Both A and B ✓

d. Hypotension

Answer: c

Erythropoietin therapy can cause hypertension and a hypercoagulable state (thrombosis, access clotting), especially if Hb rises fast or high.

Key point: ESA side effects: HTN + thrombosis.

qs.q: In patients with hypertension and proteinuria, which class of drugs is most effective in retarding the progression of chronic renal failure?
qs.a:
a. Beta-blockers

b. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors ✓

c. Calcium channel blockers

d. Nitrates

e. Thiazide diuretics

Answer: b

ACE inhibitors (and ARBs) lower intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria, so they slow progression of proteinuric CKD more than other antihypertensives.

Key point: Proteinuric CKD → ACEi/ARB.

qs.q: Deficiency of which one of the following contributes to renal osteodystrophy?
qs.a:
a. 1α-hydroxylase ✓

b. Phosphate

c. Aluminium

d. 25-hydroxycholecalciferol

e. Parathyroid hormone

Answer: a

Loss of renal 1α-hydroxylase means 25-OH vitamin D cannot be activated to calcitriol, causing hypocalcaemia, secondary hyperparathyroidism and renal osteodystrophy.

Key point: Renal osteodystrophy: no 1α-hydroxylase → no calcitriol.

qs.q: In patients with chronic renal failure, which of the following is the most important contributor to renal osteodystrophy?
qs.a:
a. Impaired renal production of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol) ✓

b. Hypophosphatemia

c. Loss of vitamin D and calcium via dialysis

d. The use of calcitriol

Answer: a

The main driver of renal osteodystrophy is impaired renal production of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol), with phosphate retention and secondary hyperparathyroidism. Phosphate is high, not low.

Key point: CKD bone disease = low calcitriol + high phosphate + high PTH.

qs.q: Oliguria is defined as a urine output of:
qs.a:
a. Less than 400 mL/24 h ✓

b. Less than 50 mL/24 h

c. Less than 100 mL/24 h

d. More than 400 mL/24 h

Answer: a

Oliguria is urine output less than 400 mL/24 h (the minimum needed to excrete the daily solute load). Anuria is less than 50–100 mL/24 h.

Key point: Oliguria <400 mL/day · anuria <50 mL/day.

qs.q: A diabetic patient (creatinine 2) underwent coronary angiography, then developed gastroenteritis with vomiting; next morning she was unwell with creatinine 3. What is the diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Contrast-induced nephropathy ✓

b. Renal tubular acidosis

c. Chronic interstitial nephritis

d. Atheroembolic renal disease

Answer: a

Creatinine rising 24–72 h after angiography in a diabetic with CKD, worsened by volume loss from vomiting, fits contrast-induced nephropathy.

Key point: AKI 1–3 days after contrast (DM, CKD, dehydration) = contrast nephropathy.

qs.q: All of the following cause acute tubular necrosis (ATN) EXCEPT:
qs.a:
a. Corticosteroids ✓

b. Prolonged hypovolemia

c. Aminoglycosides

d. Rhabdomyolysis

Answer: a

ATN is caused by ischaemia (prolonged hypovolaemia) and nephrotoxins (aminoglycosides, myoglobin from rhabdomyolysis, contrast). Corticosteroids do not cause ATN.

Key point: ATN: ischaemia, aminoglycosides, myoglobin, contrast.

qs.q: A 50-year-old female presents with fever, cough, and yellow purulent sputum for 1 week. Urea and creatinine are normal, but she has hyponatremia and hypokalemia. She is admitted for IV gentamicin. After 1 day, she becomes hypotensive and is treated with IV saline and gentamicin. After 6 hours, urea and creatinine become elevated. What is the cause of the kidney affection?
qs.a:
a. Gentamicin nephrotoxicity

b. IgA nephropathy

c. SIADH with pneumonia

d. Acute tubular necrosis (ATN) due to persistent hypotension ✓

Answer: d

Creatinine rose within hours of a period of persistent hypotension, so the keyed cause is ischaemic ATN. Gentamicin nephrotoxicity usually takes 5–7 days of therapy to appear.

Key point: AKI soon after hypotension → ischaemic ATN; aminoglycoside ATN appears after ~1 week.

qs.q: AKI developing 24–72 hours after IV contrast in a diabetic patient with CKD is due to:
qs.a:
a. Atheroembolic disease

b. Acute interstitial nephritis

c. Contrast-induced nephropathy ✓

d. Renal vein thrombosis

Answer: c

AKI 24–72 hours after IV contrast in a diabetic with CKD is contrast-induced nephropathy. Atheroembolic disease appears later with livedo, eosinophilia and low complement.

Key point: 24–72 h after contrast = contrast nephropathy.

qs.q: AKI after cardiac catheterization with epigastric pain and diminished peripheral pulses suggests:
qs.a:
a. Contrast-induced nephropathy

b. Acute interstitial nephritis

c. Post-streptococcal GN

d. Atheroembolic renal disease (cholesterol emboli) ✓

Answer: d

After catheterisation, AKI with abdominal (mesenteric) pain and poor peripheral pulses/blue toes suggests cholesterol emboli (atheroembolic disease) showering from the aorta.

Key point: Post-catheter AKI + blue toes/abdominal pain = cholesterol emboli.

qs.q: A patient with non-specific symptoms and serum creatinine 9 mg/dL. What is the next step?
qs.a:
a. Repeat creatinine after one month

b. Start oral corticosteroids

c. Initiate dialysis ✓

d. Do nothing and observe

Answer: c

Creatinine 9 mg/dL with uraemic symptoms indicates advanced/end-stage kidney failure — dialysis is indicated (after checking hyperkalaemia, acidosis, fluid overload).

Key point: Symptomatic very high creatinine = start dialysis.

qs.q: An African American woman with joint pain presents with renal impairment. What is the most common urinalysis finding in acute renal failure?
qs.a:
a. Hyaline casts

b. Protein 4+ / hematuria / RBC casts

c. Muddy brown casts ✓

d. Fatty casts only

Answer: c

The question asks for the commonest urinalysis finding in acute renal failure: muddy brown granular casts of ATN (the commonest intrinsic AKI). RBC casts and heavy proteinuria are more specific for lupus/GN.

Key point: Commonest AKI cast = muddy brown (ATN).

qs.q: Which of the following is correct in management of radiocontrast induced kidney injury?
qs.a:
a. Acetylcysteine

b. Hydration

c. Minimize contrast volume

d. All of the above ✓

Answer: d

Contrast nephropathy is prevented by hydration (IV saline), using the least possible contrast volume, and N-acetylcysteine. All three are correct.

qs.q: Anuria is defined as:
qs.a:
a. Urine output < 50 ml/6 hr

b. Urine output < 50 ml/12 hr

c. Urine output < 50 ml/24 hr ✓

d. Urine output < 100 ml/24 hr

Answer: c

Anuria is urine output less than 50 mL/24 h (some texts use <100 mL/day).

Key point: Anuria <50 mL/24 h.

qs.q: Analgesic increases the risk of:
qs.a:
a. Tubulointerstitial nephritis ✓

b. Glomerulonephritis

c. Acute tubular necrosis

d. Renal artery stenosis

Answer: a

Chronic analgesic use (NSAIDs, phenacetin combinations) causes tubulointerstitial nephritis and papillary necrosis (analgesic nephropathy).

Key point: Analgesics → interstitial nephritis / papillary necrosis.

qs.q: 1st step in management of tubulointerstitial nephritis:
qs.a:
a. Stop offending drug ✓

b. Start steroids

c. Dialysis

d. IV fluids

Answer: a

The first and most important step in drug-induced tubulointerstitial nephritis is stopping the offending drug; steroids may be added if there is no improvement.

Key point: AIN: stop the drug first.

qs.q: A patient with pancreatitis was given an antibiotic and later had high creatinine. What is the most likely antibiotic given?
qs.a:
a. Aminoglycosides & Vancomycin ✓

b. Penicillins

c. Macrolides

d. Cephalosporins

Answer: a

Aminoglycosides and vancomycin are the classic nephrotoxic antibiotics (ATN), so a rising creatinine after antibiotics points to them.

Key point: Nephrotoxic antibiotics: aminoglycosides, vancomycin.

qs.q: An African American woman with joint pain comes with serum tests of renal impairment. What is the most common finding to be seen in urinalysis in acute renal failure?
qs.a:
a. Hyaline casts

b. Muddy brown casts

c. Protein 4+/hematuria/RBC casts ✓

d. Fatty casts only

Answer: c

In this version the keyed finding is heavy proteinuria with haematuria and RBC casts, i.e. an active glomerulonephritis (lupus nephritis fits a woman with joint pain).

Key point: Woman + arthralgia + renal impairment + RBC casts → lupus nephritis.

qs.q: A man with suprapubic mass, high BUN and K, and high creatinine. What is the management?
qs.a:
a. Dialysis ✓

b. Diuretics

c. IV fluids

d. Antibiotics

Answer: a

A suprapubic mass means urinary retention (post-renal AKI), so relieving the obstruction with a catheter is the first step; the keyed answer is dialysis because of the dangerous hyperkalaemia and uraemia, which need urgent treatment if they do not settle.

Key point: Palpable bladder → catheter; dangerous K+/uraemia → dialysis.

qs.q: Prerenal failure is associated with:
qs.a:
a. Postural hypotension ✓

b. Hypertension

c. Hyperkalemia

d. Metabolic alkalosis

Answer: a

Pre-renal failure comes from low effective volume — postural hypotension, tachycardia, dry mucosa. Hypertension does not fit.

Key point: Pre-renal AKI: volume depletion → postural hypotension.

qs.q: Renal Artery Stenosis:
qs.a:
a. Treatment with ACE I deteriorates renal function ✓

b. Treatment with ACE I improves renal function

c. Treatment with beta blockers is contraindicated

d. It is caused by hypovolemia

Answer: a

In (bilateral) renal artery stenosis GFR depends on angiotensin II constricting the efferent arteriole; ACE inhibitors remove this and renal function deteriorates.

Key point: Renal artery stenosis + ACEi → rising creatinine.

qs.q: When is ACE I contraindicated?
qs.a:
a. Hyperkalemia ✓

b. Hypertension

c. Proteinuria

d. Diabetes

Answer: a

ACE inhibitors raise potassium and are contraindicated in hyperkalaemia (also in bilateral renal artery stenosis and pregnancy). They are used in hypertension, proteinuria and diabetes.

Key point: ACEi contraindications: hyperkalaemia, bilateral RAS, pregnancy.

qs.q: Palpable Bladder:
qs.a:
a. Urine Catheter (Retention) ✓

b. Diuretics

c. IV fluids

d. Dialysis

Answer: a

A palpable bladder means urinary retention (post-renal obstruction); the treatment is urinary catheterisation.

Key point: Palpable bladder → catheterise.

qs.q: After performing imaging, patient presents with signs of renal failure:
qs.a:
a. Contrast nephropathy ✓

b. Acute interstitial nephritis

c. Rhabdomyolysis

d. Renal artery thrombosis

Answer: a

Renal failure appearing after an imaging study with contrast = contrast-induced nephropathy.

Key point: AKI after contrast imaging = contrast nephropathy.

qs.q: A 49-year-old woman presents with acute kidney injury after an acute illness manifested by myalgia, diarrhoea and vomiting. Her BP is 84/50 mmHg and she has dry mucous membranes. She was taking ibuprofen, paracetamol and domperidone during the illness. Her renal function improves rapidly with intravenous (IV) fluids. Which one of the following findings are likely to be present?
qs.a:
a. Dense granular ('muddy brown') casts on urinalysis

b. Hypercalcaemia

c. Hyponatraemia

d. Low (< 1%) fractional excretion of sodium ✓

e. Low urine specific gravity

Answer: d

Rapid improvement with IV fluids means pre-renal AKI: the tubules are intact and avidly reabsorb sodium, so fractional excretion of sodium is below 1% and urine is concentrated. Muddy brown casts mean ATN.

Key point: Pre-renal: FENa <1%, high urine SG, bland sediment.

qs.q: Oliguria is:
qs.a:
a. <50 ml urine/24 hrs

b. <100 ml urine/24 hrs

c. <200 ml urine/24 hrs

d. <400 ml urine/24 hrs ✓

Answer: d

Oliguria = urine output below 400 mL/24 h.

Key point: Oliguria <400 mL/day.

qs.q: A previously fit and well 70-year-old woman has been admitted due to a fractured neck of femur, and she has recently returned to the ward after a cemented hemiarthroplasty. You are bleeped to the ward to see her, as it is noted that she has had only 30 ml urine output in the last 3 hours. She is asleep on the ward, with a patient-controlled analgesic device in situ. Her airway is intact and her respiratory rate is 12/min with normal saturations and good air entry bilaterally. Her pulse is 125 bpm with a blood pressure of 95/68 mmHg and she has delayed capillary refill. She has pale conjunctiva and a temperature of 37.3°C. She has a 12-hourly bag of normal saline running. Her catheter is draining concentrated urine. An abdominal examination is normal. Which of the following interventions would you try first to increase the urine output?
qs.a:
a. Fluid challenge of 500 ml 5% dextrose over 10 minutes

b. Fluid challenge of 500 ml normal saline over 10 minutes ✓

c. Flush the catheter

d. Start antibiotics for presumed sepsis

e. Stop the patient-controlled analgesic device

Answer: b

She is tachycardic, hypotensive with delayed capillary refill after surgery = hypovolaemia, so give a fluid challenge of 500 mL normal saline quickly. Dextrose does not stay in the circulation; the catheter is already draining concentrated urine.

Key point: Post-op oliguria + shock signs → crystalloid fluid challenge.

qs.q: A 55-year-old man with significant cardiovascular disease and diabetes has acute kidney injury in the context of a viral illness. He was at a social gathering where he consumed alcohol and woke the next morning unwell. He had fever, aches and pains, headache and felt thirsty. He takes atorvastatin, lansoprazole, amlodipine, bisoprolol, warfarin, digoxin regularly. He passed a small amount of dark urine. His creatinine is 190 µmol/L (2.15 mg/dL), potassium 6.8 mmol/L, corrected calcium 1.97 mmol/L (7.90 mg/dL), international normalised ratio (INR) 2.0. Urine dipstick shows haematuria but no proteinuria. Direct urinalysis revealed no cells or casts. What is the likely cause of his kidney injury?
qs.a:
a. Acute interstitial nephritis

b. ATN due to viral infection

c. Haemorrhage into the kidneys

d. Pre-renal injury due to dehydration from alcohol

e. Rhabdomyolysis ✓

Answer: e

Dipstick 'blood' with no RBCs on microscopy = myoglobinuria. With statin use, alcohol, aches, high potassium and low calcium, this is rhabdomyolysis causing AKI.

Key point: Dipstick blood + no RBCs = myoglobin → rhabdomyolysis.

qs.q: A 62-year-old man presents with a large myocardial infarction and undergoes primary coronary angiography and stenting. Two days later he develops a low-grade fever and dusky discolouration of the toes on both feet, although peripheral pulses are palpable. eGFR was 52 mL/min/1.73 m2 pre-procedure and falls to 25 mL/min/1.73 m2 2 days later. Other investigations reveal: urinalysis: blood 1+, protein 1+; haemoglobin 12 g/L; white cell count 10.6x10^9/L with eosinophilia; platelet count 109. Creatine kinase is elevated at 640 U/L. What is the most likely cause of his acute kidney injury?
qs.a:
a. Cholesterol embolisation ✓

b. Contrast nephropathy

c. Haemolytic uraemic syndrome

d. Renal artery thrombosis

e. Rhabdomyolysis

Answer: a

Days after coronary angiography: blue toes, fever, eosinophilia, falling eGFR and low-grade proteinuria = cholesterol embolisation from the aorta.

Key point: Angiography + blue toes + eosinophilia = cholesterol emboli.

qs.q: A 58-year-old man presents with breathlessness, he reports feeling unwell over the last three months with nausea, vomiting and difficulty breathing. You notice his ankles are swollen and he has bruises on his arms. The patient mentions he has not been urinating as often as normal. The most appropriate investigation is:
qs.a:
a. Urine microscopy

b. Renal ultrasound

c. Serum electrolytes, urea and creatinine ✓

d. Renal biopsy

e. Chest x-ray

Answer: c

Months of nausea, vomiting, breathlessness, oedema, bruising and reduced urine output suggest renal failure, so the first test is serum urea, creatinine and electrolytes.

Key point: Suspected renal failure → U&E and creatinine first.

qs.q: A case of Rhabdomyolysis:
qs.a:
a. CK was very high and metabolic acidosis ✓

b. Normal CK and metabolic alkalosis

c. Low CK and respiratory acidosis

d. High CK and metabolic alkalosis

Answer: a

Rhabdomyolysis: very high CK (often >5× normal) with high anion gap metabolic acidosis, hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia and hypocalcaemia.

Key point: Rhabdomyolysis: CK very high + metabolic acidosis.

qs.q: A patient presents with acute renal failure. Which urinary cast is most characteristic of acute tubular necrosis (ATN)?
qs.a:
a. Hyaline casts

b. Muddy brown granular casts ✓

c. RBC casts

d. WBC casts

Answer: b

Muddy brown granular (epithelial) casts are the hallmark of ATN. Hyaline = pre-renal/normal; RBC casts = GN; WBC casts = pyelonephritis/AIN.

Key point: ATN = muddy brown granular casts.

qs.q: A patient undergoes angiography. After 48 hours, renal function starts deteriorating. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Acute glomerulonephritis

b. Contrast-associated acute kidney injury ✓

c. Chronic interstitial nephritis

d. Postrenal AKI

Answer: b
