Creatinine rising about 48 hours after angiography = contrast-associated AKI.

Key point: AKI 24–72 h post-contrast.

qs.q: Which of the following drugs can cause rhabdomyolysis?
qs.a:
a. Statins ✓

b. Paracetamol

c. Omeprazole

d. Amoxicillin

Answer: a

Statins can cause myopathy and rhabdomyolysis (higher risk with fibrates, macrolides, high doses).

Key point: Statins → rhabdomyolysis.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic finding in rhabdomyolysis?
qs.a:
a. Elevated creatine kinase

b. Elevated urinary WBC casts ✓

c. Myoglobinuria

d. Acute kidney injury

Answer: b

Rhabdomyolysis gives high CK, myoglobinuria and AKI (pigmented granular casts). WBC casts point to pyelonephritis or interstitial nephritis.

Key point: WBC casts are not a rhabdomyolysis feature.

qs.q: Which of the following factors suggests that a patient has established acute tubular necrosis (ATN) rather than pre-renal uraemia?
qs.a:
a. Urine sodium = 10 mmol/L

b. Fractional urea excretion = 20%

c. Increase in urine output following fluid challenge

d. Specific gravity = 1025

e. Fractional sodium excretion = 1.5% ✓

Answer: e

FeNa 1.5% is above the prerenal cut-off but below the ATN threshold, so it is the value that tilts toward ATN among the options. The key is that FeNa is more than 1% and no fluid response occurs. ⚠️ The source point is grey: 1.5% sits between the cut-offs, so review the question.

Key point: FeNa > 1% → ATN (grey zone at 1–2%).

qs.q: A 72-year-old woman was admitted with pneumonia five days ago and has since developed diarrhoea and oliguria. Her creatinine has increased from 98 to 172 µmol/L. Which test is most useful in differentiating pre-renal uraemia from acute tubular necrosis?
qs.a:
a. Serum urea level

b. Haemoglobin concentration

c. Plasma osmolality

d. Urinary urea

e. Urinary sodium ✓

Answer: e

Urinary sodium separates them: pre-renal kidneys conserve sodium (urine Na <20, FENa <1%); in ATN damaged tubules waste sodium (urine Na >40).

Key point: Pre-renal vs ATN → urinary sodium / FENa.

qs.q: In acute renal failure, dietary protein should be restricted in which of the following situations?
qs.a:
a. All patients

b. All patients with BUN above 100

c. All patients with creatinine above 10

d. Only in patients who are well nourished on hospital admission

e. If azotemia is advanced and dialysis is not an option ✓

Answer: e

Protein restriction in AKI is only considered when azotemia is advanced and dialysis is not an option; otherwise patients need adequate protein because AKI is catabolic.

Key point: AKI: don't restrict protein unless dialysis isn't possible.

qs.q: A patient develops acute kidney injury shortly after receiving iodinated contrast during an imaging procedure. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Pre-renal AKI

b. Contrast-associated AKI ✓

c. Acute interstitial nephritis

d. Post-renal AKI

Answer: b

AKI shortly after iodinated contrast = contrast-associated AKI.

Key point: Recent contrast + AKI = contrast nephropathy.

qs.q: Which is correct regarding thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP)?
qs.a:
a. It is caused by factor VIII deficiency

b. It is caused by ADAMTS13 deficiency or inhibition ✓

c. It is caused by antibodies against platelet factor 4

d. It presents with normal platelet count

Answer: b

TTP is caused by deficiency or inhibition (autoantibodies) of ADAMTS13, so ultra-large vWF multimers cause platelet microthrombi. Low platelets are typical; anti-PF4 antibodies cause HIT.

Key point: TTP = ADAMTS13 deficiency.

qs.q: AKI after cardiac catheterization with epigastric pain and diminished peripheral pulses suggests:
qs.a:
a. Contrast-induced nephropathy

b. Acute interstitial nephritis

c. Post-streptococcal GN

d. Atheroembolic renal disease (cholesterol emboli) ✓

Answer: d

After catheterisation, AKI with abdominal pain and reduced peripheral pulses/blue toes suggests cholesterol emboli (atheroembolic renal disease).

Key point: Post-catheter AKI + ischaemic signs = cholesterol emboli.

qs.q: A 10-year-old boy is admitted to hospital with diarrhoea and lethargy. There is a known local outbreak of E. coli O157:H7, and his initial blood tests show evidence of acute renal failure. Which investigation result would be expected?
qs.a:
a. Increased prothrombin time

b. Thrombocytosis

c. Fragmented red blood cells ✓

d. Right shift of the white blood cells

e. Raised serum haptoglobin

Answer: c

E. coli O157:H7 (Shiga toxin) causes haemolytic uraemic syndrome: microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia with fragmented red cells (schistocytes), thrombocytopenia and AKI. PT is normal, platelets are low and haptoglobin is low.

Key point: HUS triad: MAHA (schistocytes) + low platelets + AKI.

qs.q: Hyperkalemic renal tubular acidosis is type:
qs.a:
a. Type II (proximal)

b. Type I (distal)

c. Type IV ✓

d. Type III (mixed)

Answer: c

Type IV RTA (hypoaldosteronism / aldosterone resistance, common in diabetics) is the hyperkalaemic RTA. Types I and II cause hypokalaemia.

Key point: Type 4 RTA = hyperkalaemic.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the metabolic acidosis seen in RTA?
qs.a:
a. High–anion-gap metabolic acidosis

b. Normal–anion-gap metabolic acidosis ✓

c. Mixed anion-gap and non–anion-gap metabolic acidosis

d. Metabolic alkalosis

Answer: b

All RTAs cause a normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis, because the problem is bicarbonate loss or failure of acid excretion, not an added unmeasured acid.

Key point: RTA = normal anion gap, hyperchloraemic acidosis.

qs.q: A case of prolonged analgesic abuse and kidney impairment. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Chronic interstitial nephritis ✓

b. Renal tubular acidosis

c. Acute tubular necrosis

d. IgA nephropathy

Answer: a

Long-term analgesic abuse causes chronic interstitial nephritis with papillary necrosis (analgesic nephropathy).

Key point: Analgesic abuse → chronic interstitial nephritis.

qs.q: A young male with intermittent flank pain and hypertension has kidney impairment; his father died from subarachnoid hemorrhage. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. ADPKD (autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease) ✓

b. IgA nephropathy

c. Medullary cystic kidney disease

d. Simple renal cyst

Answer: a

A young man with flank pain, hypertension and renal impairment whose father died of subarachnoid haemorrhage (berry aneurysm) = autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.

Key point: Flank pain + HTN + family SAH = ADPKD.

qs.q: All of the following are true about acquired cystic kidney disease EXCEPT:
qs.a:
a. It is not associated with cancer ✓

b. It occurs in long-term dialysis patients

c. It causes multiple bilateral cysts

d. It is usually asymptomatic

Answer: a

Acquired cystic kidney disease develops in long-term dialysis patients (bilateral multiple cysts, often asymptomatic) and IS associated with renal cell carcinoma — so 'not associated with cancer' is false.

Key point: Acquired cystic disease on dialysis ↑ risk of RCC.

qs.q: A patient with flank pain has a renal cyst on imaging and everything else is normal. The diagnosis is:
qs.a:
a. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease

b. Simple renal cyst ✓

c. Acquired cystic kidney disease

d. Renal cell carcinoma

Answer: b

A single cyst with everything else normal is a simple renal cyst — common and benign. ADPKD gives multiple bilateral cysts and a family history.

Key point: Single cyst, normal kidneys = simple cyst.

qs.q: The most common cause of acute interstitial nephritis is:
qs.a:
a. Glomerular immune complex deposition

b. Prolonged hypotension

c. Drug allergy (hypersensitivity) ✓

d. Urinary tract obstruction

Answer: c

Drug hypersensitivity (penicillins, NSAIDs, PPIs, diuretics, allopurinol) is the commonest cause of acute interstitial nephritis.

Key point: AIN commonest cause = drugs.

qs.q: Which of the following is a complication of polycystic kidney disease OUTSIDE the kidney?
qs.a:
a. Pulmonary fibrosis

b. Sensorineural hearing loss

c. Intracranial berry aneurysm ✓

d. Optic neuritis

Answer: c

Extrarenal ADPKD complications: intracranial berry aneurysms (SAH), liver cysts, mitral valve prolapse, colonic diverticula and hernias.

Key point: ADPKD outside the kidney: berry aneurysm, liver cysts, MVP.

qs.q: What is the main cause of death in polycystic kidney disease?
qs.a:
a. Renal failure and its cardiovascular complications ✓

b. Hepatic failure from liver cysts

c. Malignant transformation of cysts

d. Cyst rupture

Answer: a

Most ADPKD patients die from end-stage renal failure and its cardiovascular complications (hypertension, LVH, coronary disease); SAH is a less common cause.

Key point: ADPKD death: renal failure + cardiovascular disease.

qs.q: A 12-year-old boy had a strep infection 1 week ago and received ampicillin. He now has fever, morbilliform rash, abnormal kidney function, hematuria, WBC casts and eosinophiluria (ASOT positive). The diagnosis is:
qs.a:
a. Acute tubular necrosis

b. Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) ✓

c. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

d. IgA nephropathy

Answer: b

Fever, rash, eosinophiluria, WBC casts and AKI after a beta-lactam (ampicillin) = drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis. Post-strep GN would show RBC casts after 1–3 weeks without rash/eosinophilia.

Key point: Drug + fever + rash + eosinophiluria = AIN.

qs.q: A patient with chronic interstitial nephritis presents for treatment. What is the treatment?
qs.a:
a. Stop offending drug ✓

b. Give corticosteroids

c. Dialysis

d. IV fluids

Answer: a

Management of interstitial nephritis starts with stopping the offending drug/toxin; steroids may help acute drug-induced cases.

Key point: Interstitial nephritis: remove the cause.

qs.q: A patient with polycystic kidney disease presents for evaluation. What is the first investigation?
qs.a:
a. Renal ultrasound ✓

b. Renal biopsy

c. CT scan

d. MRI

Answer: a

Renal ultrasound is the first-line, cheap and radiation-free test for polycystic kidney disease and is used for screening relatives.

Key point: ADPKD: ultrasound first.

qs.q: A patient with adult-type polycystic kidney disease presents. Which of the following is correct regarding inheritance?
qs.a:
a. Autosomal dominant ✓

b. Autosomal recessive

c. X-linked dominant

d. X-linked recessive

Answer: a

Adult-type polycystic kidney disease is autosomal dominant (PKD1 on chromosome 16, PKD2 on chromosome 4). The infantile type is autosomal recessive.

Key point: Adult PKD = autosomal dominant.

qs.q: A patient with polycystic kidney disease presents. Which investigation confirms the diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Ultrasound ✓

b. Renal biopsy

c. CT scan

d. MRI

Answer: a

Ultrasound confirms ADPKD by showing multiple bilateral cysts (age-specific criteria). CT/MRI are for complications or volume measurement; biopsy is not needed.

Key point: ADPKD diagnosis = ultrasound.

qs.q: A patient with polycystic kidney disease presents with abdominal or flank pain and haematuria. What is the clinical finding?
qs.a:
a. Hypertension (HTN)

b. Haematuria

c. asymptomatic

d. all of the above ✓

Answer: d

ADPKD may be asymptomatic, or present with hypertension, haematuria (cyst rupture), flank/abdominal pain, stones and infection — all of the listed findings occur.

Key point: ADPKD: pain, haematuria, HTN — or no symptoms.

qs.q: Which is the function of the kidney?
qs.a:
a. Maintains homeostasis ✓

b. Produces bile

c. Produces insulin

d. Stores glycogen

Answer: a

The kidney maintains homeostasis: water, electrolytes, acid–base, blood pressure, waste excretion and hormones (EPO, calcitriol, renin). Bile, insulin and glycogen storage are liver/pancreas functions.

Key point: Kidney = homeostasis organ.

qs.q: A patient with a palpable right mass and a palpable left smaller mass, his father died of renal failure and his uncle has a renal transplant. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Renal cell carcinoma

b. PCKD ✓

c. Simple cyst

d. Nephrolithiasis

Answer: b

Bilateral palpable kidneys with a family history of renal failure and transplantation = polycystic kidney disease (autosomal dominant).

Key point: Bilateral kidney masses + family history = PCKD.

qs.q: The most common presentation of PCKD is:
qs.a:
a. HTN & Hematuria ✓

b. Oliguria

c. Edema

d. Proteinuria

Answer: a

PCKD commonly presents with hypertension and haematuria (with flank pain). Oedema and heavy proteinuria are not typical.

Key point: PCKD: HTN + haematuria.

qs.q: Which of the following is not a clinical manifestation of PCKD?
qs.a:
a. Periorbital edemaE ✓

b. Hematuria

c. Hypertension

d. Flank pain

Answer: a

Periorbital oedema is a nephrotic/nephritic feature, not PCKD. PCKD gives haematuria, hypertension and flank pain.

Key point: No periorbital oedema in PCKD.

qs.q: A man with PCKD complains of dysuria, loin pain and heaviness:
qs.a:
a. Cyst infection ✓

b. Renal stone

c. Renal cell carcinoma

d. Urinary tract infection

Answer: a

In PCKD, fever-free dysuria with loin pain and heaviness fits infection of a cyst (cyst infection), which needs lipid-soluble antibiotics such as quinolones.

Key point: PCKD + loin pain + urinary symptoms → cyst infection.

qs.q: Which indicates a prerenal cause?
qs.a:
a. Postural hypotension ✓

b. Hypertension

c. Hyperkalemia

d. Metabolic alkalosis

Answer: a

Pre-renal AKI is due to reduced perfusion — postural hypotension is a sign of volume depletion.

Key point: Postural hypotension → pre-renal.

qs.q: A 68-year-old woman has used large amounts of analgesics for years to relieve severe headaches and arthritis. She now has an elevated urea and creatinine consistent with chronic renal failure. Which of the following changes in the kidney is most likely seen with her diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Glomerulosclerosis

b. Chronic interstitial nephritis ✓

c. Cortical necrosis

d. Nephrolithiasis

Answer: b

Long-term high-dose analgesic (phenacetin/NSAID) use causes analgesic nephropathy: chronic tubulointerstitial injury with papillary necrosis.

Key point: Analgesics → chronic interstitial nephritis.

qs.q: A 43-year-old man has just been diagnosed with polycystic kidney disease and is keen to know about potential risks or associated health problems. Which of the following is not an extrarenal complication of polycystic kidney disease?
qs.a:
a. Bladder diverticuli ✓

b. Cerebral aneurysms

c. Hepatic cysts

d. Mitral valve prolapse

e. Pancreatic cysts

Answer: a

Extrarenal ADPKD features include cerebral aneurysms, hepatic and pancreatic cysts, mitral valve prolapse and colonic diverticula — but not bladder diverticula.

Key point: ADPKD: colonic (not bladder) diverticula.

qs.q: A 68-year-old woman develops malaise and a low-grade fever. She has no rash and appears euvolaemic. She takes atorvastatin, omeprazole, amlodipine and digoxin regularly and takes ibuprofen intermittently. Urinalysis shows some leucocytes but no casts, haematuria or proteinuria. She has a creatinine of 320 µmol/L (3.62 mg/dL), which has been 68 µmol/L (0.77 mg/dL) 1 year previously. What is the likely cause of renal injury?
qs.a:
a. Acute interstitial nephritis ✓

b. ATN due to rhabdomyolysis

c. Glomerulonephritis

d. Pre-renal injury due to NSAIDs

e. Urinary obstruction

Answer: a

New-onset AKI with sterile leucocyturia in a patient on omeprazole (a PPI) and intermittent NSAIDs, euvolaemic and without casts or haematuria, is most likely acute interstitial nephritis. PPIs are a common modern cause, and rash/eosinophilia are often absent.

Key point: PPI or NSAID + sterile pyuria + AKI = AIN (rash often absent).

qs.q: Which of the following is a well-known cause of chronic interstitial nephritis?
qs.a:
a. Analgesic nephropathy ✓

b. Acute glomerulonephritis

c. Minimal change disease

d. Renal artery stenosis

Answer: a

Analgesic nephropathy (chronic NSAID/phenacetin use) is a classic cause of chronic interstitial nephritis with papillary necrosis.

Key point: Chronic interstitial nephritis ← analgesics.

qs.q: Which of the following statements about ADPKD is INCORRECT?
qs.a:
a. Most patients require dialysis within two years of diagnosis. ✓

b. It can present with hypertension.

c. Intracranial aneurysms may occur.

d. It can occur without a positive family history.

Answer: a

ADPKD progresses slowly; most patients reach ESRD in their 50s–60s, not within two years of diagnosis — so that statement is incorrect. HTN, intracranial aneurysms and de novo mutations (no family history) all occur.

Key point: ADPKD progresses slowly over decades.

qs.q: Which chromosome is associated with the PKD1 gene responsible for ADPKD?
qs.a:
a. Chromosome 18, long arm

b. Chromosome 22, long arm

c. Chromosome 16, long arm

d. Chromosome 16, short arm ✓

Answer: d

PKD1 lies on the short arm of chromosome 16 (16p13.3) and causes ~85% of ADPKD; PKD2 is on chromosome 4.

Key point: PKD1 = 16p · PKD2 = chromosome 4.

qs.q: Which investigation compares serum creatinine with urinary creatinine excretion over 24 hours to assess renal function?
qs.a:
a. Serum urea

b. Creatinine clearance ✓

c. Serum uric acid

d. Urinary albumin

Answer: b

Creatinine clearance compares a 24-hour urinary creatinine excretion with serum creatinine to estimate GFR: CrCl = (U × V) / P.

Key point: Creatinine clearance = 24-h urine creatinine vs serum creatinine.

qs.q: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease type 2 (ADPKD type 2) is associated with a gene defect in which chromosome?
qs.a:
a. Chromosome 4 ✓

b. Chromosome 8

c. Chromosome 12

d. Chromosome 16

e. Chromosome 20

Answer: a

⚠️ The source prints no key; answer chosen from the lecture. PKD2, coding polycystin-2, lies on chromosome 4. It causes about 15% of ADPKD with milder, later disease.

Key point: PKD2 = chromosome 4, milder.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT associated with adult polycystic kidney disease (APKD)?
qs.a:
a. Hepatomegaly

b. Hypertension

c. Subarachnoid haemorrhage

d. Urinary tract infection

e. Renal cell carcinoma ✓

Answer: e

⚠️ The source prints no key; answer chosen from the lecture. ADPKD is associated with hepatomegaly (liver cysts), hypertension, SAH and UTI or cyst infection. It does not carry a specifically increased risk of renal cell carcinoma.

Key point: ADPKD does not specifically raise RCC risk.

qs.q: Which of the following statements about polycystic kidney disease is TRUE?
qs.a:
a. Polycystic kidney disease is an autosomal recessive disorder linked to a causative gene on the short arm of chromosome 16.

b. Erythropoietin levels are often low due to progressive renal failure.

c. Chronic diverticular disorder is a rare finding.

d. Nephrotic-range proteinuria is an uncommon finding. ✓

e. Intracranial saccular aneurysms have no specific association with polycystic kidney disease.

Answer: d

⚠️ The source prints no key; answer chosen from the lecture. In PKD, proteinuria is usually mild; nephrotic-range proteinuria is uncommon. PKD is autosomal dominant, erythropoietin is often preserved or high (polycythaemia), diverticular disease is common, and berry aneurysm is a specific association.

Key point: PKD: mild proteinuria, EPO preserved, diverticula common.

qs.q: Which of the following is an extrarenal complication of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD)?
qs.a:
a. Hepatic cysts ✓

b. Renal stones

c. Renal papillary necrosis

d. Renal tubular acidosis

Answer: a

Hepatic cysts are the commonest extrarenal manifestation of ADPKD. Stones occur but are renal; papillary necrosis and RTA are not ADPKD features.

Key point: Commonest extrarenal ADPKD = liver cysts.

qs.q: What is the most common presenting symptom of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD)?
qs.a:
a. Flank or abdominal pain ✓

b. Severe oliguria

c. Nephrotic syndrome

d. Dysuria

Answer: a

Flank or abdominal pain (cyst enlargement, bleeding, stones, infection) is the most common presenting symptom of ADPKD.

Key point: ADPKD presents with flank pain.

qs.q: Most common complication of dialysis in a diabetic patient:
qs.a:
a. Hypotension ✓

b. Disequilibrium syndrome

c. Air embolism

d. Peritonitis

Answer: a

Hypotension is the commonest complication of haemodialysis, especially in diabetics (autonomic neuropathy, impaired vasoconstriction).

Key point: Dialysis + diabetic → hypotension (commonest).

qs.q: Criteria for hemodialysis include:
qs.a:
a. Hyperkalemia that is responding to treatment

b. Uremic encephalopathy ✓

c. Metabolic acidosis that is responding to treatment

d. Mild anemia

Answer: b

Uraemic encephalopathy is a true indication for dialysis. Hyperkalaemia and acidosis count only when they do NOT respond to medical treatment.

Key point: Dialysis for REFRACTORY K/acidosis/fluid + uraemic encephalopathy/pericarditis.

qs.q: A diabetic patient underwent dialysis, then developed hypotension, headache, confusion, and seizures; CT confirms brain edema. What is the cause of the complication?
qs.a:
a. Hypotension

b. Disequilibrium syndrome ✓

c. Air embolism

d. Access infection

Answer: b

Headache, confusion, seizures and brain oedema after dialysis = dialysis disequilibrium syndrome, from rapid urea removal causing water shift into the brain.

Key point: Brain oedema after dialysis = disequilibrium.

qs.q: Which of the following peritoneal fluid findings confirm peritoneal dialysis peritonitis?
qs.a:
a. Cell count more than 100/mm³ with neutrophils more than 50% ✓

b. Cell count less than 100/mm³ with neutrophils less than 50%

c. Cell count less than 100/mm³ with neutrophils more than 50%

d. Cell count more than 100/mm³ with neutrophils less than 50%

Answer: a

PD peritonitis is diagnosed by effluent white cells > 100/mm³ with > 50% neutrophils (plus cloudy fluid, pain, and a positive culture).

Key point: PD peritonitis: WBC > 100, neutrophils > 50%.

qs.q: A patient on peritoneal dialysis develops complications. What should she be expected to have?
qs.a:
a. Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome

b. Peritonitis ✓

c. Air embolism

d. Vascular access thrombosis

Answer: b

The characteristic complication of peritoneal dialysis is peritonitis (cloudy fluid, abdominal pain). The other options are haemodialysis complications.

Key point: PD → peritonitis.

qs.q: A patient with non-specific symptoms and serum creatinine 9 mg/dL. What is the next step?
qs.a:
a. Repeat creatinine after one month

b. Start oral corticosteroids

c. Initiate dialysis ✓

d. Do nothing and observe

Answer: c

Creatinine 9 mg/dL with uraemic symptoms indicates advanced/end-stage kidney failure — dialysis is indicated (after checking hyperkalaemia, acidosis, fluid overload).

Key point: Symptomatic very high creatinine = start dialysis.

qs.q: A patient with acute kidney injury has been anuric for 12 hours despite fluid challenges. Potassium is 5.2 mmol/L, urea is very high and a pericardial rub is audible. The patient appears euvolaemic. A decision is made to commence haemodialysis due to concerns regarding uraemia and specifically uraemic pericarditis. What will the first dialysis session involve?
qs.a:
a. A large surface area dialyser

b. A short 2-hour session initially ✓

c. Heparin anticoagulation

d. High blood flow rate of 400 ml/min

e. Ultrafiltration of 2 L (fluid removal)

Answer: b

The first session in a very uraemic patient is short (about 2 hours) with low blood flow and a small dialyser. A rapid fall in urea causes dialysis disequilibrium (cerebral oedema). In pericarditis, heparin is avoided because of pericardial bleeding risk, and a euvolaemic patient does not need fluid removed.

Key point: First dialysis: short, slow, small; no heparin in pericarditis.

qs.q: A patient is taking a statin, diuretics, and 3 anti-hypertensive drugs. What is the cause of death in renal dialysis patients?
qs.a:
a. Occult malignancy

b. GIT bleeding

c. Pulmonary embolism

d. Cardiovascular ✓

Answer: d

Cardiovascular disease is the commonest cause of death in dialysis patients (accelerated atherosclerosis, LVH, arrhythmia, sudden death).

Key point: Dialysis patient dies of → cardiovascular.

qs.q: Which of the following is a common complication of hemodialysis in diabetic patients?
qs.a:
a. Hypotension ✓

b. Hypercalcemia

c. Hyperthyroidism

d. Polycythemia

Answer: a

Intradialytic hypotension is the commonest haemodialysis complication, especially in diabetics (autonomic neuropathy, poor vascular reactivity).

Key point: Diabetic on HD → hypotension.

qs.q: Which of the following is not an absolute contraindication for renal transplant?
qs.a:
a. Active infection

b. Active glomerulonephritis

c. Hepatitis C chronicity ✓

d. Overt hepatitis

Answer: c

Chronic hepatitis C reduces graft and patient survival, but is not an absolute contraindication; it can be treated with antivirals. Active infection, active glomerulonephritis and overt (active) hepatitis are absolute contraindications.

Key point: Not absolute CI: chronic HCV. Absolute: active infection, active malignancy, HIV (old teaching), active GN.

qs.q: A patient undergoing peritoneal dialysis presents with abdominal pain and increased leucocyte count in peritoneal fluid. What is the diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Peritonitis ✓

b. Pancreatitis

c. Appendicitis

d. Cholecystitis

Answer: a

Abdominal pain with a raised leucocyte count (>100/µL, mostly neutrophils) in PD effluent = PD peritonitis.

Key point: PD + cloudy fluid/WBC >100 = peritonitis.

qs.q: A patient develops severe metabolic acidosis, hyperkalemia and renal failure. Which treatment may be required?
qs.a:
a. Oral iron

b. Calcium supplementation

c. Hemodialysis ✓

d. Erythropoietin

Answer: c

Severe metabolic acidosis and hyperkalaemia from renal failure that do not respond to medical treatment are indications for haemodialysis.

Key point: Refractory acidosis/hyperkalaemia → dialysis.

qs.q: Which of the following is an indication for dialysis?
qs.a:
a. Refractory hyperkalemia ✓

b. Mild anemia

c. Mild hypertension

d. Asymptomatic proteinuria

Answer: a

Dialysis indications (AEIOU): refractory Acidosis, Electrolytes (hyperkalaemia), Intoxications, fluid Overload, Uraemic complications. Mild anaemia, mild HTN or proteinuria are not indications.

Key point: Dialysis: AEIOU.

qs.q: Which of the following is an indication for urgent dialysis?
qs.a:
a. Uremic pericarditis ✓

b. Mild anemia

c. Asymptomatic azotemia

d. Mild proteinuria

Answer: a

Uraemic pericarditis is an urgent dialysis indication (risk of tamponade). Mild anaemia, asymptomatic azotaemia and mild proteinuria are not.

Key point: Uraemic pericarditis → urgent dialysis.

qs.q: A patient on peritoneal dialysis develops abdominal pain and fever. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
qs.a:
a. Comparison of abdominal fluid amylase with serum amylase activity

b. Gram stain of peritoneal fluid ✓

c. Ultrasonography of the abdomen

d. CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis

Answer: b

Abdominal pain and fever on PD = PD peritonitis. First step: send effluent for cell count, Gram stain and culture, then start intraperitoneal antibiotics.

Key point: PD peritonitis → effluent count + Gram + culture.

qs.q: Which of the following statements about the differences between peritoneal dialysis (PD) and haemodialysis (HD) is TRUE?
qs.a:
a. PD requires a more restrictive diet than HD.

b. PD enables a more efficient transfer of solutes than HD.

c. PD may be performed less frequently than HD.

d. Symptomatic fluid shift is less common with PD than HD. ✓

e. Previous abdominal surgery is more likely to impede HD than PD.

Answer: d

PD is slow and continuous, so fluid and solute shifts are gentle: less hypotension and disequilibrium than HD.

Key point: PD = gentle, daily; HD = efficient, 3×/week.

qs.q: Mixed cryoglobulinemia is associated with:
qs.a:
a. HCV ✓

b. HBV

c. HIV

d. Cytomegalovirus

Answer: a

Mixed cryoglobulinaemia is most strongly associated with hepatitis C infection.

Key point: Cryoglobulinaemia ↔ HCV.

qs.q: A known case of rheumatoid arthritis for 15 years on methotrexate & sulfa for 3 years presented with severe weakness, loss of appetite, breathlessness, swelling of legs, face and abdomen. On exam: puffy face, marked anemia, pitting lower limb edema, BP 160/110 mmHg, pulse 76/min. Serum creatinine 2, BUN 30, albumin 2.8, total cholesterol 375, protein +++. What is the diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Nephritic

b. Nephrotic ✓

c. Renal tubular acidosis

d. Goodpasture syndrome

Answer: b (no answer in the file — suggested)

Albumin 2.8, cholesterol 375, protein +++ and generalised oedema = nephrotic syndrome (in RA, consider secondary amyloidosis or drug-induced membranous nephropathy). The file gives no key; nephrotic is the clear answer from the data.

Key point: Oedema + low albumin + high lipids + heavy proteinuria = nephrotic.

qs.q: A case of low back pain, bony pain and trivial falls with renal affection:
qs.a:
a. Multiple myeloma ✓

b. Primary osteoporosis

c. Osteomalacia

d. Hodgkin lymphoma

Answer: a

Bone pain, pathological fractures/falls and renal impairment in an older patient = multiple myeloma (lytic lesions, light-chain cast nephropathy, hypercalcaemia).

Key point: Bone pain + renal failure → myeloma.

qs.q: A case of malar rash, photosensitivity then developed renal affection. What is the diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Lupus nephritis ✓

b. IgA nephropathy

c. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

d. Minimal change disease

Answer: a

Malar rash and photosensitivity point to SLE; renal involvement is lupus nephritis.

Key point: Malar rash + renal disease = lupus nephritis.

qs.q: Specific biopsy findings for diabetic nephropathy?
qs.a:
a. Eosinophilic nodules called nodular glomerulosclerosis ✓

b. Diffuse thickening of glomerular basement membrane

c. Focal thickening and sclerosing of the basement membrane

d. Spike and dome appearance of the basement membrane

Answer: a

Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules (nodular intercapillary glomerulosclerosis) are specific for diabetic nephropathy.

Key point: Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules = diabetic nephropathy.

qs.q: A patient with multiple myeloma (plasma cell dyscrasia) is at risk of:
qs.a:
a. Amyloidosis ✓

b. Glomerulonephritis

c. Pyelonephritis

d. Nephrolithiasis

Answer: a

Plasma cell dyscrasias produce light chains that can deposit as AL amyloid, causing nephrotic syndrome; myeloma also causes cast nephropathy.

Key point: Myeloma → AL amyloidosis.

qs.q: Which condition does NOT cause hemoptysis with renal involvement?
qs.a:
a. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (ANCA)

b. Microscopic polyangiitis (ANCA)

c. IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease) ✓

d. Goodpasture syndrome

Answer: c

IgA nephropathy affects only the kidney. ANCA vasculitis (GPA, MPA) and Goodpasture's cause pulmonary haemorrhage with GN.

Key point: Not pulmonary–renal: IgA nephropathy.

qs.q: IgG is raised (about 1600 mg/dL) while all other immunoglobulins are normal. The most likely diagnosis is:
qs.a:
a. Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) ✓

b. Multiple myeloma

c. Waldenström macroglobulinemia

d. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia

Answer: a

A modest isolated IgG rise with other immunoglobulins normal (no end-organ damage) fits MGUS. Myeloma usually suppresses the other immunoglobulins and causes CRAB features.

Key point: Small M-protein, no CRAB = MGUS.

qs.q: A patient has more than 46% plasma cells in the bone marrow. The diagnosis is:
qs.a:
a. MGUS

b. Multiple myeloma ✓

c. Waldenström macroglobulinemia

d. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia

Answer: b

Bone marrow clonal plasma cells ≥10% (here 46%) with myeloma features = multiple myeloma. MGUS has <10%.

Key point: Marrow plasma cells ≥10% → myeloma.

qs.q: A case with bone pain, hypercalcemia, renal dysfunction and anemia typical of multiple myeloma. Which investigation is needed?
qs.a:
a. PTH level

b. Serum ferritin

c. Serum protein electrophoresis ✓

d. Bone scan only

Answer: c

CRAB features (Calcium high, Renal failure, Anaemia, Bone pain) → confirm myeloma with serum protein electrophoresis (M-band), immunofixation and free light chains.

Key point: Suspected myeloma → serum protein electrophoresis.

qs.q: Which antibodies are found in antiphospholipid syndrome (APS)?
qs.a:
a. Anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm

b. Anti-Scl-70 and anti-centromere

c. Anticardiolipin, anti-β2 glycoprotein I and lupus anticoagulant ✓

d. Anti-Jo-1 and anti-Mi-2

Answer: c

APS antibodies: anticardiolipin, anti-β2 glycoprotein I and lupus anticoagulant.

Key point: APS: aCL + anti-β2GPI + lupus anticoagulant.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT a criterion for the diagnosis of SLE?
qs.a:
a. Malar rash

b. Photosensitivity

c. Positive ANA

d. Kayser-Fleischer ring ✓

Answer: d

Kayser–Fleischer rings are copper deposits of Wilson's disease, not an SLE criterion. Malar rash, photosensitivity and ANA are.

Key point: KF ring = Wilson's disease.

qs.q: Which type of anemia is included in the diagnostic criteria of SLE?
qs.a:
a. Hemolytic anemia ✓

b. Iron-deficiency anemia

c. Megaloblastic anemia

d. Aplastic anemia

Answer: a

Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (with reticulocytosis/positive Coombs) is the haematological anaemia criterion in SLE.

Key point: SLE criterion anaemia = haemolytic.

qs.q: A woman on hydroxychloroquine for SLE needs follow-up of which organ?
qs.a:
a. Liver

b. Retina (eye) ✓

c. Kidney

d. Lung

Answer: b

Hydroxychloroquine can cause retinopathy (bull's-eye maculopathy), so regular eye/retinal screening is needed.

Key point: Hydroxychloroquine → retinal screening.

qs.q: Which condition is associated with large kidney size despite advanced kidney damage?
qs.a:
a. Chronic pyelonephritis

b. Amyloidosis ✓

c. Hypertensive nephrosclerosis

d. Reflux nephropathy

Answer: b

Amyloidosis keeps kidneys large despite advanced damage.

Key point: Large kidneys + CKD = amyloidosis.

qs.q: A patient with stage V (membranous) lupus nephritis typically presents with:
qs.a:
a. Nephrotic syndrome ✓

b. Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis

c. Isolated hematuria

d. Acute nephritic syndrome

Answer: a

Class V (membranous) lupus nephritis presents with nephrotic syndrome (heavy proteinuria, edema).

Key point: Lupus class V = nephrotic.

qs.q: A patient with diabetes mellitus is at risk of developing diabetic nephropathy. Which medication can help prevent or delay its progression, particularly in the presence of albuminuria?
qs.a:
a. ACE inhibitors ✓

b. NSAIDs

c. Corticosteroids

d. Loop diuretics

Answer: a

ACE inhibitors (or ARBs) reduce intraglomerular pressure and albuminuria, delaying diabetic nephropathy progression. NSAIDs worsen renal function.

Key point: Diabetic albuminuria → ACEi/ARB.

qs.q: A patient with systemic lupus erythematosus has class V lupus nephritis (membranous lupus nephritis). What is the typical clinical presentation?
qs.a:
a. Nephrotic syndrome ✓

b. Acute nephritic syndrome

c. Isolated haematuria

d. Acute renal colic

Answer: a

Class V (membranous) lupus nephritis presents with nephrotic syndrome (heavy proteinuria, oedema), often with little haematuria.

Key point: Class V lupus nephritis = nephrotic.

qs.q: What is the commonest renal lesion in diabetic nephropathy?
qs.a:
a. Diffuse glomerulosclerosis ✓

b. Chronic interstitial nephritis

c. Arterionephrosclerosis

d. Nodular glomerulosclerosis

Answer: a

Diffuse mesangial expansion is commonest, whereas the nodular Kimmelstiel–Wilson lesion is more specific but less frequent. (Source: Kumar Ch.6 Q43)

Key point: Diffuse mesangial expansion is commonest, whereas the nodular Kimmelstiel–Wilson lesion is more specific but less frequent.

qs.q: A patient with type 1 diabetes mellitus is known to have stage 1 diabetic nephropathy. Which of the following best describes his degree of renal involvement?
qs.a:
a. Latent phase

b. Hyperfiltration ✓

c. Established renal failure

d. End-stage renal disease

Answer: b

Mogensen stage 1 = hyperfiltration (GFR raised, kidneys enlarged).

Key point: Stage 1 hyperfiltration → 2 latent → 3 micro → 4 overt → 5 ESRD.

qs.q: A 54-year-old man with end-stage diabetic nephropathy is being assessed for renal transplantation. Which HLA antigen is the most important to match between donor and recipient?
qs.a:
a. HLA-DP

b. HLA-B

c. HLA-DR ✓

d. HLA-C

e. HLA-A

Answer: c

For kidney transplantation, HLA-DR matching matters most for graft survival, followed by HLA-B and then HLA-A.

Key point: Most important HLA match = DR.

qs.q: Which one of the following is a contraindication to renal biopsy?
qs.a:
a. Haematuria

b. Kidneys less than 60% of normal size ✓

c. Anaemia

d. Rapid deterioration in renal function

e. ACE inhibitor therapy

Answer: b

Small kidneys (shrunken, chronic disease) are a contraindication to biopsy: high bleeding risk and little diagnostic benefit. Haematuria and rapid deterioration are indications.

Key point: Small kidneys → don't biopsy.

qs.q: All of the following are causes of metabolic alkalosis EXCEPT:
qs.a:
a. Massive blood transfusion

b. Vomiting

c. Renal failure ✓

d. Hypokalemia

Answer: c

Renal failure causes metabolic ACIDOSIS (failure to excrete acid). Vomiting, hypokalaemia and massive transfusion (citrate → bicarbonate) cause metabolic alkalosis.

Key point: Renal failure = acidosis, not alkalosis.

qs.q: Low serum potassium level is least likely to cause which of the following?
qs.a:
a. Muscle weakness

b. Palpitations

c. Paresthesias

d. Diarrhoea ✓

Answer: d

Hypokalaemia causes weakness, palpitations/arrhythmias, paraesthesiae and constipation/ileus — not diarrhoea (diarrhoea is a cause, not an effect).

Key point: Low K → ileus/constipation, not diarrhoea.

qs.q: Which of the following is the only source of blood cells in a normal adult?
qs.a:
a. Liver

b. Spleen

c. Bone marrow ✓

d. Lymph nodes

Answer: c

In normal adults, bone marrow is the only site of haematopoiesis. Liver and spleen produce blood only in the fetus or in extramedullary haematopoiesis.

Key point: Adult haematopoiesis = bone marrow.

qs.q: What is the normal lifespan of a red blood cell (RBC)?
qs.a:
a. 30 days

b. 60 days

c. 90 days

d. 120 days ✓

Answer: d

Red blood cells live about 120 days before removal by splenic macrophages.

Key point: RBC lifespan 120 days.

qs.q: Red cell distribution width (RDW) is usually increased in which of the following conditions?
qs.a:
a. Iron deficiency anemia ✓

b. Aplastic anemia

c. Acute blood loss

d. Hereditary spherocytosis in all cases

Answer: a

RDW (variation in red cell size) rises early in iron deficiency (anisocytosis), helping to separate it from thalassaemia trait (normal RDW).

Key point: High RDW → iron deficiency.

qs.q: What does the reticulocyte count provide information about?
qs.a:
a. Platelet production in the bone marrow

b. Erythroid activity in the bone marrow ✓

c. WBC production

d. Iron stores in the body

Answer: b

The reticulocyte count reflects erythroid activity of the marrow: high in haemolysis/bleeding, low in marrow failure or deficiency.

Key point: Reticulocytes = marrow red-cell output.

qs.q: Teardrop-shaped RBCs (dacrocytes) are classically associated with which condition?
qs.a:
a. Thalassemia

b. Myelofibrosis ✓

c. G6PD deficiency

d. Hereditary spherocytosis

Answer: b

Tear-drop cells (dacrocytes) are classic for myelofibrosis (cells squeezed out of a fibrotic marrow).

Key point: Tear-drop cells = myelofibrosis.

qs.q: In an SLE patient, the normocytic anemia is due to:
qs.a:
a. Anemia of chronic disease ✓

b. Blood loss

c. Nutritional deficiency (folate / B12)

d. Aplastic anemia

Answer: a

In chronic inflammatory disease like SLE, normocytic anaemia is usually anaemia of chronic disease (hepcidin-mediated iron trapping).

Key point: SLE normocytic anaemia → anaemia of chronic disease.

qs.q: Which of the following is a clinical feature of long-standing iron deficiency anemia?
qs.a:
a. Brittle nails and hair with spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia) ✓

b. Hair-on-end skull appearance

c. Subacute combined degeneration of the cord

d. Painful vaso-occlusive crises

Answer: a

Long-standing iron deficiency causes epithelial changes: brittle hair and nails, koilonychia (spoon nails), angular stomatitis, glossitis. Hair-on-end skull = thalassaemia; SACD = B12; vaso-occlusive crises = sickle cell.

Key point: Koilonychia → chronic iron deficiency.

qs.q: A boy diagnosed with TB, after starting anti-TB drugs, developed sudden fatigue, rapid heart rate, breathlessness and jaundice. CBC shows anemia and bite cells on the peripheral blood smear. What is the most likely cause?
qs.a:
a. Enzyme deficiency ✓

b. Globin chain deficiency

c. Abnormal hemoglobin structure

d. Membrane defect

Answer: a

Acute haemolysis with bite cells after an oxidant drug (e.g. anti-TB drugs) = G6PD deficiency, an enzyme deficiency.

Key point: Oxidant drug + bite cells = G6PD (enzyme) deficiency.

qs.q: A patient workup for unexplained hemolysis and pancytopenia reveals a deficiency of CD55 & CD59. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. PNH ✓

b. Antiphospholipid syndrome

c. Hereditary spherocytosis

d. G6PD deficiency

Answer: a

CD55 and CD59 deficiency (GPI anchor loss, PIG-A mutation) = paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria: complement-mediated haemolysis, pancytopenia and thrombosis.

Key point: CD55/CD59 deficient = PNH.

qs.q: A type 2 diabetic patient taking metformin developed neurological manifestations. Which of the following side effects of metformin causes these manifestations?
qs.a:
a. Vitamin B12 malabsorption ✓

b. Folic acid deficiency

c. Iron deficiency

d. Vitamin B6 excess

Answer: a

Long-term metformin impairs vitamin B12 absorption, which can cause peripheral neuropathy and subacute combined degeneration.

Key point: Metformin → B12 deficiency → neuropathy.

qs.q: A strict vegetarian complains of fatigue and anemia over the last 2 months. Which of the following is deficient?
qs.a:
a. Vit B12 ✓

b. Vit B6

c. Folic acid

d. Vit K

Answer: a

Vitamin B12 is found only in animal products, so strict vegans are at risk of B12 deficiency (megaloblastic anaemia).

Key point: Strict vegetarian → B12 deficiency.

qs.q: A case of bleeding with a low reticulocyte count. What does this indicate?
qs.a:
a. Inadequate bone marrow production ✓

b. Adequate erythropoiesis

c. Iron deficiency anemia

d. Hemolytic anemia

Answer: a

After bleeding the marrow should raise reticulocytes; a low count means the marrow is not responding — inadequate production (marrow suppression, lack of iron/B12/folate, or low EPO).

Key point: Anaemia + low retics = production problem.

qs.q: Which of these findings is most likely to be found in iron deficiency anemia?
qs.a:
a. Low serum ferritin and decreased iron saturation ✓

b. Low serum ferritin and decreased TIBC

c. High serum ferritin and increased iron saturation

d. High serum ferritin and decreased iron saturation

Answer: a

Iron deficiency: low ferritin (depleted stores), low serum iron and low transferrin saturation, with HIGH TIBC.

Key point: IDA: ferritin ↓, saturation ↓, TIBC ↑.

qs.q: Which finding characterizes megaloblastic anemia?
qs.a:
a. Hypersegmented neutrophils ✓

b. Teardrop cells

c. Auer rods

d. Spherocytes

Answer: a

Hypersegmented neutrophils (≥5 lobes) are characteristic of megaloblastic anaemia (B12/folate deficiency).

Key point: Hypersegmented neutrophils = megaloblastic.

qs.q: Which type of anemia rarely results from decreased dietary intake?
qs.a:
a. Iron deficiency anemia

b. Vitamin B12 deficiency ✓

c. Folate deficiency

d. Anemia of chronic disease

Answer: b

B12 stores last years and dietary lack is rare (only vegans); pernicious anaemia is the main cause.

Key point: B12 = absorption problem; folate = diet.

qs.q: Koilonychia is seen in:
qs.a:
a. Vitamin B12 deficiency

b. Long-standing iron deficiency anemia ✓

c. Hemolytic anemia

d. Aplastic anemia

Answer: b

Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails) is a sign of long-standing iron deficiency anaemia.

Key point: Spoon nails = iron deficiency.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT a complication of iron overload from chronic blood transfusion?
qs.a:
a. Pulmonary fibrosis ✓

b. Cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia

c. Liver cirrhosis

d. Diabetes mellitus

Answer: a

Transfusional iron overload deposits iron in the heart (cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia), liver (cirrhosis), pancreas (diabetes), pituitary and gonads — not in the lungs, so pulmonary fibrosis is not a complication.

Key point: Iron overload: heart, liver, pancreas, endocrine — not lungs.

qs.q: Deficiency of CD55 and CD59 is related to:
qs.a:
a. Hereditary spherocytosis

b. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia

c. Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) ✓

d. G6PD deficiency

Answer: c

Loss of the GPI-anchored complement regulators CD55 (DAF) and CD59 (MIRL) is the defect in PNH, leaving red cells open to complement lysis.

Key point: CD55/CD59 ↓ = PNH.

qs.q: A peripheral blood smear showing bite cells suggests:
qs.a:
a. Globin-chain defect (thalassemia)

b. Enzyme-deficiency anemia (G6PD deficiency) ✓

c. Abnormal hemoglobin (sickle cell)

d. Membrane defect (hereditary spherocytosis)

Answer: b

Bite cells (and Heinz bodies) form when splenic macrophages remove denatured haemoglobin after oxidant stress — classic for G6PD deficiency.

Key point: Bite cells = G6PD deficiency.

qs.q: In a case with a picture of a thalassemia patient with jaundice, what is the cause of the jaundice?
qs.a:
a. Hemolysis ✓

b. Obstructive biliary disease

c. Acute viral hepatitis

d. Hepatocellular failure

Answer: a

Jaundice in thalassaemia is unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia from haemolysis and ineffective erythropoiesis (pigment gallstones may add obstruction later).

Key point: Thalassaemia jaundice = haemolytic.

qs.q: In a case with a picture of a thalassemia patient, which investigation is used to confirm the diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Hemoglobin electrophoresis ✓

b. Osmotic fragility test

c. Ham's test

d. G6PD enzyme assay

Answer: a

Haemoglobin electrophoresis (or HPLC) confirms thalassaemia: raised HbA2 (β-trait) and HbF, absent/low HbA in major. Osmotic fragility is for spherocytosis, Ham's test for PNH.

Key point: Thalassaemia → Hb electrophoresis.

qs.q: Which of the following is a complication associated with thalassemia?
qs.a:
a. Bone marrow suppression

b. Iron deficiency

c. Iron overload (transfusion haemosiderosis) ✓

d. Polycythemia

Answer: c

Repeated transfusions and increased iron absorption cause iron overload (haemosiderosis) in thalassaemia, damaging heart, liver and endocrine glands.

Key point: Thalassaemia major → iron overload.

qs.q: A 47-year-old perimenopausal female presents with leg discomfort of three months duration. It is aggravated by sitting still and is relieved by moving her legs. Her husband reports that she kicks all night. The patient has no past medical history and is on no medication. Vital signs and exam are normal. Labs show microcytic hypochromic anemia, normal chemistry panel, and normal thyroid-stimulating hormone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Neuropathy secondary to B12 deficiency

b. Restless leg syndrome secondary to iron deficiency ✓

c. Perimenopause

d. Osteoarthritis

Answer: b

An urge to move the legs at rest, relieved by movement, with night-time kicking = restless legs syndrome; microcytic hypochromic anaemia points to iron deficiency as the cause.

Key point: Restless legs + microcytic anaemia → iron deficiency.

qs.q: A 17-year-old female patient presents to the hospital with easy fatigability. She mentioned that she has a regular menstrual cycle every 28 days lasting for 10 days. Complete blood count shows a hemoglobin of 7 mg/dL, hematocrit 40% and an MCV of 60 micrometers and serum ferritin of 25 micrograms/L. How long iron therapy should be continued after restoration of normal hematologic values to replenish iron stores?
qs.a:
a. 36 to 48 hours

b. 3 to 5 days

c. 14 to 28 days

d. 3 to 6 months ✓

Answer: d

After Hb normalises, oral iron is continued for about 3–6 months to refill body iron stores (ferritin).

Key point: Continue iron 3–6 months after Hb normalises.

qs.q: A 17-year-old woman presents to the hospital with a history of dyspnea and fatigue for a month. Her past medical history is unremarkable. Physical examination reveals pallor, scleral icterus, and jaundice. Hematocrit is 25%, total bilirubin is 7.5 mg/dl, direct bilirubin is 1.5 mg/dl, serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is 300 U/L, reticulocyte count is 7%. The direct Coombs test is positive. What is the underlying diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Hereditary spherocytosis

b. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia ✓

c. Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria

d. Sickle cell anemia

Answer: b

Haemolytic anaemia (unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, reticulocytosis, jaundice) with a positive direct Coombs test = autoimmune haemolytic anaemia.

Key point: Haemolysis + positive DAT = AIHA.

qs.q: An adult woman of Mediterranean descent has asymptomatic anemia discovered on routine lab testing. Which of the following lab values is most supportive of a diagnosis of thalassemia trait?
qs.a:
a. Low red cell count on a CBC

b. Increased hemoglobin A2 on electrophoresis ✓

c. Low ferritin

d. Increased hemoglobin A on electrophoresis

Answer: b

β-thalassaemia trait shows raised HbA2 (>3.5%) on electrophoresis, with microcytosis but normal ferritin and a relatively high red cell count.

Key point: β-thal trait = HbA2 ↑.

qs.q: Which of the following can cause macrocytosis with megaloblastic changes?
qs.a:
a. Reticulocytosis

b. Excess alcohol intake

c. Folic acid deficiency ✓

d. Chronic liver disease

Answer: c

Megaloblastic macrocytosis is caused by B12 or folate deficiency (impaired DNA synthesis). Alcohol, liver disease and reticulocytosis cause macrocytosis WITHOUT megaloblastic change.

Key point: Megaloblastic = B12/folate deficiency.

qs.q: A strict vegetarian complains of fatigue and anemia in the last 2 months. Which of the following is deficient?
qs.a:
a. Vit b12 ✓

b. Vit b6

c. Folic acid

d. Vit C

Answer: a

B12 comes only from animal foods, so strict vegetarians develop B12 deficiency.

Key point: Vegan → B12 deficiency.

qs.q: To differentiate between Thalassemia trait and iron deficiency anemia:
qs.a:
a. Increased hemoglobin A2 synthesis ✓

b. Splenomegaly

c. Low ferritin

d. High TIBC

Answer: a

Raised HbA2 identifies β-thalassaemia trait; iron deficiency has low ferritin and high TIBC with normal or low HbA2.

Key point: Thal trait vs IDA → HbA2.

qs.q: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia is?
qs.a:
a. Type I hypersensitivity

b. Type II hypersensitivity ✓

c. Type III hypersensitivity

d. Type IV hypersensitivity

Answer: b

AIHA is a type II (antibody-mediated, cytotoxic) hypersensitivity: IgG/IgM bind red cell antigens leading to destruction.

Key point: AIHA = type II hypersensitivity.

qs.q: Bone marrow aplasia in sickle cell anemia is most commonly follow infection with?
qs.a:
a. Parvovirus B19 ✓

b. H. influenza

c. Streptococcus pneumoniae

d. Salmonella

Answer: a

Parvovirus B19 infects erythroid precursors and causes aplastic crisis in chronic haemolysis.

Key point: Aplastic crisis = parvovirus B19.

qs.q: Patient takes sulfa drug and develop anemia and jaundice with peripheral blood smear shows bite cells and Heinz bodies most likely diagnosis is?
qs.a:
a. G6PD deficiency ✓

b. Spherocytosis

c. Thalassemia

d. Sickle cell anemia

Answer: a

Oxidant drug (sulfa) + haemolysis + bite cells = G6PD deficiency.

Key point: Oxidant drug + bite cells = G6PD.

qs.q: Which of the following is a characteristic manifestation of iron deficiency anemia?
qs.a:
a. Koilonychia ✓

b. Glossitis

c. Angular cheilitis

d. Pica

Answer: a

Koilonychia (spoon nails) is the classic sign of chronic iron deficiency. Glossitis and angular cheilitis also occur in B-vitamin deficiencies; pica is suggestive but less specific.

Key point: Iron deficiency hallmark: koilonychia.

qs.q: Which of the following is characteristic for macrocytic anemia:
qs.a:
a. Hypersegmented neutrophils ✓

b. Teardrop cells

c. Target cells

d. Schistocytes

Answer: a

Hypersegmented neutrophils characterise megaloblastic (macrocytic) anaemia. Tear-drop = myelofibrosis; target cells = thalassaemia/liver disease; schistocytes = MAHA.

Key point: Macrocytic/megaloblastic → hypersegmented neutrophils.

qs.q: Which of the following is correct about hereditary spherocytosis?
qs.a:
a. Deficiency of cell membrane protein spectrin ✓

b. Deficiency of G6PD

c. Abnormal hemoglobin structure

d. Iron deficiency

Answer: a

Hereditary spherocytosis is a red cell membrane cytoskeleton defect (spectrin, ankyrin, band 3), producing spherocytes that the spleen destroys.

Key point: HS = membrane protein (spectrin/ankyrin) defect.

qs.q: A 28-year-old female machinist complaining of weight loss and amenorrhea for the past year. Otherwise she's healthy. Her hemoglobin is 9 and all other labs were normal (Electrolytes, enzymes etc.,). What is the diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Hypopituitarism

b. Anorexia nervosa ✓

c. Iron deficiency anemia

d. Hyperthyroidism

Answer: b

A young woman with weight loss and amenorrhoea for a year, otherwise well with normal labs apart from mild anaemia, fits anorexia nervosa (hypothalamic amenorrhoea).

Key point: Weight loss + amenorrhoea + normal labs → anorexia nervosa.

qs.q: How to differentiate between micro, macro and normocytic anemia?
qs.a:
a. MCV ✓

b. MCH

c. MCHC

d. RDW

Answer: a

MCV (mean cell volume) classifies anaemia: <80 fL microcytic, 80–100 normocytic, >100 macrocytic.

Key point: Classify anaemia by MCV.

qs.q: Elevated stercobilinogen is caused by:
qs.a:
a. Hemolytic anemia ✓

b. Obstructive jaundice

c. Hepatitis

d. Iron deficiency

Answer: a

Haemolysis increases bilirubin production, so more stercobilinogen appears in stool (and urobilinogen in urine). Obstructive jaundice reduces stercobilinogen (pale stools).

Key point: Haemolysis → ↑ stercobilinogen.

qs.q: Which decreases iron absorption:
qs.a:
a. Tannate in tea ✓

b. Vitamin C

c. Meat

d. Gastric acid

Answer: a

Tannates in tea (and phytates, calcium) bind non-haem iron and reduce absorption. Vitamin C, meat and gastric acid increase it.

Key point: Tea tannates ↓ iron absorption.

qs.q: A 65-year-old woman presents to her GP complaining of tiredness, shortness of breath and loss of sensation in her feet. On examination she is visibly pale, has mild jaundice and glossitis. She has loss of joint position sense and vibration distally, with extensor plantar reflexes, absent ankle jerks and brisk knee jerks bilaterally. What is the most likely cause for her symptoms?
qs.a:
a. Chronic sickle cell disease

b. G6PD deficiency

c. Heart failure

d. Renal failure

e. Vitamin B12 deficiency ✓

Answer: e

Anaemia with mild jaundice (ineffective erythropoiesis), glossitis and combined dorsal column + pyramidal signs (subacute combined degeneration) = vitamin B12 deficiency.

Key point: Anaemia + glossitis + SACD = B12 deficiency.

qs.q: Which increases absorption of iron?
qs.a:
a. Vitamin C ✓

b. Tannate in tea

c. Phytates

d. Calcium

Answer: a

Vitamin C reduces ferric to ferrous iron and increases absorption; tannates, phytates and calcium decrease it.

Key point: Vitamin C ↑ iron absorption.

qs.q: Beta thalassemia is a cause of:
qs.a:
a. Microcytic Anemia ✓

b. Macrocytic Anemia

c. Normocytic Anemia

d. Hemolytic Anemia with normal MCV

Answer: a

β-thalassaemia reduces globin chain production, so cells are small and pale: microcytic hypochromic anaemia.

Key point: Thalassaemia = microcytic.

qs.q: Commonest Anemia:
qs.a:
a. Iron Deficiency Anemia ✓

b. Vitamin B12 deficiency

c. Thalassemia

d. Aplastic anemia

Answer: a

Iron deficiency anaemia is the commonest anaemia worldwide.

Key point: Commonest anaemia = iron deficiency.

qs.q: In a pregnant woman exhibiting macrocytic anemia, which nutrient deficiency is commonly associated with an increase in mean corpuscular volume (MCV)?
qs.a:
a. Iron

b. Vitamin B12

c. Folic acid ✓

d. Vitamin C

Answer: c

Folate demand rises in pregnancy, so folate deficiency is the usual cause of macrocytic (megaloblastic) anaemia in pregnancy.

Key point: Pregnancy macrocytosis → folate deficiency.

qs.q: A patient took Quinidine and hemolysis happened. Blood film shows:
qs.a:
a. Bite cells and Heinz bodies ✓

b. Target cells

c. Sickle cells

d. Spherocytes

Answer: a

Drug-induced oxidant haemolysis (e.g. quinidine, primaquine) in G6PD deficiency shows bite cells and Heinz bodies.

Key point: Oxidant drug haemolysis → bite cells + Heinz bodies.

qs.q: In Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH):
qs.a:
a. Pt will have thrombosis & hemorrhage + decrease CD55 CD59 ✓

b. Pt will have isolated anemia only

c. Pt will have splenomegaly

d. Pt will have normal complement regulation

Answer: a

PNH: CD55/CD59 deficiency leads to complement haemolysis, thrombosis (often hepatic/abdominal veins) and marrow failure (pancytopenia with bleeding).

Key point: PNH triad: haemolysis, thrombosis, cytopenias.

qs.q: A case of sickle cell Anemia:
qs.a:
a. Hyposplenism with no splenectomy (functional hyposplenism) + leg ulcers + Howell-Jolly bodies ✓

b. Splenomegaly + leg ulcers

c. Hypersplenism

d. Normal spleen function

Answer: a

Repeated splenic infarction in sickle cell anaemia leads to autosplenectomy (functional hyposplenism with Howell–Jolly bodies); leg ulcers are typical.

Key point: Sickle cell adult: autosplenectomy + Howell–Jolly bodies.

qs.q: Which condition is not typically associated with lymphocytosis?
qs.a:
a. Infectious mononucleosis

b. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)

c. Post-splenectomy state ✓

d. Pertussis infection

Answer: c

Lymphocytosis occurs in viral infections (EBV), pertussis and CLL. Post-splenectomy blood shows Howell–Jolly bodies, thrombocytosis and neutrophilia — not typically lymphocytosis.

Key point: Lymphocytosis: EBV, pertussis, CLL.

qs.q: In a case of sickle cell disease it will has:
qs.a:
a. Urine with increased hemosiderin ✓

b. Urine with decreased hemosiderin

c. Normal urine

d. Urine with increased urobilinogen only

Answer: a

Intravascular haemolysis in sickle cell disease filters haemoglobin into the urine, where tubular cells store it as haemosiderin, so urinary haemosiderin is increased.

Key point: Urinary haemosiderin ↑ = intravascular haemolysis.

qs.q: Which of the following can cause vitamin B12 deficiency?
qs.a:
a. Pernicious anemia

b. Strict vegan diet

c. Malabsorption

d. All of the above ✓

Answer: d

B12 deficiency results from pernicious anaemia (no intrinsic factor), strict vegan diet and malabsorption (ileal disease/resection, metformin).

Key point: B12 deficiency: PA, vegan diet, malabsorption.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT typically found in megaloblastic anemia?
qs.a:
a. Macrocytosis

b. Hypersegmented neutrophils

c. Megaloblasts in bone marrow

d. Microcytic red blood cells ✓

Answer: d

Megaloblastic anaemia gives macrocytosis, hypersegmented neutrophils and megaloblasts in the marrow — not microcytic cells.

Key point: Megaloblastic = macrocytic, never microcytic.

qs.q: Which of the following is a characteristic finding in megaloblastic anemia?
qs.a:
a. Hyposegmented neutrophils

b. Hypersegmented neutrophils ✓

c. Spherocytes

d. Schistocytes

Answer: b

Hypersegmented neutrophils (≥5 lobes) are the characteristic blood film finding in megaloblastic anaemia.

Key point: Hypersegmented neutrophils → B12/folate deficiency.

qs.q: Which of the following is correct regarding megaloblastic anemia?
qs.a:
a. Folate deficiency is a consequence of vitamin B12 deficiency

b. Vitamin B12 deficiency may cause neurological manifestations ✓

c. Vitamin B12 deficiency causes microcytosis

d. Folate deficiency causes peripheral neuropathy

Answer: b

B12 deficiency can cause neurological damage (SACD, neuropathy, dementia); folate deficiency does not cause neuropathy. Both are macrocytic.

Key point: Neurology → B12, not folate.

qs.q: What is the underlying defect in hereditary spherocytosis?
qs.a:
a. Deficiency of spectrin ✓

b. Deficiency of hemoglobin A

c. Deficiency of G6PD

d. Deficiency of iron

Answer: a

Hereditary spherocytosis is mainly a deficiency of the membrane protein spectrin (or ankyrin/band 3), making cells spherical and fragile.

Key point: HS = spectrin defect.

qs.q: A patient with sickle cell anemia develops acute chest syndrome. Which of the following is a characteristic feature?
qs.a:
a. Acute chest pain, fever and pulmonary infiltrates ✓

b. Isolated abdominal pain

c. Severe hematuria only

d. Isolated thrombocytopenia

Answer: a

Acute chest syndrome = new pulmonary infiltrate with chest pain, fever, cough or hypoxia in sickle cell disease; a leading cause of death.

Key point: Acute chest syndrome: chest pain + fever + new infiltrate.

qs.q: What is the most common cause of microcytic anemia?
qs.a:
a. Vitamin B12 deficiency

b. Iron deficiency anemia ✓

c. Aplastic anemia

d. Folate deficiency

Answer: b

Iron deficiency is the commonest cause of microcytic anaemia. B12/folate deficiency cause macrocytic anaemia.

Key point: Microcytic → iron deficiency first.

qs.q: What is the average lifespan of a normal RBC?
qs.a:
a. 60 days

b. 90 days

c. 120 days ✓

d. 180 days

Answer: c

Normal red cells live about 120 days.

Key point: RBC lifespan 120 days.

qs.q: A patient has pancytopenia with anemia. Which of the following is a possible diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Aplastic anemia ✓

b. Iron deficiency anemia

c. Thalassemia trait

d. Hereditary spherocytosis

Answer: a

Pancytopenia (low RBCs, WBCs and platelets) fits aplastic anaemia (marrow failure). IDA, thal trait and spherocytosis affect red cells only.

Key point: Pancytopenia → think aplastic anaemia.

qs.q: Which of the following is an early presentation of aplastic anemia?
qs.a:
a. Decrease in all three blood cell lines simultaneously

b. Decrease in one or two blood cell lines ✓

c. Isolated increase in platelets

d. Increased reticulocyte count

Answer: b

Aplastic anaemia often starts with one or two lines falling (often platelets or neutrophils) before full pancytopenia develops; reticulocytes are low.

Key point: Early aplastic anaemia: 1–2 cell lines low.

qs.q: Which type of antibody is responsible for warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia?
qs.a:
a. IgA

b. IgM

c. IgG ✓

d. IgE

Answer: c

Warm AIHA is caused by IgG antibodies active at 37°C (extravascular splenic destruction); cold AIHA is IgM.

Key point: Warm AIHA = IgG · cold = IgM.

qs.q: A patient presents with episodes of dark urine, especially in the morning. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia

b. G6PD deficiency

c. Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria ✓

d. Hereditary spherocytosis

Answer: c

Dark urine on waking (haemoglobinuria from nocturnal complement haemolysis) is the classic presentation of paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria.

Key point: Morning dark urine = PNH.

qs.q: All of the following can produce microcytic anemia EXCEPT:
qs.a:
a. Sideroblastic anemia

b. Thalassemia

c. Pernicious anemia ✓

d. Iron deficiency anemia

Answer: c

Pernicious anaemia is macrocytic (B12 deficiency).

Key point: PA = macrocytic.

qs.q: Which of the following is an inherited platelet function abnormality?
qs.a:
a. Glanzmann's thrombasthenia

b. Bernard–Soulier syndrome

c. Congenital macrothrombocytopenia

d. All of the above ✓

Answer: d

Inherited platelet function disorders include Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GPIIb/IIIa), Bernard–Soulier syndrome (GPIb) and congenital macrothrombocytopenias.

Key point: Glanzmann, Bernard–Soulier, macrothrombocytopenias.

qs.q: Which of the following is also an inherited disorder affecting platelet adhesion?
qs.a:
a. von Willebrand disease ✓

b. Iron deficiency anemia

c. Hemophilia A

d. DIC

Answer: a

von Willebrand disease is an inherited disorder of platelet ADHESION (vWF bridges platelet GPIb to collagen).

Key point: vWD = adhesion defect.

qs.q: A patient presents with joint and muscle bleeding, prolonged PTT and normal factor VIII level. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Hemophilia A

b. Hemophilia B ✓

c. von Willebrand disease

d. ITP

Answer: b

Joint/muscle bleeding with prolonged PTT and normal factor VIII means factor IX deficiency — haemophilia B.

Key point: ↑PTT + normal FVIII = haemophilia B.

qs.q: A female patient presents with heavy menstrual bleeding that does not respond to tranexamic acid or contraceptive pills. Platelet count is normal and PTT is prolonged. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. von Willebrand factor deficiency ✓

b. Hemophilia A

c. ITP

d. DIC

Answer: a

Menorrhagia resistant to tranexamic acid/pill, normal platelets and prolonged PTT in a woman = von Willebrand disease (low vWF lowers factor VIII).

Key point: Female + menorrhagia + ↑PTT, normal PLT → vWD.

qs.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with a 12-month history of heavy menstrual bleeding that has not responded to medical treatment. During the last two months, she has developed increased bleeding and bruising. Examination reveals multiple papular rashes over the buttocks and sacrum. There is no abdominal pain, joint pain or hepatosplenomegaly. Urine dipstick is normal. Laboratory investigations show Hb 12 g/dL, platelets 18,000/mm³ and WBCs 5,000/mm³. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) ✓

b. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP)

c. Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS)

d. Henoch–Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis)

Answer: a

Isolated severe thrombocytopenia (18,000) with normal Hb and WBC, normal urine, no organomegaly and mucocutaneous bleeding = immune thrombocytopenia.

Key point: Isolated low platelets in a well adult = ITP.

qs.q: Which of the following is characteristic of iron deficiency anemia?
qs.a:
a. Koilonychia ✓

b. Target cells

c. Spherocytes

d. Bite cells

Answer: a

Koilonychia (spoon nails) is characteristic of iron deficiency. Target cells = thalassaemia; spherocytes = HS/AIHA; bite cells = G6PD.

Key point: Koilonychia = iron deficiency.

qs.q: Which test is classically used to diagnose hereditary spherocytosis?
qs.a:
a. Osmotic fragility test ✓

b. Coombs test

c. Ham test

d. Sickling test

Answer: a

The osmotic fragility test (and EMA binding) diagnoses hereditary spherocytosis: spherocytes lyse in hypotonic saline. Coombs = AIHA, Ham = PNH.

Key point: HS → osmotic fragility test.

qs.q: Which of the following is a feature of sickle cell disease without previous splenectomy?
qs.a:
a. Functional hyposplenism ✓

b. Splenomegaly throughout life

c. Increased splenic function

d. No splenic changes

Answer: a

Repeated splenic infarcts cause functional hyposplenism (autosplenectomy) in sickle cell disease, even without surgery.

Key point: Sickle cell → functional hyposplenism.

qs.q: Which RBC morphology may be seen in sickle cell disease?
qs.a:
a. Target cells

b. Sickle-shaped cells

c. Both A and B ✓

d. Bite cells only

Answer: c (no answer in the file — suggested)

Sickle cell disease shows sickle cells and target cells on the film (plus Howell–Jolly bodies from hyposplenism). The file gives no key; 'both' fits the standard teaching.

Key point: Sickle film: sickle + target cells.

qs.q: A patient with sickle cell disease has increased urinary hemosiderin. What does this indicate?
qs.a:
a. Intravascular hemolysis ✓

b. Iron deficiency

c. Decreased RBC destruction

d. Vitamin B12 deficiency

Answer: a

Urinary haemosiderin means haemoglobin was filtered at the glomerulus — evidence of intravascular haemolysis.

Key point: Haemosiderinuria = intravascular haemolysis.

qs.q: Which of the following substances inhibits or decreases iron absorption?
qs.a:
a. Sugar

b. Citric acid

c. Vitamin C

d. Tannate ✓

Answer: d

Tannates (tea) inhibit iron absorption; vitamin C, citric acid and sugars enhance it.

Key point: Tannate ↓ iron absorption.

qs.q: Anemia of chronic disease is characterized by which of the following findings?
qs.a:
a. Low serum ferritin

b. Low serum iron ✓

c. Increased TIBC

d. Increased serum transferrin

Answer: b

Anaemia of chronic disease: low serum iron and low TIBC with normal/high ferritin (iron trapped by hepcidin).

Key point: ACD: iron ↓, TIBC ↓, ferritin normal/↑.

qs.q: Which of the following ferritin levels is expected in anemia of chronic disease?
qs.a:
a. Decreased serum ferritin

b. Normal or increased serum ferritin ✓

c. Absent serum ferritin

d. Extremely low serum ferritin

Answer: b

Ferritin is normal or raised in anaemia of chronic disease (iron is stored but unavailable, and ferritin is an acute-phase reactant).

Key point: ACD ferritin = normal or high.

qs.q: A patient with Crohn's disease presents with anemia. Which of the following findings helps differentiate iron deficiency anemia from anemia of chronic disease?
qs.a:
a. High ferritin level ✓

b. Increased hepcidin level

c. Low serum iron

d. Low hemoglobin level

Answer: a

A high ferritin argues for anaemia of chronic disease; a low ferritin confirms iron deficiency. Low serum iron and low Hb occur in both.

Key point: Ferritin separates IDA (low) from ACD (normal/high).

qs.q: Which of the following mechanisms plays an important role in the development of anemia of chronic disease?
qs.a:
a. Decreased hepcidin production

b. Increased hepcidin production ✓

c. Increased intestinal iron absorption

d. Increased iron release from macrophages

Answer: b

Inflammation (IL-6) increases hepcidin, which blocks ferroportin: iron absorption falls and iron stays locked in macrophages.

Key point: ACD mechanism = ↑ hepcidin.

qs.q: Which of the following is the most common cause of anemia globally?
qs.a:
a. Vitamin B12 deficiency

b. Folic acid deficiency

c. Iron deficiency anemia ✓

d. Aplastic anemia

Answer: c

Iron deficiency anaemia is the commonest anaemia globally.

Key point: Global #1 anaemia = iron deficiency.

qs.q: What is the most important cause of iron deficiency anemia in adults?
qs.a:
a. Increased iron absorption

b. Chronic blood loss ✓

c. Increased RBC destruction

d. Decreased erythropoietin production

Answer: b

In adults, iron deficiency is mainly due to chronic blood loss (menstrual, GI). In men and post-menopausal women, GI bleeding must be excluded.

Key point: Adult IDA = chronic blood loss until proven otherwise.

qs.q: Which of the following is an important cause of chronic blood loss leading to iron deficiency anemia in adults?
qs.a:
a. Menstrual blood loss

b. Gastrointestinal blood loss

c. Both A and B ✓

d. Increased dietary iron intake

Answer: c

Both menstrual and gastrointestinal blood loss are major causes of chronic blood loss leading to iron deficiency.

Key point: IDA: menstrual + GI losses.

qs.q: Which of the following is usually required during pregnancy to prevent nutritional anemia?
qs.a:
a. Iron and folic acid ✓

b. Vitamin C only

c. Vitamin B12 only

d. Calcium and vitamin D only

Answer: a

Iron and folic acid supplements are given in pregnancy to prevent iron-deficiency and megaloblastic anaemia (folate also prevents neural tube defects).

Key point: Pregnancy: iron + folic acid.

qs.q: Which of the following deficiencies causes abnormally large red blood cells and megaloblastic anemia?
qs.a:
a. Oxygen deficiency

b. Vitamin C deficiency

c. Vitamin B12 and folic acid deficiency ✓

d. Carbon dioxide deficiency

Answer: c

Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency impair DNA synthesis, producing large red cells and megaloblastic marrow.

Key point: B12/folate deficiency → megaloblastic anaemia.

qs.q: Which of the following is the most common cause of vitamin B12 deficiency in adults in many Western populations?
qs.a:
a. Inadequate dietary intake

b. Pernicious anemia ✓

c. Chronic blood loss

d. Iron malabsorption

Answer: b

In Western populations, pernicious anaemia (autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor) is the commonest cause of B12 deficiency.

Key point: West: B12 deficiency = pernicious anaemia.

qs.q: Pernicious anemia is mainly caused by:
qs.a:
a. Excessive intrinsic factor production

b. Failure of intrinsic factor production ✓

c. Increased iron absorption

d. Increased folic acid absorption

Answer: b

Pernicious anaemia is autoimmune gastritis destroying parietal cells, so intrinsic factor is not produced and B12 cannot be absorbed.

Key point: PA = no intrinsic factor.

qs.q: Pernicious anemia is primarily associated with which of the following mechanisms?
qs.a:
a. Vitamin B12 malabsorption ✓

b. Excessive vitamin B12 excretion

c. Increased RBC destruction

d. Decreased folic acid production

Answer: a

Pernicious anaemia causes B12 malabsorption because intrinsic factor is absent.

Key point: PA = B12 malabsorption.

qs.q: Antiparietal cell antibodies are found in approximately what percentage of patients with pernicious anemia?
qs.a:
a. 10%

b. 30%

c. 50%

d. 90% ✓

Answer: d

Anti-parietal cell antibodies are found in ~90% of pernicious anaemia (sensitive but not specific); anti-intrinsic factor antibodies (~50%) are more specific.

Key point: Parietal cell Ab ~90% (sensitive) · IF Ab ~50% (specific).

qs.q: Which of the following is a common neurological complication of vitamin B12 deficiency?
qs.a:
a. Peripheral neuropathy only

b. Subacute combined degeneration ✓

c. Cerebral hemorrhage

d. Myasthenia gravis

Answer: b

Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (dorsal columns + corticospinal tracts) is the classic neurological complication of B12 deficiency.

Key point: B12 → subacute combined degeneration.

qs.q: What is the most common cause of folic acid deficiency?
qs.a:
a. Inadequate dietary intake ✓

b. Excessive vitamin B12 intake

c. Chronic blood loss

d. Increased intrinsic factor production

Answer: a

Folate stores last only months, so inadequate dietary intake (poor diet, alcoholism) is the commonest cause of folate deficiency.

Key point: Folate deficiency = poor intake.

qs.q: A red blood cell folate level below which of the following values is suggestive of folic acid deficiency?
qs.a:
a. 50 ng/mL

b. 100 ng/mL

c. 150 ng/mL ✓

d. 500 ng/mL

Answer: c

Red cell folate reflects tissue stores; a level below about 150 ng/mL suggests folate deficiency.

Key point: RBC folate <150 ng/mL = deficiency.

qs.q: Why should large doses of folic acid be avoided as the sole treatment in patients with vitamin B12 deficiency?
qs.a:
a. They cause severe iron deficiency

b. They may correct anemia while neurological damage continues to progress ✓

c. They cause hemolysis

d. They inhibit intrinsic factor production

Answer: b

Folic acid alone can correct the anaemia of B12 deficiency while the neurological damage (SACD) keeps progressing — so B12 must be replaced first.

Key point: Never give folate alone in B12 deficiency.

qs.q: Which of the following is a characteristic finding in sideroblastic anemia?
qs.a:
a. Hairy lymphoid cells

b. Ring sideroblasts in the bone marrow ✓

c. Spherocytes in peripheral blood

d. Target cells only

Answer: b

Sideroblastic anaemia shows ring sideroblasts (iron-laden mitochondria around the nucleus) on Prussian blue stain of the marrow.

Key point: Ring sideroblasts = sideroblastic anaemia.

qs.q: Which of the following substances can cause acquired sideroblastic anemia?
qs.a:
a. Lead ✓

b. Vitamin C

c. Vitamin D

d. Calcium

Answer: a

Lead poisoning inhibits haem synthesis enzymes (ALA dehydratase, ferrochelatase), causing acquired sideroblastic anaemia with basophilic stippling. Alcohol, isoniazid and copper deficiency also cause it.

Key point: Acquired sideroblastic: lead, alcohol, isoniazid.

qs.q: Which of the following is characteristic of aplastic anemia?
qs.a:
a. Hypercellular bone marrow

b. Hypocellular bone marrow ✓

c. Increased production of all blood cells

d. Increased megakaryocytes in all cases

Answer: b

Aplastic anaemia = hypocellular (fatty) bone marrow with pancytopenia.

Key point: Aplastic anaemia = empty marrow.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic finding of aplastic anemia?
qs.a:
a. Pancytopenia

b. Hypocellular bone marrow

c. Hypercellular bone marrow ✓

d. Decreased hematopoietic cells

Answer: c

Aplastic anaemia has a hypocellular (fatty) marrow with pancytopenia; a hypercellular marrow is NOT a feature (it suggests leukaemia/MDS or peripheral destruction).

Key point: Aplastic = hypocellular marrow.

qs.q: Abnormal hairy lymphoid cells in the bone marrow are characteristic of which of the following diseases?
qs.a:
a. Aplastic anemia

b. Hairy cell leukemia ✓

c. Iron deficiency anemia

d. Pernicious anemia

Answer: b

Hairy cells (B-lymphocytes with cytoplasmic projections, TRAP/CD103-positive) in marrow are characteristic of hairy cell leukaemia, which often gives a 'dry tap'.

Key point: Hairy cells = hairy cell leukaemia.

qs.q: Hereditary spherocytosis is commonly associated with a deficiency of which of the following proteins?
qs.a:
a. Hemoglobin

b. Spectrin ✓

c. Albumin

d. Fibrinogen

Answer: b

Hereditary spherocytosis is mostly due to deficiency of the membrane skeleton protein spectrin (or ankyrin/band 3).

Key point: HS ↔ spectrin.

qs.q: Which of the following tests is classically used to diagnose hereditary spherocytosis?
qs.a:
a. Osmotic fragility test ✓

b. Coombs test

c. Bleeding time

d. Prothrombin time

Answer: a

Spherocytes have less surface area per volume and lyse earlier in hypotonic saline — increased osmotic fragility diagnoses HS.

Key point: HS → ↑ osmotic fragility.

qs.q: A patient with hereditary spherocytosis develops sudden severe anemia following a viral infection. Which virus is most likely responsible?
qs.a:
a. Epstein-Barr virus

b. Parvovirus B19 ✓

c. Hepatitis B virus

d. Cytomegalovirus

Answer: b

Parvovirus B19 infects erythroid progenitors, stopping red cell production for a few days; in chronic haemolysis (HS, sickle cell) this causes an aplastic crisis.

Key point: Aplastic crisis in haemolytic anaemia = parvovirus B19.

qs.q: Which of the following is recommended before splenectomy in patients with hereditary spherocytosis?
qs.a:
a. No vaccination is required

b. Appropriate immunization against encapsulated organisms ✓

c. Antiviral therapy

d. Routine anticoagulation

Answer: b

Before splenectomy patients must be vaccinated against encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, Hib, meningococcus), ideally 2 weeks before surgery.

Key point: Pre-splenectomy: vaccinate against encapsulated bacteria.

qs.q: Which of the following may be recommended after splenectomy in patients with hereditary spherocytosis?
qs.a:
a. Lifelong penicillin prophylaxis ✓

b. Lifelong corticosteroids

c. Iron chelation therapy

d. Vitamin B12 injections

Answer: a

After splenectomy, penicillin prophylaxis (often lifelong, at least in children) protects against overwhelming post-splenectomy infection.

Key point: Post-splenectomy: penicillin prophylaxis.

qs.q: Which of the following laboratory findings is characteristic of heterozygous beta-thalassemia (beta-thalassemia trait)?
qs.a:
a. Decreased HbA2

b. Increased HbA2 ✓

c. Increased HbF only

d. Absent HbA

Answer: b

β-thalassaemia trait shows raised HbA2 (>3.5%), often with slightly raised HbF; HbA is still present.

Key point: β-thal trait = ↑ HbA2.

qs.q: Which of the following is usually true about beta-thalassemia trait?
qs.a:
a. It is usually asymptomatic ✓

b. It always requires blood transfusion

c. It causes severe anemia in all patients

d. It requires bone marrow transplantation

Answer: a

β-thalassaemia trait is usually asymptomatic with mild microcytosis and needs no transfusion; it matters for genetic counselling.

Key point: Thal trait: asymptomatic carrier.

qs.q: Which of the following radiological findings is characteristic of thalassemia major?
qs.a:
a. Ground-glass appearance

b. Hair-on-end appearance of the skull ✓
