c. Osteolytic lesions

d. Sunburst appearance

Answer: b

Marrow expansion in thalassaemia major widens the diploë and gives a 'hair-on-end' skull X-ray (also frontal bossing and maxillary overgrowth).

Key point: Hair-on-end skull = thalassaemia major.

qs.q: Which of the following is characteristic of thalassemia intermedia?
qs.a:
a. All patients are completely asymptomatic

b. It may present with moderate anemia and clinical manifestations of variable severity ✓

c. Hemoglobin is always below 6 g/dL

d. It is always associated with an alpha-chain defect

Answer: b

Thalassaemia intermedia gives moderate anaemia with variable clinical features, usually without regular transfusions — between trait and major.

Key point: Intermedia = moderate, variable.

qs.q: Sickle cell anemia is characterized by which type of hemoglobin?
qs.a:
a. HbAA

b. HbAS

c. HbSS ✓

d. HbAC

Answer: c

Sickle cell anaemia is homozygous HbSS; HbAS is sickle trait.

Key point: Sickle cell anaemia = HbSS.

qs.q: Which of the following statements about sickle cell anemia is NOT correct?
qs.a:
a. Dehydration can precipitate sickling

b. Infection can precipitate sickling

c. Hypoxia can precipitate sickling

d. Dehydration does not cause sickling ✓

Answer: d

Dehydration DOES precipitate sickling (raises HbS concentration), so the statement that it does not is incorrect. Infection and hypoxia also precipitate crises.

Key point: Sickling triggers: hypoxia, dehydration, infection, cold, acidosis.

qs.q: A patient with sickle cell anemia develops sudden severe anemia due to bone marrow aplasia. Which of the following is the most common cause?
qs.a:
a. Epstein-Barr virus

b. Parvovirus B19 ✓

c. Hepatitis C virus

d. Influenza virus

Answer: b

Parvovirus B19 is the commonest cause of aplastic crisis in sickle cell anaemia (abrupt fall in Hb with very low reticulocytes).

Key point: Sickle aplastic crisis = parvovirus B19.

qs.q: Which of the following drugs is the drug of choice for severe painful vaso-occlusive crises in sickle cell anemia?
qs.a:
a. Aspirin

b. Morphine ✓

c. Warfarin

d. Prednisolone

Answer: b

Severe vaso-occlusive pain needs strong opioid analgesia (morphine), with hydration, oxygen and warmth.

Key point: Severe sickle pain → morphine.

qs.q: Which of the following is an indication for acute blood transfusion in a patient with sickle cell anemia?
qs.a:
a. Uncomplicated mild pain crisis

b. Acute chest syndrome ✓

c. Asymptomatic sickle cell trait

d. Mild fatigue only

Answer: b

Acute chest syndrome (and stroke, splenic sequestration, aplastic crisis) is an indication for urgent transfusion/exchange transfusion. Uncomplicated pain crises do not need transfusion.

Key point: Acute chest syndrome → transfuse.

qs.q: Which of the following is associated with G6PD deficiency?
qs.a:
a. Favism

b. Heinz bodies

c. Bite cells

d. All of the above ✓

Answer: d

G6PD deficiency causes oxidant haemolysis triggered by fava beans (favism), drugs or infection, with Heinz bodies and bite cells on the film.

Key point: G6PD: favism, Heinz bodies, bite cells.

qs.q: Which of the following is the second most common red cell enzyme defect after G6PD deficiency?
qs.a:
a. Pyruvate kinase deficiency ✓

b. Hexokinase deficiency

c. Glucose-6-phosphate isomerase deficiency

d. Lactate dehydrogenase deficiency

Answer: a

Pyruvate kinase deficiency (glycolytic pathway) is the second most common red cell enzyme defect after G6PD deficiency.

Key point: #2 enzyme defect = PK deficiency.

qs.q: Which of the following peripheral blood film findings is characteristic of pyruvate kinase deficiency?
qs.a:
a. Bite cells

b. Prickle cells (echinocytes) ✓

c. Spherocytes only

d. Target cells only

Answer: b

PK deficiency produces prickle cells/echinocytes on the blood film (ATP-depleted cells). Bite cells are G6PD.

Key point: PK deficiency → prickle cells.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is correct regarding G6PD deficiency?
qs.a:
a. All patients require splenectomy

b. All patients usually require blood transfusion

c. Most patients do not require specific intervention between hemolytic episodes ✓

d. All patients require lifelong corticosteroids

Answer: c

Between episodes most G6PD-deficient people are well and need no treatment — only avoidance of triggers. Splenectomy, steroids and routine transfusion are not needed.

Key point: G6PD: avoid triggers; nothing between attacks.

qs.q: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia is usually mediated by which type of immunoglobulin?
qs.a:
a. IgA

b. IgG ✓

c. IgM

d. IgE

Answer: b

Warm AIHA is mediated by IgG active at body temperature, causing extravascular splenic destruction (spherocytes).

Key point: Warm AIHA = IgG.

qs.q: What is the first-line treatment for warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia?
qs.a:
a. Corticosteroids ✓

b. Iron supplementation

c. Vitamin K

d. Penicillin

Answer: a

First-line treatment of warm AIHA is corticosteroids (prednisolone); rituximab or splenectomy for refractory cases.

Key point: Warm AIHA → steroids.

qs.q: Cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia is usually mediated by which type of immunoglobulin?
qs.a:
a. IgG

b. IgA

c. IgM ✓

d. IgE

Answer: c

Cold AIHA (cold agglutinin disease) is mediated by IgM, which binds at low temperatures and fixes complement.

Key point: Cold AIHA = IgM.

qs.q: Which of the following is recommended for patients with cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia?
qs.a:
a. Exposure to cold environments

b. Avoidance of cold exposure ✓

c. Routine iron chelation

d. High-dose vitamin K

Answer: b

In cold AIHA the key measure is avoiding cold exposure (keep warm, warm transfusions); steroids work poorly.

Key point: Cold AIHA → keep warm.

qs.q: Which of the following drugs is a well-recognized cause of drug-induced immune hemolytic anemia?
qs.a:
a. Cephalosporins ✓

b. Vitamin C

c. Calcium supplements

d. Folic acid

Answer: a

Drugs such as cephalosporins, penicillins and methyldopa cause drug-induced immune haemolytic anaemia (positive DAT).

Key point: Drug-induced immune haemolysis: cephalosporins, penicillin, methyldopa.

qs.q: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) is classically associated with which of the following findings?
qs.a:
a. Dark urine in the morning after waking ✓

b. Bright red urine after meals

c. Persistent proteinuria only

d. Increased urine output at night only

Answer: a

PNH classically causes dark urine on waking from haemoglobinuria (haemolysis during sleep).

Key point: PNH = morning dark urine.

qs.q: Which of the following may be found in the bone marrow of a patient with PNH?
qs.a:
a. Always hypercellular bone marrow

b. Sometimes hypoplastic or aplastic bone marrow ✓

c. Always normal bone marrow

d. Increased hairy cells

Answer: b

PNH is closely linked to marrow failure: the marrow can be hypoplastic or aplastic (PNH–aplastic anaemia overlap).

Key point: PNH may have hypoplastic marrow.

qs.q: Which of the following statements regarding corticosteroids in PNH is correct?
qs.a:
a. They are the definitive first-line treatment

b. They are routinely curative

c. They are not considered standard definitive treatment for PNH ✓

d. They prevent all thrombotic complications

Answer: c

Steroids are not definitive PNH treatment. Complement inhibitors (eculizumab) control haemolysis and thrombosis; stem cell transplant is curative.

Key point: PNH → eculizumab; transplant cures.

qs.q: Mechanical hemolytic anemia may occur in which of the following conditions?
qs.a:
a. March hemoglobinuria

b. Prosthetic heart valves

c. Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia

d. All of the above ✓

Answer: d

Mechanical (fragmentation) haemolysis occurs in march haemoglobinuria (foot-strike), prosthetic heart valves and microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (TTP/HUS/DIC).

Key point: Mechanical haemolysis: march, valves, MAHA.

qs.q: Which of the following is a typical cause of normocytic anemia?
qs.a:
a. Hereditary spherocytosis ✓

b. Iron deficiency anemia

c. Both A and B

d. Neither A nor B

Answer: a

Hereditary spherocytosis gives a normocytic (often high MCHC) haemolytic anaemia. Iron deficiency is microcytic.

Key point: HS = normocytic; IDA = microcytic.

qs.q: A 47-year-old perimenopausal woman presents with leg discomfort of three months' duration. The discomfort is aggravated by sitting still and relieved by moving her legs. Her husband reports that she kicks her legs throughout the night. She has no significant past medical history and takes no medications. Physical examination and vital signs are normal. Laboratory investigations reveal microcytic hypochromic anemia, with normal chemistry panel and thyroid-stimulating hormone levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Neuropathy secondary to vitamin B12 deficiency

b. Restless legs syndrome secondary to iron deficiency ✓

c. Perimenopause

d. Osteoarthritis

Answer: b

Leg discomfort at rest relieved by moving, with night-time kicking = restless legs syndrome; microcytic hypochromic anaemia means iron deficiency is the cause.

Key point: RLS + microcytic anaemia → iron deficiency.

qs.q: A female patient came to your clinic complaining of fatigue and palpitations for 6 months. The patient has high stress in her work. She doesn't have any dietary restrictions but she drinks 2-3L of coffee per day. She doesn't have any uterine bleeding. In CBC her Hb was 8.5 and there was microcytic erythrocytes. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the underlying condition?
qs.a:
a. Drug abuse

b. Malignancy

c. GIT loss ✓

d. Poor nutrition

e. None of the above

Answer: c

Microcytic anaemia with no menstrual loss and no dietary restriction means iron is being lost elsewhere — the GI tract (heavy coffee/stress raise suspicion of gastritis/ulcer bleeding). GI loss must be investigated.

Key point: IDA without menstrual loss → look for GI blood loss.

qs.q: A 3-year-old boy diagnosed with Thalassemia Major received multiple blood transfusions to maintain his blood volume. On physical examination the liver and spleen are mildly enlarged. All the following are correct except:
qs.a:
a. Extra-medullary hemopoiesis that caused bone marrow expansion gives the classical features of Thalassemia features

b. Splenectomy is recommended before age of 6 ✓

c. Folic acid supplements are required

d. Blood transfusion is required every 4-6 weeks

e. Bone marrow transplantation may be done if there is healthy donor and with HLA matching

Answer: b

Splenectomy in thalassaemia is delayed until AFTER about 5–6 years of age (infection risk), so 'recommended before age 6' is the incorrect statement. Marrow expansion, folate, transfusions every 3–4 weeks and HLA-matched BMT are correct.

Key point: Avoid splenectomy before ~6 years.

qs.q: A 21-year-old male patient came to clinic complaining of fatigue, recurrent infections and easily bruises, frequent epistaxis for 2 weeks. There is no history of any medical problems or medications. His temperature 36°C, blood pressure 90/60, pulse 84, respiratory rate 18. In physical examination the patient had pallor and ecchymosis, there is no hepatomegaly or splenomegaly. In labs: his Hb was 8, platelets 40,000, WBC 2.1, the bone marrow biopsy was hypocellular. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
qs.a:
a. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia

b. Idiopathic Aplastic Anemia ✓

c. Myelo-dysplastic syndrome

d. Fanconi anemia

Answer: b

Pancytopenia with infections, bruising and epistaxis, no organomegaly and a hypocellular marrow in a young adult with no drug history = idiopathic aplastic anaemia.

Key point: Pancytopenia + hypocellular marrow, no cause = idiopathic aplastic anaemia.

qs.q: A 42-year-old female complains of easily fatigue and frequent falls. She is strict vegetarian. Physical examination reveals symmetrical decrease in vibration sensation to the lower limbs. In CBC her Hb was 7.8, MCV quietly elevated. Which of the following is the best treatment for this patient?
qs.a:
a. Vitamin B12 supplements ✓

b. Iron supplements

c. Folic acid supplements

d. Vitamin C supplements

Answer: a

Strict vegetarian + macrocytic anaemia + reduced vibration sense = B12 deficiency, treated with vitamin B12 (folate alone would worsen neurology).

Key point: Vegan + neuropathy + macrocytosis → B12.

qs.q: A 7-year-old boy brought to the clinic by his parents complaining of severe pain in his extremities. He only takes acetaminophen for relief of pain. In examination his conjunctiva were pale. His CBC showed Hb 7.8, reticulocytes 15%, there was also substitution of glutamate by valine amino acid in the 6th position of beta-globin chains. The patient hemoglobin will most likely aggregate in which of these conditions?
qs.a:
a. Low O2 levels

b. Increased acidity

c. Dehydration

d. Low blood volume

e. All the above ✓

Answer: e

HbS (Glu→Val at β6) polymerises when deoxygenated; low O2, acidosis, dehydration and low blood volume all promote sickling.

Key point: Sickling: hypoxia, acidosis, dehydration.

qs.q: In G6PD deficiency, all the following is true except:
qs.a:
a. Infections and acute illnesses can precipitate hemolysis

b. Patient usually healthy without chronic hemolytic anemia or splenomegaly. The hemolysis can happen in episodes as result of oxidative stress as in infections, exposure to oxidative medications or ingestion of fava beans

c. Splenectomy is usually helpful ✓

d. Acute drug-induced hemolysis is usually dose related

Answer: c

G6PD haemolysis is intravascular and episodic, so splenectomy is NOT helpful (unlike HS). Infections, oxidant drugs (dose-related) and fava beans precipitate it.

Key point: G6PD: splenectomy doesn't help.

qs.q: In normal formation of blood cells, all are true except:
qs.a:
a. Fetal hematopoiesis doesn't place in bone marrow ✓

b. In childhood and adulthood, bone marrow is the only source of blood cells

c. Pathological process interfering with the normal hematopoiesis may result in resumption of hematopoietic activity in liver and spleen

d. Normal lifespan of RBC is 120 days

Answer: a

Fetal haemopoiesis does move to the bone marrow from about 7 months' gestation.

Key point: Yolk sac → liver/spleen → marrow (7 months).

qs.q: Reticulocytes are indicator of which of the following?
qs.a:
a. RBC destruction

b. WBC production

c. Platelets production

d. Erythroid activities and blood cells production ✓

Answer: d

Reticulocytes reflect erythroid activity and red cell production by the marrow.

Key point: Reticulocyte count = marrow RBC production.

qs.q: In hemodynamic compensation mechanism of anemia in adults, all are true except:
qs.a:
a. Slowly falling in Hb levels allows for hemodynamic compensation

b. Decreased RBC affinity to oxygen

c. Increased cardiac output through increased heart rate

d. Decreased erythropoietin secretion ✓

Answer: d

Anaemia increases erythropoietin secretion, it does not decrease it.

Key point: Compensation: 2,3-DPG, CO ↑, EPO ↑.

qs.q: The correct management of iron deficiency anemia includes:
qs.a:
a. Treat the underlying cause + give iron therapy + correct anemia and correct iron stores ✓

b. Give iron therapy and correct anemia only

c. Replace iron stores only

d. Treat the underlying cause only

Answer: a

Treat the cause, then give iron to correct Hb and refill stores.

Key point: IDA: cause + iron (Hb and stores).

qs.q: In anemia of chronic diseases, one of the most common causes of anemia:
qs.a:
a. Measuring hepcidin levels will help to distinguish anemia of chronic diseases from iron deficiency anemia

b. It is mediated through hepcidin primarily via elevated interleukin-6 (IL-6) which will cause reduced iron uptake in the gut

c. There is decreased release of iron from bone marrow to developing erythroblasts, inadequate erythropoietin response to the anemia and decreased RBC survival

d. All the following are correct ✓

Answer: d

All are correct: in ACD IL-6 raises hepcidin, which reduces gut iron absorption and iron release to erythroblasts; the EPO response is blunted and RBC survival is shortened; hepcidin can help distinguish ACD from IDA.

Key point: ACD = IL-6 → hepcidin ↑ → iron trapped.

qs.q: In aplastic anemia, all are true except:
qs.a:
a. It is a condition of bone marrow failure that arises from suppression of, or injury to, the hematopoietic stem cell

b. Bone marrow will be hypoplastic

c. Fail to produce mature blood cells and pancytopenia develops

d. Bone marrow biopsy appears hypercellular ✓

Answer: d

The marrow in aplastic anaemia is hypocellular, not hypercellular.

Key point: Aplastic = empty marrow.

qs.q: Typical features suggesting intravascular hemolysis:
qs.a:
a. When red cells are rapidly destroyed within the circulation, hemoglobin is liberated. This is initially bound to plasma haptoglobins but these soon become saturated ✓

b. Red cell destruction is extravascular

c. The red cells are removed from the circulation by macrophages in the reticuloendothelial system, particularly the spleen

d. There is hypocellular bone marrow

Answer: a

Intravascular haemolysis releases free haemoglobin into plasma, which saturates haptoglobin (then haemoglobinaemia, haemoglobinuria, haemosiderinuria). Splenic macrophage removal is extravascular.

Key point: Intravascular: free Hb, low haptoglobin, haemoglobinuria.

qs.q: Features of beta thalassemia include:
qs.a:
a. Microcytic anemia

b. Splenomegaly

c. Bone deformity

d. Gallbladder stones can develop with chronic hemolysis

e. Recurrent leg ulcers

f. All the above ✓

Answer: f

β-thalassaemia causes microcytic anaemia, splenomegaly, bone deformities (marrow expansion), pigment gallstones and leg ulcers — all the above.

Key point: β-thal: microcytosis, spleen, bones, stones, ulcers.

qs.q: Anemia is a reduction of total circulating red cell mass below the normal limits. The classical symptoms include palpitation, dizziness, angina, pallor of skin and nails, weakness, etc. Which of the following laboratory parameter is used to classify anemia into microcytic, normocytic, or macrocytic?
qs.a:
a. Mean Corpuscular Volume ✓

b. Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin

c. Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin Concentration

d. Red Cell Distribution Width

Answer: a

MCV classifies anaemia as microcytic (<80), normocytic or macrocytic (>100).

Key point: MCV classifies anaemia.

qs.q: Based on the size of the red blood cells, microcytic anemia is defined when the mean corpuscular volume (MCV) is:
qs.a:
a. Less than 80 fL/cell ✓

b. Less than 120 fL/cell

c. Less than 160 fL/cell

d. Less than 200 fL/cell

Answer: a

Microcytic anaemia means MCV below 80 fL.

Key point: Microcytic = MCV < 80 fL.

qs.q: Which of the following condition is not associated with microcytic anemia?
qs.a:
a. Iron Deficiency Anemia

b. Aplastic Anemia ✓

c. Sideroblastic Anemia

d. Thalassemia

Answer: b

Aplastic anaemia is normocytic (or mildly macrocytic) marrow failure, not microcytic.

Key point: Microcytic = TAILS: Thalassaemia, ACD, Iron, Lead, Sideroblastic.

qs.q: Identify the pathological condition associated with normocytic anemia:
qs.a:
a. Sickle Cell Anemia

b. G6PD deficiency

c. Aplastic Anemia

d. All of the above ✓

e. None of the above

Answer: d

Sickle cell, G6PD deficiency (haemolytic) and aplastic anaemia are all normocytic normochromic.

Key point: Haemolysis and marrow failure = normocytic.

qs.q: Identify the pathological condition associated with macrocytic anemia:
qs.a:
a. Sideroblastic anemia

b. Folic acid deficiency ✓

c. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia

d. Myelofibrosis

Answer: b

Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic (macrocytic) anaemia from defective DNA synthesis.

Key point: Macrocytic megaloblastic = B12 or folate.

qs.q: Identify the anemia caused by diminished erythropoiesis:
qs.a:
a. Megaloblastic anemia

b. Iron deficiency anemia

c. Aplastic Anemia

d. All of the above ✓

e. None of the above

Answer: d

Reduced production causes megaloblastic anaemia (impaired DNA synthesis), iron deficiency (no iron for haem) and aplastic anaemia (marrow failure) — all of the above.

Key point: Production failure: B12/folate, iron, aplastic.

qs.q: Identify the underlying cause of hemolytic anemia from the following choices:
qs.a:
a. Sickle-cell Disease

b. G6PD deficiency

c. Thalassemia

d. All of the above ✓

e. None of the above

Answer: d

Sickle cell disease, G6PD deficiency and thalassaemia all cause haemolytic anaemia (thalassaemia via haemolysis and ineffective erythropoiesis).

Key point: Haemoglobinopathies and enzymopathies are haemolytic.

qs.q: Which of the following iron testing panel represents the diagnosis of iron deficiency anemia?
qs.a:
a. Increased Iron, Increased TIBC, Decreased % Saturation & Decreased Serum Ferritin

b. Decreased Iron, Increased TIBC, Decreased % Saturation & Decreased Serum Ferritin ✓

c. Decreased Iron, Decreased TIBC, Decreased % Saturation & Increased Serum Ferritin

d. Decreased Iron, Normal TIBC, Normal % Saturation, Decreased Serum Ferritin

Answer: b

Iron deficiency: low serum iron, HIGH TIBC, low transferrin saturation and low ferritin.

Key point: IDA: iron ↓, TIBC ↑, sat ↓, ferritin ↓.

qs.q: Which of the following iron testing panel represents the diagnosis of anemia of chronic disease?
qs.a:
a. Increased Iron, Increased TIBC, Decreased % Saturation & Decreased Serum Ferritin

b. Decreased Iron, Increased TIBC, Decreased % Saturation & Decreased Serum Ferritin

c. Decreased Iron, Decreased TIBC, Decreased % Saturation & Increased Serum Ferritin ✓

d. Decreased Iron, Normal TIBC, Normal % Saturation, Decreased Serum Ferritin

Answer: c

Anaemia of chronic disease: low iron, LOW TIBC, low saturation, normal/raised ferritin.

Key point: ACD: iron ↓, TIBC ↓, ferritin ↑.

qs.q: Hereditary spherocytosis (HS) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by a defect involving ankyrin and spectrin in the erythrocyte membrane; this causes a decrease in the erythrocyte surface membrane. Which of the following statement is true regarding spherocytosis?
qs.a:
a. Decreased Osmotic Fragility

b. Mild Hemolytic Anemia ✓

c. Normal MCH

d. All of the above

e. None of the above

Answer: b

HS usually causes a mild haemolytic anaemia. Osmotic fragility is INCREASED and MCHC is raised, so the other statements are wrong.

Key point: HS: mild haemolysis, ↑ osmotic fragility, ↑ MCHC.

qs.q: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) is hemolytic anemia caused by an acquired somatic mutation of a gene (PIGA) that encodes an anchor for proteins (CD55 and CD59) in the cell membrane. Identify the correct statement regarding PNH:
qs.a:
a. Mutation of PIGA gene causes complement-mediated lysis of red blood cells

b. May causes pancytopenia and venous thrombosis

c. Increases the antibodies against Rh antigen on erythrocytes

d. All of the above ✓

Answer: d

PIGA mutation removes CD55/CD59, giving complement-mediated lysis, pancytopenia and venous thrombosis. PNH does not raise anti-Rh antibodies, so 'all of the above' is the keyed answer only as the file gives it.

Key point: PNH: complement lysis + cytopenias + thrombosis.

qs.q: Identify the underlying cause of hemolytic anemia from the following?
qs.a:
a. Pyruvate kinase deficiency

b. Hereditary elliptocytosis

c. Hereditary spherocytosis

d. All of the above ✓

e. None of the above

Answer: d

Pyruvate kinase deficiency (enzyme), hereditary elliptocytosis and spherocytosis (membrane) are all inherited haemolytic anaemias.

Key point: Inherited haemolysis: membrane + enzyme defects.

qs.q: Hereditary elliptocytosis is caused by:
qs.a:
a. Mutation of gene encoding pyruvate dehydrogenase

b. Mutation of gene encoding spectrin ✓

c. Mutation of gene encoding ankyrin

d. All of the above

e. None of the above

Answer: b

Hereditary elliptocytosis is mostly due to spectrin mutations (defective spectrin dimer association), sometimes protein 4.1.

Key point: Elliptocytosis ↔ spectrin.

qs.q: Polycythemia refers to increased red cell mass. Polycythemia can occur from which of the following conditions?
qs.a:
a. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

b. Cyanotic congenital heart disease

c. Renal cell carcinoma

d. All of the above ✓

e. None of the above

Answer: d

Secondary polycythaemia comes from hypoxia (COPD, cyanotic heart disease) or inappropriate EPO (renal cell carcinoma) — all of the above.

Key point: Secondary polycythaemia: hypoxia or EPO-secreting tumour.

qs.q: Aplastic anemia refers to a syndrome of chronic primary hematopoietic failure and attendant pancytopenia. Which of the following is not the acquired etiology of aplastic anemia?
qs.a:
a. Alkylating agents

b. Chloramphenicol

c. Fanconi syndrome ✓

d. Cytomegalovirus infection

Answer: c

Fanconi ANAEMIA is an inherited cause; 'Fanconi syndrome' is a proximal tubular disorder — either way it is not an acquired cause. Alkylating agents, chloramphenicol and viruses are acquired causes.

Key point: Acquired aplastic: drugs, chemicals, viruses, radiation.

qs.q: The most common cause of iron deficiency anemia in men is:
qs.a:
a. Chronic intravascular hemolysis

b. Vegetarian diet

c. Chronic occult bleeding ✓

d. Vitamin C deficiency

Answer: c

In men (and post-menopausal women) IDA is chronic occult GI bleeding until proven otherwise → endoscopy.

Key point: IDA in a man = look for GI blood loss.

qs.q: Aplastic anemia involves panhypoplasia of the marrow with anemia, leukopenia, and which of the following?
qs.a:
a. Anisocytosis

b. RBC fragmentation

c. Reticulocytosis

d. Thrombocytopenia ✓

Answer: d

Aplastic anaemia = pancytopenia: anaemia, leucopenia and thrombocytopenia, with low reticulocytes.

Key point: Aplastic: all three lines low.

qs.q: True aplastic anemia is most common in adolescents and young adults. Which of the following is the most likely etiology in about half of cases?
qs.a:
a. Chemical exposure

b. Drug hypersensitivity

c. Idiopathic ✓

d. Radiation therapy

Answer: c

About half or more of aplastic anaemia cases are idiopathic (immune-mediated T-cell attack on stem cells).

Key point: Commonest aplastic cause = idiopathic.

qs.q: Onset of aplastic anemia usually is insidious, often occurring over weeks or months. However, a life-threatening risk is associated with which of the following signs/symptoms?
qs.a:
a. Agranulocytosis ✓

b. Bleeding into conjunctivae

c. Ecchymoses

d. Splenomegaly

Answer: a

Severe neutropenia/agranulocytosis carries the greatest immediate risk — overwhelming infection. Splenomegaly is not a feature.

Key point: Aplastic anaemia: infection from neutropenia kills.

qs.q: The first stage of iron deficiency is marked by which of the following?
qs.a:
a. Progressive depletion of bone marrow iron stores ✓

b. Gradual decline in transferrin functioning

c. Slowing in iron elimination

d. Sharp decline in hematocrit levels

Answer: a

Iron deficiency develops in stages: first depletion of marrow/storage iron (low ferritin), then iron-deficient erythropoiesis, then anaemia.

Key point: Stage 1 IDA = stores depleted (ferritin ↓).

qs.q: The response to treatment of iron deficiency anemia is assessed by:
qs.a:
a. Serial serum iron measurements

b. Serial hemoglobin measurements ✓

c. Serial iron-binding capacity measurements

d. Serial serum ferritin measurements

Answer: b

Response to iron is monitored by a rising reticulocyte count (5–10 days) and haemoglobin (about 1 g/dL per week).

Key point: Monitor iron therapy with Hb (and reticulocytes).

qs.q: Which of the following symptoms suggests bleeding as a cause of acute anemia?
qs.a:
a. Melena ✓

b. Heart murmur

c. Jaundice

d. Chest pain

Answer: a

Melaena (black tarry stool) indicates upper GI bleeding as the cause of acute anaemia. Jaundice suggests haemolysis.

Key point: Melaena → GI bleeding.

qs.q: Which of the following symptoms suggest hemolysis?
qs.a:
a. Melena

b. Jaundice ✓

c. Hematemesis

d. Epistaxis

Answer: b

Haemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin, causing jaundice.

Key point: Anaemia + jaundice = haemolysis.

qs.q: In addition to blood loss and hemolysis, anemia can result from which of the following conditions?
qs.a:
a. Asthma

b. Deficient red blood cell production ✓

c. Low blood pressure

d. Congestive heart failure

Answer: b

Anaemia results from blood loss, haemolysis or deficient red cell production.

Key point: Anaemia = loss, destruction or underproduction.

qs.q: Which of the following signifies anemia?
qs.a:
a. A low white blood cell count

b. A low platelet count

c. A low hemoglobin level ✓

d. A low sodium level

Answer: c

Anaemia is defined by a low haemoglobin concentration (below ~13 g/dL in men, ~12 g/dL in women).

Key point: Anaemia = low Hb.

qs.q: Anemia arises due to deficiency of:
qs.a:
a. Iron

b. Vitamin B12

c. Folic acid

d. Any of the above ✓

Answer: d

Nutritional anaemia can result from iron, vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.

Key point: Nutritional anaemia: iron, B12, folate.

qs.q: Anemia due to deficiency of iron or vitamin B12 can be differentiated based on the examination of the blood cells.
qs.a:
a. True ✓

b. False

Answer: a

True: iron deficiency gives small pale cells (microcytic hypochromic, pencil cells); B12 deficiency gives macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils.

Key point: Blood film separates IDA from B12 deficiency.

qs.q: A person can develop iron-deficiency anemia despite eating food that contains adequate iron.
qs.a:
a. True ✓

b. False

Answer: a

True: iron deficiency can occur despite an adequate diet through blood loss, malabsorption (coeliac, gastrectomy) or increased needs (pregnancy).

Key point: Good diet doesn't exclude IDA.

qs.q: Which vitamin enhances iron absorption?
qs.a:
a. Vitamin A

b. Vitamin B

c. Vitamin C ✓

d. Vitamin D

Answer: c

Vitamin C enhances non-haem iron absorption by keeping iron in the ferrous form.

Key point: Vitamin C ↑ iron absorption.

qs.q: Aplastic anemia is a condition where:
qs.a:
a. The bone marrow does not produce enough blood cells ✓

b. Red blood cells are destroyed very fast in the circulation

c. There is deficiency of iron

d. There is deficiency of vitamin B12

Answer: a

Aplastic anaemia: the bone marrow fails to produce enough blood cells (all lines).

Key point: Aplastic = marrow failure.

qs.q: Anemia is a common condition. What happens when a person has anemia?
qs.a:
a. The body produces too much iron

b. The blood does not have enough red blood cells ✓

c. The blood becomes thick

d. Too many white blood cells are produced

Answer: b

In anaemia the blood has too few red cells/too little haemoglobin to carry adequate oxygen.

Key point: Anaemia = too few RBCs/Hb.

qs.q: What is the most common cause of anemia?
qs.a:
a. Too little sleep

b. Too much sugar

c. Too little iron in the blood ✓

d. Exposure to X-ray radiation

Answer: c

Iron deficiency is the most common cause of anaemia.

Key point: #1 cause = iron deficiency.

qs.q: Which of these groups is the most likely to have anemia?
qs.a:
a. Men

b. Women ✓

c. Teenagers

d. Older adults

Answer: b

Women (menstruation, pregnancy) are most likely to have anaemia.

Key point: Women at highest risk.

qs.q: How does anemia affect the body?
qs.a:
a. The blood doesn't deliver enough oxygen to the body ✓

b. Blood becomes thin

c. Tissues retain fluids

d. None of the above

Answer: a

Anaemia reduces oxygen delivery to tissues, causing fatigue, breathlessness and palpitations.

Key point: Anaemia → poor O2 delivery.

qs.q: A lack of which of these will result in abnormally large red blood cells and a condition called megaloblastic anemia?
qs.a:
a. Oxygen

b. Vitamin C

c. Vitamin B-12 and folic acid ✓

d. Carbon dioxide

Answer: c

Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency cause megaloblastic anaemia with large red cells.

Key point: B12/folate → megaloblastic.

qs.q: Which of these are signs of anemia?
qs.a:
a. Pale gums ✓

b. Dark circles under the eyes

c. Bleeding

d. Numbness in hands and feet

Answer: a

Pallor of mucous membranes (gums, conjunctivae) is a sign of anaemia.

Key point: Anaemia sign: pale mucosa.

qs.q: How does iron-deficiency anemia affect children and teens?
qs.a:
a. More fatigue

b. Increased irritability

c. Aggravates hyperactivity

d. A and B ✓

Answer: d

Iron deficiency in children and teens causes fatigue and irritability (and poor concentration/school performance).

Key point: Child IDA: fatigue + irritability.

qs.q: Iron-deficiency anemia can cause pica, a rare condition in which a person craves eating nonfood items. Which of these would he or she eat?
qs.a:
a. Ice

b. Soil

c. Clay

d. Any of the above ✓

Answer: d

Pica in iron deficiency includes craving ice (pagophagia), soil or clay (geophagia) — any of these.

Key point: Pica: ice, soil, clay.

qs.q: Anemia can contribute to which of these among older adults?
qs.a:
a. More falls ✓

b. High blood pressure

c. Diminished eyesight

d. Diabetes

Answer: a

In older adults anaemia contributes to weakness, dizziness and more falls.

Key point: Elderly anaemia → falls.

qs.q: A boy was playing, fell, and developed a hematoma. PT is normal, PTT is prolonged and factor VIII activity is normal. What is the diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Hemophilia A

b. Hemophilia B ✓

c. von Willebrand disease

d. Vitamin K deficiency

Answer: b

Haemarthrosis/haematoma after minor trauma in a boy with isolated prolonged PTT points to haemophilia; normal factor VIII activity means factor IX deficiency = haemophilia B.

Key point: Prolonged PTT + normal VIII in a boy = haemophilia B (IX).

qs.q: A boy underwent gingival manipulation and then developed bleeding; factor VIII is deficient. What is the diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Hemophilia A ✓

b. Hemophilia B

c. von Willebrand disease

d. Glanzmann thrombasthenia

Answer: a

Bleeding after gum manipulation in a boy with factor VIII deficiency = haemophilia A.

Key point: Low FVIII in a boy = haemophilia A.

qs.q: A case of recent antibiotic intake presenting with epistaxis and gingival bleeding, prolonged PT and mildly elevated PTT with a normal platelet count. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Vitamin K deficiency ✓

b. DIC

c. Liver failure

d. Thrombocytopenia

Answer: a

Broad-spectrum antibiotics kill gut flora that make vitamin K2, so factor VII falls first (prolonged PT) with a mild PTT rise and normal platelets = vitamin K deficiency.

Key point: Antibiotics + prolonged PT, normal platelets = vitamin K deficiency.

qs.q: A female with menorrhagia and bleeding; all labs are normal except low platelets. The diagnosis is:
qs.a:
a. ITP ✓

b. DIC

c. vWD

d. Hemophilia A

Answer: a

Mucosal bleeding with isolated thrombocytopenia and otherwise normal labs is immune thrombocytopenia (ITP).

Key point: Isolated low platelets + mucosal bleeding = ITP.

qs.q: A known liver patient presents with bleeding; his PT, PTT and bleeding time are prolonged. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Liver cirrhosis ✓

b. Hemophilia

c. vWD

d. Thrombocytopenia

Answer: a

Cirrhosis reduces synthesis of most clotting factors (PT and PTT prolonged) and causes thrombocytopenia from hypersplenism (bleeding time prolonged), so all three tests are abnormal.

Key point: Liver disease: PT + PTT + BT all prolonged.

qs.q: All of the following cause thrombosis followed by thrombocytopenia EXCEPT:
qs.a:
a. DIC

b. Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) ✓

c. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)

d. TTP

Answer: b

DIC, HIT and TTP consume platelets in widespread thromboses (thrombosis with thrombocytopenia). ITP destroys antibody-coated platelets without thrombosis — it causes bleeding.

Key point: Thrombosis + low platelets: DIC, HIT, TTP — not ITP.

qs.q: All of the following cause thrombocytopenia EXCEPT:
qs.a:
a. ITP

b. TTP

c. Henoch-Schönlein purpura ✓

d. DIC

Answer: c

Henoch-Schönlein purpura is a small-vessel IgA vasculitis with palpable purpura and NORMAL platelets.

Key point: HSP = purpura with normal platelets.

qs.q: A patient with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-weber-Rendu syndrome) presents with recurrent epistaxis and gastrointestinal bleeding. Which Of the following findings is NOT typically associated with this condition?
qs.a:
a. Recurrent epistaxis

b. Mucocutaneous telangiectasia

c. Iron-deficiency (microcytic) anemia

d. Macrocytosis ✓

Answer: d

HHT causes recurrent epistaxis, mucocutaneous telangiectasia and chronic blood loss → microcytic iron-deficiency anaemia; macrocytosis is not typical.

Key point: HHT → iron deficiency (microcytic).

qs.q: Which of the following is an inherited coagulation disorder?
qs.a:
a. Disseminated intravascular coagulation

b. Vitamin K deficiency

c. Hemophilia A ✓

d. Liver disease coagulopathy

Answer: c

Haemophilia A (X-linked factor VIII deficiency) is inherited; DIC, vitamin K deficiency and liver disease are acquired coagulopathies.

Key point: Inherited coagulopathy: haemophilia A/B, vWD.

qs.q: A 32-year-old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding, bruises and papular petechial rash on buttocks. Hb 12, platelets 18,000, WBC 5000, normal urine dipstick. The diagnosis is:
qs.a:
a. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

b. Hemolytic uremic syndrome

c. Henoch-Schönlein purpura

d. Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) ✓

Answer: d

Isolated severe thrombocytopenia with normal Hb, WBC and urine, and mucocutaneous bleeding in a well adult = ITP. TTP/HUS need haemolysis and organ involvement; HSP has a normal platelet count.

Key point: Isolated thrombocytopenia = ITP.

qs.q: A patient has joint and muscle bleeding, high PTT and normal factor VIII. The diagnosis is:
qs.a:
a. Hemophilia A

b. Hemophilia B ✓

c. von Willebrand disease

d. Factor VII deficiency

Answer: b (factor IX deficiency)

Joint/muscle bleeding with prolonged PTT and normal factor VIII = factor IX deficiency (haemophilia B).

Key point: Normal FVIII + ↑PTT + haemarthrosis = haemophilia B.

qs.q: An 18-year-old girl with menorrhagia didn't improve on tranexamic acid and oral contraceptive pills. Low hemoglobin, normal platelets count, normal WBCs, normal PT, prolonged APTT. Which of the following is most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. VWF disease ✓

b. Hemophilia A

c. DIC

d. Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura

Answer: a

Menorrhagia unresponsive to tranexamic acid/pill, normal platelets and PT, prolonged APTT in a teenage girl = von Willebrand disease.

Key point: Girl + menorrhagia + ↑APTT = vWD.

qs.q: What is the treatment strategy for von Willebrand disease?
qs.a:
a. Factor VIII replacement therapy

b. Platelet transfusion

c. Fibrinogen concentrate

d. Cryoprecipitate and desmopressin (DDAVP) ✓

Answer: d

vWD: mild bleeds → DDAVP (± tranexamic acid); serious bleeds → vWF-containing factor VIII concentrate or cryoprecipitate (rich in vWF).

Key point: vWD: DDAVP (mild) · cryo / vWF-rich concentrate (severe).

qs.q: A female patient presents with a family history of bleeding, bleeding in between cycles, and increased blood flow in menstruation:
qs.a:
a. Von Willebrand disease ✓

b. Hemophilia A

c. ITP

d. DIC

Answer: a

A woman with heavy, irregular bleeding and a family history of bleeding most likely has von Willebrand disease, the commonest inherited bleeding disorder (autosomal).

Key point: Female inherited bleeding → vWD.

qs.q: A patient with vWD is going for a dental procedure. What should be given for prophylaxis?
qs.a:
a. Cryo + DDAVP

b. Cryo + tranexamic acid

c. DDAVP + tranexamic acid ✓

d. Platelet transfusion

Answer: c

For a dental procedure in vWD: DDAVP raises vWF/FVIII and tranexamic acid protects the clot from the fibrinolysis-rich oral mucosa.

Key point: vWD dental: DDAVP + tranexamic acid.

qs.q: All of the following conditions can prolong bleeding time EXCEPT:
qs.a:
a. Thrombocytopenia

b. von Willebrand disease

c. Platelet function disorders

d. Hemophilia A ✓

Answer: d

Haemophilia A is a factor VIII deficiency: APTT prolonged, but platelets and bleeding time are normal.

Key point: Haemophilia = normal bleeding time.

qs.q: Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) mainly contains which of the following coagulation factors?
qs.a:
a. Factors II, VII, IX and X ✓

b. Factors I, V, VIII and XIII

c. Factors VIII, IX, XI and XII

d. Factors I, II, V and VIII

Answer: a

Prothrombin complex concentrate contains the vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX and X (4-factor PCC).

Key point: PCC = factors II, VII, IX, X.

qs.q: Which of the following coagulation factors is present in cryoprecipitate?
qs.a:
a. Factor IX

b. Fibrinogen ✓

c. Factor II

d. Factor X

Answer: b

Cryoprecipitate is rich in fibrinogen (its main use), plus factor VIII, vWF and factor XIII.

Key point: Cryo = fibrinogen + VIII + vWF + XIII.

qs.q: Which of the following is also present in cryoprecipitate?
qs.a:
a. Factor VIII ✓

b. Factor IX

c. Factor II

d. Factor VII

Answer: a

Besides fibrinogen, cryoprecipitate contains factor VIII (and vWF, factor XIII).

Key point: Cryo contains factor VIII.

qs.q: A patient taking warfarin presents with severe hemorrhage despite receiving vitamin K. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional treatment?
qs.a:
a. Prothrombin complex concentrate ✓

b. Platelet transfusion

c. Fresh frozen plasma only in all cases

d. Cryoprecipitate

Answer: a

Severe warfarin bleeding needs immediate factor replacement with prothrombin complex concentrate in addition to IV vitamin K (vitamin K takes hours to work).

Key point: Warfarin + severe bleed → PCC + IV vitamin K.

qs.q: Which of the following does NOT usually prolong activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)?
qs.a:
a. Unfractionated heparin

b. Warfarin ✓

c. Antiphospholipid syndrome

d. Factor VIII deficiency

Answer: b

Warfarin mainly prolongs the PT/INR (factor VII has the shortest half-life). Heparin, lupus anticoagulant (APS) and factor VIII deficiency prolong the aPTT.

Key point: Warfarin → PT; heparin → aPTT.

qs.q: Which of the following conditions is associated with increased bleeding time?
qs.a:
a. Hemophilia A

b. Von Willebrand disease ✓

c. Factor IX deficiency

d. Vitamin K deficiency

Answer: b

vWD gives an adhesion defect, so the bleeding time is prolonged (and APTT often prolonged from low factor VIII).

Key point: Prolonged BT + normal platelets → vWD or a platelet function defect.

qs.q: Which of the following coagulation parameters is typically prolonged in hemophilia A?
qs.a:
a. Bleeding time

b. Prothrombin time

c. Activated partial thromboplastin time ✓

d. Thrombin time only

Answer: c

Haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency, intrinsic pathway) prolongs the aPTT; PT and bleeding time are normal.

Key point: Haemophilia: ↑aPTT only.

qs.q: A patient presents with fever, hemorrhage, and renal manifestations. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP)

b. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) ✓

c. Iron deficiency anemia

d. Hemophilia A

Answer: b

Fever, haemorrhage (low platelets) and renal involvement point to TTP (pentad: fever, MAHA, thrombocytopenia, renal and neurological signs). ITP lacks fever and renal disease.

Key point: Fever + bleeding + renal = TTP.

qs.q: Cryoprecipitate mainly consists of:
qs.a:
a. Platelets

b. Factor IX

c. Factor V

d. Fibrinogen ✓

Answer: d

Cryoprecipitate is rich in fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF, factor XIII and fibronectin; fibrinogen is its main use.

Key point: Cryo = fibrinogen + VIII + vWF + XIII.

qs.q: A case of low platelets, schistocytes and creatinine 9, D-dimer normal, clotting normal. What is the cause?
qs.a:
a. Crescentic glomerulonephritis

b. Thrombotic microangiopathy ✓

c. DIC

d. Immune thrombocytopenic purpura

Answer: b

Thrombocytopenia + schistocytes + severe renal failure with NORMAL clotting and D-dimer = thrombotic microangiopathy (HUS/TTP). DIC would prolong PT/PTT and raise D-dimer.

Key point: MAHA + low PLT + normal clotting = TMA.

qs.q: A 45-year-old female taking OCPs presented with DVT and normal labs. What is the best next step?
qs.a:
a. Start anticoagulants for 3 months and thrombophilia screening after 3-6 months ✓

b. Start anti-platelet therapy only

c. Observe as it is provoked

d. Anticoagulants for life

Answer: a

DVT with a transient provoking factor (OCP) is treated with about 3 months of anticoagulation; thrombophilia screening, if done, is delayed until anticoagulation is completed or stopped, as acute clot and anticoagulants distort the results.

Key point: Provoked DVT: anticoagulate 3 months; thrombophilia screen later.

qs.q: Which of the following is true regarding TTP?
qs.a:
a. ADAMTS13 enzyme deficiency ✓

b. Thrombocytosis

c. A genetic disorder causing a deficiency of factor VIII

d. Caused by antibodies against platelet factor 4

Answer: a

TTP is due to deficiency (often autoantibody) of ADAMTS13, the vWF-cleaving protease. Platelets are low; anti-PF4 = HIT.

Key point: TTP = ADAMTS13 deficiency.

qs.q: A patient workup for unexplained hemolysis and pancytopenia reveals a deficiency of CD55 & CD59. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. PNH ✓

b. Antiphospholipid syndrome

c. Hereditary spherocytosis

d. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia

Answer: a

Haemolysis with pancytopenia and CD55/CD59 deficiency = paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria.

Key point: CD55/CD59 ↓ = PNH.

qs.q: A case presented with DVT after delivery, no history of gestational abnormalities or HTN; labs show low platelet count and prolonged PT & PTT. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. DIC ✓

b. ITP

c. TTP

d. PNH

Answer: a

Postpartum thrombosis with low platelets and prolonged PT and PTT = DIC (obstetric trigger, consumption of platelets and factors). ITP/TTP have normal clotting times.

Key point: Low PLT + long PT & PTT + thrombosis = DIC.

qs.q: A case about factor V Leiden is mentioned directly in the case with other labs. What is the diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Factor V Leiden mutation ✓

b. Protein C deficiency

c. Antithrombin III deficiency

d. Antiphospholipid syndrome

Answer: a

When factor V Leiden is reported in the case, the diagnosis is factor V Leiden thrombophilia — activated protein C resistance, the commonest inherited thrombophilia.

Key point: Factor V Leiden = APC resistance.

qs.q: A patient develops severe bleeding due to heparin therapy. Which of the following is the specific antidote?
qs.a:
a. Cryoprecipitate

b. Fresh frozen plasma (FFP)

c. Protamine sulfate ✓

d. Vitamin K

Answer: c

Protamine sulphate binds and neutralises heparin; it is the specific antidote.

Key point: Heparin → protamine.

qs.q: A patient develops thrombocytopenia after receiving heparin therapy. Despite the low platelet count, the patient develops a thrombotic event. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP)

b. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP)

c. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) ✓

d. Aplastic anemia

Answer: c

Falling platelets 5–10 days after heparin with new thrombosis = heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (antibodies to heparin–PF4 activate platelets). Stop heparin, use argatroban/fondaparinux.

Key point: Heparin + low PLT + thrombosis = HIT.

qs.q: All of the following cause thrombocytopenia EXCEPT:
qs.a:
a. ITP

b. TTP

c. Henoch-Schönlein purpura ✓

d. DIC

Answer: c

Henoch-Schönlein purpura is a small-vessel IgA vasculitis with palpable purpura and NORMAL platelets.

Key point: HSP = purpura with normal platelets.

qs.q: A patient passes bloody (dark) urine at night and in the early morning. The diagnosis is:
qs.a:
a. Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) ✓

b. Hereditary spherocytosis

c. G6PD deficiency

d. Cold agglutinin disease

Answer: a

Dark urine at night/early morning (haemoglobinuria) = paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria.

Key point: Night/morning dark urine = PNH.

qs.q: Hypercoagulability is most characteristic of which nephrotic disease?
qs.a:
a. Minimal change disease

b. IgA nephropathy

c. Membranous nephropathy ✓

d. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

Answer: c

Membranous nephropathy carries the highest risk of venous thrombosis, especially renal vein thrombosis.

Key point: Renal vein thrombosis = membranous.

qs.q: Which is correct regarding thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP)?
qs.a:
a. It is caused by factor VIII deficiency

b. It is caused by ADAMTS13 deficiency or inhibition ✓

c. It is caused by antibodies against platelet factor 4

d. It presents with normal platelet count

Answer: b

TTP is caused by ADAMTS13 deficiency or inhibition; platelets are low and factor VIII is normal.

Key point: TTP = ADAMTS13.

qs.q: Which antibodies are found in antiphospholipid syndrome (APS)?
qs.a:
a. Anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm

b. Anti-Scl-70 and anti-centromere

c. Anticardiolipin, anti-β2 glycoprotein I and lupus anticoagulant ✓

d. Anti-Jo-1 and anti-Mi-2

Answer: c

APS is defined by anticardiolipin, anti-β2 glycoprotein I and lupus anticoagulant antibodies.

Key point: APS antibodies: aCL, anti-β2GPI, LA.

qs.q: A 16-year-old female presents with complaints of generalized fatigue and exertional dyspnea for the past four weeks. For the past two weeks, she has also started to pass dark-colored urine, especially at night and in the morning on waking up. Laboratory investigations were carried out which show hemoglobin 7.1 g/dL, white blood cells 2200 per cubic millimeter, and platelets 80,000 per cubic millimeter. What is the most likely complication of this condition that can lead to death?
qs.a:
a. Liver cell failure

b. Thrombosis ✓

c. Respiratory failure

d. Acute kidney injury

Answer: b

Dark morning urine, haemolysis and pancytopenia in a young woman = PNH. Thrombosis (especially hepatic/abdominal veins) is the main cause of death.

Key point: PNH: haemolysis + pancytopenia + thrombosis (leading cause of death).

qs.q: Heparin toxicity therapy:
qs.a:
a. Protamine sulphate ✓

b. Vitamin K

c. PCC

d. Fresh frozen plasma

Answer: a

Heparin overdose/bleeding is reversed with protamine sulphate. Vitamin K and PCC reverse warfarin.

Key point: Heparin toxicity → protamine.

qs.q: All of the following cause paradoxical thrombocytopenia (thrombosis then thrombocytopenia) except:
qs.a:
a. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

b. Disseminated intravascular coagulopathy

c. Immune thrombocytopenic purpura ✓

d. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia

Answer: c

TTP, DIC and HIT cause thrombosis with platelet consumption; ITP causes thrombocytopenia with bleeding, not thrombosis.

Key point: ITP = bleeding, not thrombosis.

qs.q: Heparin action:
qs.a:
a. Binding via a specific pentasaccharide to antithrombin which potentiates its natural anticoagulant activity. Increased cleavage of activated proteases, particularly factor Xa and thrombin (IIa), accounts for the anticoagulant effect ✓

b. Inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase

c. Inhibits platelet aggregation only

d. Increases synthesis of clotting factors

Answer: a

Heparin binds antithrombin via a specific pentasaccharide, greatly accelerating inactivation of thrombin (IIa) and factor Xa. Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase.

Key point: Heparin = antithrombin activator.

qs.q: Which of these doesn't need further investigation for thrombosis?
qs.a:
a. DVT in 70 years old + hip replacement (already has a risk of DVT) ✓

b. A 25-year-old with unprovoked DVT

c. A 30-year-old with recurrent DVT

d. A 20-year-old with a strong family history of thrombosis

Answer: a

An elderly patient with DVT after hip replacement has an obvious provoking cause, so thrombophilia testing is not needed. Young, unprovoked, recurrent or familial thrombosis warrants investigation.

Key point: Provoked DVT in elderly → no thrombophilia screen.

qs.q: A patient presents to the emergency department with hematemesis. Laboratory investigations reveal an INR of 10. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
qs.a:
a. IV vitamin K only

b. Fresh frozen plasma (FFP)

c. IV vitamin K + 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) ✓

d. Stop warfarin and observe

Answer: c

Life-threatening bleeding (haematemesis) with INR 10: stop warfarin, give IV vitamin K plus 4-factor PCC for immediate reversal.

Key point: Major bleed on warfarin → IV vit K + PCC.

qs.q: A pregnant woman has been receiving heparin therapy for several days. What is the most appropriate anticoagulation management during pregnancy?
qs.a:
a. Continue heparin for 3 months ✓

b. Continue heparin for 6 months

c. Switch to warfarin for 3 months

d. Stop anticoagulation immediately

Answer: a

In pregnancy, LMW heparin is continued (warfarin is teratogenic); treatment typically continues through pregnancy and for at least ~6 weeks postpartum, minimum 3 months total — the keyed answer is continue heparin for 3 months.

Key point: Pregnancy VTE → heparin, never warfarin.

qs.q: Which of the following conditions is classically associated with paradoxical thrombosis despite thrombocytopenia?
qs.a:
a. ITP

b. DIC

c. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) ✓

d. TTP

Answer: c

HIT is the classic cause of paradoxical thrombosis despite thrombocytopenia (platelet activation by anti-PF4/heparin antibodies).

Key point: Paradoxical thrombosis = HIT.

qs.q: Which deficiency is associated with an increased risk of thrombosis?
qs.a:
a. Protein C deficiency

b. Protein S deficiency

c. Antithrombin deficiency

d. All of the above ✓

Answer: d

Deficiencies of the natural anticoagulants protein C, protein S and antithrombin all increase thrombosis risk.

Key point: Protein C/S and antithrombin deficiency → thrombophilia.

qs.q: What is the main treatment for deep vein thrombosis (DVT)?
qs.a:
a. Anticoagulants ✓

b. Antiplatelet drugs only

c. Iron supplementation

d. Corticosteroids

Answer: a

DVT is treated with anticoagulation (LMWH/DOAC, or heparin then warfarin) for at least 3 months. Antiplatelets alone are not adequate.

Key point: DVT → anticoagulate ≥3 months.

qs.q: A patient with PNH is at increased risk of which serious complication?
qs.a:
a. Thrombosis ✓

b. Hypercalcemia

c. Leukocytosis

d. Polycythemia

Answer: a

Thrombosis (hepatic, portal, cerebral veins) is the leading cause of death in PNH.

Key point: PNH → thrombosis.

qs.q: Which of the following is the mechanism of action of warfarin?
qs.a:
a. Activates antithrombin III

b. Inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase ✓

c. Directly inhibits thrombin

d. Directly inhibits factor Xa

Answer: b

Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1), preventing γ-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C, S.

Key point: Warfarin = VKOR inhibitor.

qs.q: What is the mechanism of action of heparin?
qs.a:
a. Inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase

b. Activates antithrombin III ✓

c. Inhibits platelet aggregation only

d. Increases synthesis of clotting factors

Answer: b

Heparin works by activating antithrombin III, which inactivates thrombin and factor Xa.

Key point: Heparin activates antithrombin.

qs.q: Which patient with DVT does not usually require extensive investigation for an underlying thrombophilia?
qs.a:
a. A 25-year-old with unprovoked DVT

b. A 30-year-old with recurrent DVT

c. A 70-year-old who develops DVT after hip replacement ✓

d. A 20-year-old with a strong family history of thrombosis

Answer: c

DVT after hip replacement in a 70-year-old is clearly provoked, so extensive thrombophilia testing is not needed.

Key point: Provoked DVT → no thrombophilia work-up.

qs.q: A male patient presents with bitemporal hemianopia and spade-like hands. Which of the following is the confirmatory diagnostic test?
qs.a:
a. Morning GH measurement

b. Oral glucose tolerance test with GH measurement ✓

c. Random IGF-1 level

d. MRI brain alone

Answer: b

Acromegaly (bitemporal hemianopia from a macroadenoma + spade-like hands) is confirmed by failure of GH to suppress (< 1 µg/L) after a 75 g oral glucose load. Glucose normally suppresses GH; autonomous somatotroph adenomas do not suppress.

Key point: Acromegaly: screen with IGF-1 → confirm with OGTT (GH fails to suppress) → then MRI.

qs.q: A female patient presents with greasy sweating, a large face and hands, and has developed amenorrhea. What is the most likely finding in her serum?
qs.a:
a. High levels of IGF-I ✓

b. High levels of ACTH

c. Low levels of growth hormone

d. Low levels of IGF-I

Answer: a

Greasy sweating, coarse enlarged face and hands = acromegaly. GH acts mainly through hepatic IGF-1, which is persistently high and is the best serum marker. Amenorrhea comes from co-secreted prolactin or stalk/gonadotroph compression.

Key point: Acromegaly = high IGF-1 (the stable marker of GH excess).

qs.q: GH deficiency causes:
qs.a:
a. Increased LDL levels ✓

b. Increased lean body mass

c. Increased bone density

d. Increased muscle mass

Answer: a

GH is lipolytic and lowers LDL; in GH deficiency, LDL and total cholesterol rise, central fat increases and cardiovascular risk goes up.

Key point: Adult GH deficiency → ↑LDL, ↑fat, ↓lean mass, ↓bone density, ↓well-being.

qs.q: A patient presents with postpartum hemorrhage, failure of lactation, fatigue, and amenorrhea. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Sheehan's syndrome ✓

b. Lymphocytic hypophysitis

c. Addison's disease

d. Premature ovarian failure

Answer: a

Massive postpartum hemorrhage → ischemic necrosis of the enlarged pregnancy pituitary (Sheehan). First sign is failure of lactation (↓prolactin), then amenorrhea (↓gonadotrophins) and fatigue (↓ACTH/TSH).

Key point: PPH + no lactation + amenorrhea = Sheehan syndrome.

qs.q: An emergency case presents with a macroadenoma, increased intracranial tension, bitemporal hemianopia, hypotension, and lethargy. What is the most appropriate next step?
qs.a:
a. Pulse steroid with hydrocortisone ✓

b. Transsphenoidal hypophysectomy

c. Immediate radiotherapy

d. Dopamine agonist therapy

Answer: a

Sudden headache/visual loss with a macroadenoma plus hypotension and lethargy = pituitary apoplexy with acute ACTH deficiency. Life-saving first step is IV hydrocortisone (stress-dose steroid) before anything else.

Key point: Pituitary apoplexy: give IV hydrocortisone FIRST, then think surgery.

qs.q: A patient presents with increased growth of skeletal and soft tissue, hypertension, arthritis, menstrual disturbances, and diabetes mellitus. Upon administration of oral glucose, which of the following levels would increase?
qs.a:
a. GH

b. IGF

c. GH and IGF ✓

d. ADH

e. None of the above

Answer: c

In acromegaly both GH and IGF-1 stay elevated; GH is NOT suppressed by oral glucose (it may even rise paradoxically), and IGF-1 remains high. The question's key reads 'GH and IGF'.

Key point: Acromegaly on OGTT: GH stays high (non-suppressible) and IGF-1 high.

qs.q: Which test is used to diagnose growth hormone deficiency?
qs.a:
a. Serum IGF-1 alone

b. Oral glucose tolerance test

c. Insulin tolerance test ✓

d. Water deprivation test

Answer: c

The insulin tolerance test (insulin-induced hypoglycaemia, glucose < 2.2 mmol/L) is the gold-standard stimulation test for GH (and ACTH) reserve; failure of GH to rise confirms deficiency.

Key point: GH excess → suppression test (OGTT); GH deficiency → stimulation test (ITT).

qs.q: What is associated with growth hormone deficiency?
qs.a:
a. Hyperlipidemia ✓

b. Hypolipidemia

c. Increase in lean body mass

d. Increase in bone density

Answer: a

GH deficiency causes an adverse lipid profile: ↑ total and LDL cholesterol (hyperlipidemia).

Key point: GH deficiency = hyperlipidemia + ↓lean mass + ↓bone density.

qs.q: Which is the most common type of pituitary adenoma?
qs.a:
a. Thyrotropinoma

b. Gonadotropinoma

c. Prolactinoma ✓

d. Corticotropinoma

Answer: c

Prolactinomas are the most common functioning pituitary adenomas (about 40–50%).

Key point: Most common pituitary adenoma = prolactinoma.

qs.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with secondary amenorrhea for 3 years and galactorrhea. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Craniopharyngioma

b. Prolactinoma ✓

c. Gonadotropinoma

d. Meningioma

Answer: b

Amenorrhea + galactorrhea in a young woman = hyperprolactinemia; the commonest pathological cause is a prolactinoma (prolactin inhibits GnRH pulsatility → hypogonadism).

Key point: Amenorrhea + galactorrhea → think prolactinoma.

qs.q: Which of the following decreases prolactin secretion?
qs.a:
a. Estrogen

b. Exercise

c. Dopamine ✓

d. Sleep

Answer: c

Dopamine from the hypothalamus is the main tonic INHIBITOR of prolactin release (via D2 receptors) — the basis of dopamine agonist therapy.

Key point: Dopamine is the brake on prolactin.

qs.q: All of the following increase prolactin levels EXCEPT:
qs.a:
a. Chest wall trauma

b. Hyperthyroidism ✓

c. Pregnancy

d. Renal failure

Answer: b

HYPOthyroidism (↑TRH) raises prolactin; hyperthyroidism does not.

Key point: Hypothyroidism (not hyperthyroidism) causes hyperprolactinemia.

qs.q: A woman presents with amenorrhea and galactorrhea. Her prolactin level is markedly elevated, but pituitary CT shows no visible lesion. What is the most appropriate treatment?
qs.a:
a. Trans-sphenoidal surgery

b. Radiotherapy

c. Cabergoline ✓

d. Reassurance without further assessment

Answer: c

Markedly raised prolactin with no visible lesion (idiopathic or microadenoma below CT resolution) is treated medically with a dopamine agonist; cabergoline is first-line (better tolerated, more effective).

Key point: Hyperprolactinemia → cabergoline first.

qs.q: What is the first-line medical treatment for a prolactinoma smaller than 10 mm?
qs.a:
a. Trans-sphenoidal surgery

b. Radiotherapy

c. Dopamine agonists (cabergoline or bromocriptine) ✓

d. Corticosteroids

Answer: c

Dopamine agonists (cabergoline > bromocriptine) normalise prolactin and shrink most micro- and macroprolactinomas — first-line therapy.

Key point: Prolactinoma = medical first (dopamine agonist), not surgery.

qs.q: Which of the following is correct about Sheehan syndrome?
qs.a:
a. Postpartum necrosis of the pituitary gland ✓

b. Postpartum necrosis of the thyroid gland

c. Autoimmune destruction of the adrenal gland

d. Pituitary hyperplasia during pregnancy

Answer: a

Sheehan = postpartum ischemic necrosis of the pituitary after severe PPH (the hyperplastic pregnancy pituitary is very blood-flow dependent).

Key point: Sheehan = pituitary infarction after PPH.

qs.q: All of the following may cause short stature EXCEPT:
qs.a:
a. Growth hormone deficiency

b. Hypothyroidism

c. Chronic systemic disease

d. Growth hormone hypersecretion ✓

Answer: d

GH hypersecretion before epiphyseal fusion causes GIGANTISM (tall stature), not short stature.

Key point: GH excess in children = gigantism (tall), not short.

qs.q: A patient presents with acromegalic features, including enlarged hands, prognathism, and increased ring size. Which substance is mainly responsible for these changes?
qs.a:
a. ACTH

b. IGF-1 ✓

c. Prolactin

d. TSH

Answer: b

GH exerts its growth effects through IGF-1 (somatomedin C) made in the liver — the mediator of acral and soft-tissue enlargement.

Key point: IGF-1 is the effector of acromegalic changes.

qs.q: A 33-year-old man presents with headaches, tiredness, reduced libido, enlarged hands, and a prominent lower jaw. Which is the most useful INITIAL laboratory investigation?
qs.a:
a. GH levels during oral glucose tolerance test

b. IGF-1 level ✓

c. MRI of the pituitary fossa

d. Random GH level

Answer: b

Serum IGF-1 is the best INITIAL test for suspected acromegaly — stable through the day and reflects integrated GH secretion.

Key point: First test in acromegaly = IGF-1.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT associated with acromegaly?
qs.a:
a. Mental retardation ✓

b. Hyperhidrosis

c. Organomegaly

d. Impaired glucose tolerance

Answer: a

Acromegaly does not cause mental retardation; intellect is preserved.

Key point: Acromegaly: sweating, organomegaly, IGT — but NOT mental retardation.

qs.q: A 25-year-old man presents with hypotension, malaise, and hyponatremia. CT reveals a 12-mm pituitary mass. Testosterone is low. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Prolactinoma

b. Non-functioning pituitary adenoma ✓

c. Acromegaly

d. Cushing disease

Answer: b

A 12 mm (macro) adenoma with hypopituitarism (low testosterone, hypotension and hyponatremia from ACTH deficiency) and no hormone excess syndrome = non-functioning adenoma compressing normal pituitary.

Key point: Macroadenoma + hypopituitarism, no excess = non-functioning adenoma.

qs.q: A 28-year-old woman has lost weight from 59 to 50 kg and presents with fatigue, amenorrhea for one year, and pallor. Which additional investigation is most important to establish the cause?
qs.a:
a. Complete blood count

b. Pituitary hormone profile

c. Thyroid function tests

d. All of the above ✓

Answer: d

Weight loss, amenorrhea, fatigue and pallor have a wide differential (anaemia, thyroid disease, pituitary failure, anorexia), so CBC, pituitary profile AND thyroid tests are all needed.

Key point: Weight loss + amenorrhea → full work-up (CBC, TFT, pituitary hormones).

qs.q: Which is the most commonly secreted pituitary hormone in terms of the most common functional pituitary adenoma?
qs.a:
a. TSH

b. GH

c. Prolactin ✓

d. ACTH

Answer: c

Prolactinoma is the commonest functioning pituitary adenoma, so prolactin is the most commonly secreted hormone.

Key point: Commonest functional pituitary adenoma = prolactinoma.

qs.q: What is the normal prolactin level?
qs.a:
a. 1–3 ng/mL

b. 5–15 ng/mL ✓

c. 20–30 ng/mL

d. 40–50 ng/mL

Answer: b

Normal serum prolactin is roughly 5–15 ng/mL (upper limit about 20–25 in women).

Key point: Normal prolactin ≈ 5–15 ng/mL.

qs.q: What is the normal GH level?
qs.a:
a. Less than 5 ✓

b. 10–15

c. 20–25

d. More than 30

Answer: a

Basal GH is usually low (< 5 ng/mL) between pulses.

Key point: Normal basal GH < 5 ng/mL.

qs.q: What is the effect of growth hormone on lipid metabolism?
qs.a:
a. Lipogenesis

b. Lipolysis ✓

c. Decreased fatty acid breakdown

d. No effect

Answer: b

GH is lipolytic: it mobilises free fatty acids from adipose tissue (part of its anti-insulin, fuel-sparing action).

Key point: GH = lipolysis + anti-insulin.

qs.q: Growth hormone has which effect on sodium?
qs.a:
a. Increases sodium loss

b. Has an aldosterone-like effect causing sodium retention ✓

c. Decreases sodium absorption

d. Causes severe hyponatremia directly

Answer: b

GH causes renal sodium and water retention (aldosterone-like effect) — contributing to soft-tissue swelling and hypertension in acromegaly.

Key point: GH retains sodium (→ HTN, soft-tissue swelling).

qs.q: Kallmann syndrome is classically associated with:
qs.a:
a. Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism and anosmia

b. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and anosmia ✓

c. Hyperprolactinemia and galactorrhea

d. Acromegaly and deafness

Answer: b

Kallmann syndrome = failure of GnRH neuron migration → hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (low LH/FSH) + anosmia (olfactory bulb hypoplasia).

Key point: Kallmann = low LH/FSH + anosmia.

qs.q: Which of the following may be associated with Kallmann syndrome?
qs.a:
a. Anosmia and deafness ✓

b. Exophthalmos

c. Pretibial myxedema

d. Hyperpigmentation

Answer: a

Besides anosmia, Kallmann syndrome may include sensorineural deafness, cleft palate, renal agenesis and colour blindness.

Key point: Kallmann extras: deafness, cleft lip/palate, renal agenesis.

qs.q: Which of the following is a typical presentation of Sheehan syndrome?
qs.a:
a. Lactation failure and amenorrhea after postpartum hemorrhage ✓

b. Galactorrhea and hypermenorrhea

c. Exophthalmos and weight loss

d. Polyuria and polydipsia

Answer: a

Lactation failure and amenorrhea after postpartum hemorrhage is the classic presentation.

Key point: Sheehan: no milk + no periods after PPH.

qs.q: What is the most common pathological cause of hyperprolactinemia?
qs.a:
a. Prolactinoma ✓

b. Acromegaly

c. Cushing syndrome

d. Diabetes insipidus

Answer: a

After physiological and drug causes, prolactinoma is the most common pathological cause of hyperprolactinemia.

Key point: Pathological hyperprolactinemia → prolactinoma first.

qs.q: Which of the following can cause hyperprolactinemia?
qs.a:
a. Methyldopa

b. Antipsychotic drugs

c. Metoclopramide

d. All of the above ✓

Answer: d

All are dopamine antagonists or depleters: methyldopa (↓dopamine synthesis), antipsychotics and metoclopramide (D2 blockers) → hyperprolactinemia.

Key point: Anything that blocks dopamine raises prolactin.

qs.q: Which of the following is a physiological cause of increased prolactin?
qs.a:
a. Sleep

b. Coitus

c. Stress

d. All of the above ✓

Answer: d

Sleep, coitus, stress, exercise, pregnancy and breastfeeding all physiologically raise prolactin.

Key point: Physiological ↑PRL: sleep, stress, coitus, exercise, pregnancy, suckling.

qs.q: Disconnection hyperprolactinemia is caused by:
qs.a:
a. Increased dopamine secretion

b. Decreased dopamine delivery due to pressure on the pituitary stalk ✓

c. Increased thyroid hormone secretion

d. Increased aldosterone secretion

Answer: b

A non-prolactin mass compressing the stalk blocks dopamine delivery from the hypothalamus → mild hyperprolactinemia (usually < 2000 mU/L).

Key point: Stalk compression → ↓dopamine → mild ↑prolactin (stalk effect).

qs.q: Which drugs are used in the treatment of hyperprolactinemia?
qs.a:
a. Cabergoline and bromocriptine ✓

b. Metyrapone and ketoconazole

c. Fludrocortisone and hydrocortisone

d. Carbimazole and PTU

Answer: a

Dopamine agonists cabergoline and bromocriptine are the drugs for hyperprolactinemia.

Key point: Hyperprolactinemia drugs = cabergoline, bromocriptine.

qs.q: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of acromegaly?
qs.a:
a. Greasy sweating ✓

b. Decreased skin thickness

c. Small hands and feet

d. Micrognathia

Answer: a

Greasy, sweaty skin (sebaceous and sweat gland hypertrophy) is characteristic of acromegaly.

Key point: Acromegaly skin: thick, greasy, sweaty.

qs.q: Prognathism means:
qs.a:
a. Small lower jaw

b. Prominent protrusion of the lower jaw ✓

c. Increased forehead hair

d. Decreased facial bone growth

Answer: b

Prognathism = protrusion of the lower jaw (mandibular overgrowth) with widened tooth spacing — typical of acromegaly.

Key point: Prognathism = big protruding lower jaw.

qs.q: Spade-like hands and feet are associated with:
qs.a:
a. Addison disease

b. Acromegaly ✓

c. Hypothyroidism

d. Diabetes insipidus

Answer: b

Broad spade-like hands and feet from soft tissue and bone overgrowth are classic acromegaly.

Key point: Spade hands = acromegaly.

qs.q: Mushroom-shaped enlargement of the phalanges is associated with:
qs.a:
a. Acromegaly ✓

b. Cushing syndrome

c. Addison disease

d. Sheehan syndrome

Answer: a

Tufting (mushroom-shaped enlargement) of the terminal phalanges on X-ray is a radiological sign of acromegaly.

Key point: Phalangeal tufting = acromegaly.

qs.q: Which of the following may be used in the medical treatment of acromegaly?
qs.a:
a. Octreotide

b. Pegvisomant (Somavert)

c. Dopamine agonists

d. All of the above ✓

Answer: d

Medical options for acromegaly: somatostatin analogues (octreotide, lanreotide), GH receptor antagonist (pegvisomant), and dopamine agonists (cabergoline, mild disease).

Key point: Acromegaly medical Rx: somatostatin analogue, pegvisomant, cabergoline (surgery first-line).

qs.q: Which of the following is a diagnostic approach for suspected acromegaly?
qs.a:
a. IGF-1 measurement followed by GH suppression testing with oral glucose ✓

b. Water deprivation test

c. ACTH stimulation test

d. Low-dose dexamethasone suppression test

Answer: a

Screen with IGF-1, then confirm with GH suppression on 75 g OGTT, then image with MRI.

Key point: Acromegaly pathway: IGF-1 → OGTT → MRI.

qs.q: A patient presents with increased hand size, headache, and hypertension. Which diagnosis is most likely?
qs.a:
a. Addison disease

b. Acromegaly ✓

c. Conn syndrome

d. Hypothyroidism

Answer: b

Increasing hand size with headache and hypertension = acromegaly.

Key point: Bigger hands/rings/shoes + headache = acromegaly.

qs.q: Which cancer is associated with acromegaly?
qs.a:
a. Hepatocellular carcinoma

b. Colorectal carcinoma ✓

c. Small cell lung cancer

d. Pancreatic carcinoma

Answer: b

Acromegaly carries an increased risk of colorectal carcinoma.

Key point: Acromegaly cancer = colorectal.

qs.q: A 28-year-old female machinist presents with significant weight loss (from 59 kg to 50 kg) and amenorrhea for the past year. She is otherwise healthy. Laboratory investigations reveal: Hemoglobin 9 g/dL, normal electrolytes, normal liver enzymes, and other routine investigations are unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Hypopituitarism

b. Anorexia nervosa ✓

c. Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)

d. Primary ovarian insufficiency

Answer: b

Healthy young woman with major weight loss and amenorrhea, mild anaemia and otherwise normal tests = anorexia nervosa (functional hypothalamic amenorrhea).

Key point: Young woman + weight loss + amenorrhea + normal labs = anorexia.

qs.q: A patient is diagnosed with a pituitary microprolactinoma (less than 10 mm). What is the first-line treatment?
qs.a:
a. Trans-sphenoidal surgery

b. Radiotherapy

c. Bromocriptine ✓

d. Observation in all cases

Answer: c

Microprolactinomas are treated first with dopamine agonists (cabergoline or bromocriptine), which shrink the tumour and lower prolactin. Surgery is for failure/intolerance.

Key point: Prolactinoma → dopamine agonist first.

qs.q: Which investigation is used to screen for acromegaly (growth hormone excess)?
qs.a:
a. Random serum GH

b. Serum IGF-1 ✓

c. Serum prolactin

d. Insulin tolerance test

Answer: b

Serum IGF-1 is the screening test for acromegaly.

Key point: Screen acromegaly with IGF-1.

qs.q: Bromocriptine is used in the treatment of which condition?
qs.a:
a. Acromegaly

b. Prolactinoma ✓

c. Pheochromocytoma

d. Diabetes insipidus

Answer: b

Bromocriptine (dopamine agonist) is used mainly for prolactinoma (also adjunct in acromegaly, Parkinson's, lactation suppression).

Key point: Bromocriptine = prolactinoma.

qs.q: MRI reveals a pituitary macroadenoma. The patient has diabetes mellitus, hypertension, galactorrhea, excessive sweating, and a high prolactin level. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Acromegaly ✓

b. Prolactinoma

c. Cushing disease

d. Non-functioning pituitary adenoma

Answer: a

Macroadenoma with DM, hypertension and excessive sweating = acromegaly; mild hyperprolactinaemia/galactorrhoea occurs from GH–prolactin co-secretion or stalk compression.

Key point: Sweating + DM + HTN + macroadenoma = acromegaly.

qs.q: Cases of acromegaly or excess growth hormone are best assessed by measuring:
qs.a:
a. ACTH

b. IGF-1 ✓

c. Prolactin

d. TSH

Answer: b

IGF-1 reflects 24-hour GH secretion and is the best screening/monitoring test for acromegaly (confirm with OGTT GH suppression).

Key point: Acromegaly → IGF-1.

qs.q: The syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) is characterized by all of the following EXCEPT:
qs.a:
a. Increased level of ADH

b. Hypo-osmolar urine ✓

c. Hyponatremia

d. Adequate hydration status (euvolemia)

Answer: b

In SIADH, ADH keeps urine inappropriately CONCENTRATED (> 100 mOsm/kg) despite low plasma osmolality — hypo-osmolar urine is NOT a feature.

Key point: SIADH = hyponatremia + concentrated urine + euvolemia.

qs.q: In a woman with polyuria of 6 L/day, which is the most important investigation to be done for diagnosis of the cause of polyuria (diabetes insipidus)?
qs.a:
a. Water deprivation test ✓

b. Urine osmolality

c. Plasma osmolality

d. Water loading test

Answer: a

Water deprivation test (followed by desmopressin) distinguishes primary polydipsia, cranial DI and nephrogenic DI.

Key point: Polyuria work-up = water deprivation test + desmopressin.

qs.q: What stimulates the hypothalamus to secrete arginine vasopressin (AVP)?
qs.a:
a. Hypokalemia

b. Hyperkalemia

c. Hypertonicity ✓

d. Hypotonicity

Answer: c

Osmoreceptors in the anterior hypothalamus sense a rise in plasma tonicity (as little as 1–2%) and trigger AVP release and thirst. Hypovolemia is the second, less sensitive stimulus.

Key point: AVP is released by hypertonicity (and hypovolemia).

qs.q: A patient presents with polyuria and polydipsia. A water deprivation test shows persistently high serum osmolality with inadequate urine concentration. After administration of desmopressin, urine osmolality increases by more than 50%. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a:
a. Central diabetes insipidus (DI) ✓

b. Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (DI)

c. SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone)

d. Primary polydipsia

Answer: a

During deprivation the urine fails to concentrate while plasma osmolality rises (true DI). A > 50% rise in urine osmolality after desmopressin shows the kidney responds — the defect is lack of ADH = central (cranial) DI.

Key point: Dilute urine + rises > 50% with desmopressin = central DI.

qs.q: A patient presents with polyuria and thirst. There appears to be no elevation of glucose, however, serum osmolality appears to be low. Upon performing the water deprivation test, osmolality is still low. Which of the following is true?
qs.a:
a. The problem is in the pituitary

b. The problem is in the kidneys

c. The patient has diabetes mellitus

d. The patient has high ADH in the serum

e. B and D ✓

Answer: e

The answer key is 'B and D': inability to concentrate urine despite water deprivation points to a renal (nephrogenic) problem, where ADH levels are HIGH because the kidney is resistant.

Key point: Nephrogenic DI = kidney resistance + HIGH ADH. (Note: low serum osmolality with polyuria in real practice suggests primary polydipsia.)

qs.q: A blood test is performed on a patient and it is discovered that the patient has very low levels of sodium. It is also known that the patient has just undergone an operation. In addition, he appears to have a small cell tumor of the lung. Which of the following conditions is most linked to the disease the patient has?
qs.a:
a. Diabetes mellitus

b. Cushing's syndrome

c. Hyperthyroidism

d. Diabetes insipidus ✓

e. None of the above

Answer: d

The file's key is 'Diabetes insipidus'. Be careful: post-operative state + small cell lung cancer + very LOW sodium is the classic picture of SIADH (ectopic/inappropriate ADH). DI produces HIGH sodium. The key likely treats this as a disorder of the ADH axis.

Key point: Small cell lung cancer + post-op + low Na⁺ = SIADH (the ADH-axis disorder). DI = high Na⁺.

qs.q: Which of the following has the greatest effect on plasma osmolality?
qs.a:
a. Progesterone

b. Cortisol

c. Vasopressin ✓

d. Aldosterone

e. Dehydroepiandrosterone

Answer: c

Vasopressin (ADH) controls free water reabsorption via aquaporin-2 in the collecting duct — the main hormonal regulator of plasma osmolality.

Key point: Osmolality = ADH; volume = aldosterone.

qs.q: In central diabetes insipidus, the water deprivation test shows:
qs.a:
a. Urine concentrates normally during water deprivation

b. Urine stays dilute during deprivation, then becomes concentrated (about 720 mOsm/kg) after vasopressin ✓

c. Urine stays dilute even after vasopressin is given

d. Serum osmolality falls below 275 mOsm/kg during deprivation

Answer: b

In cranial DI the urine stays dilute while plasma osmolality rises during deprivation; after desmopressin it concentrates (e.g. ~700 mOsm/kg) because the kidney is normal.

Key point: Central DI: dilute → concentrates after desmopressin.

qs.q: Which test is used to differentiate cranial (central) from nephrogenic diabetes insipidus?
qs.a:
a. Insulin tolerance test

b. Water deprivation test followed by desmopressin ✓

c. Short Synacthen test

d. 72-hour supervised fast

Answer: b
